Prerenal AKI

Pathophysiology

Too little blood reaches the glomeruli at too low a pressure, so GFR falls although the kidney itself is healthy; the tubules still work and hold on to Na+, water, and urea, so the urine is concentrated and low in Na+, and the injury reverses once perfusion returns.

  1. Perfusion fallsBaroreceptors raise sympathetic tone; the afferent arteriole releases renin; ADH rises
  2. Autoregulation holds GFRAngiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and prostaglandins dilate the afferent, until systolic pressure falls below about 80 mmHg
  3. GFR fallsFurther angiotensin II and sympathetic drive constrict the afferent arteriole too
  4. The tubules conserveNa+ and water are reabsorbed avidly, and urea follows passively in the proximal tubule, raising the UCR
  5. Prolonged hypoperfusionTubular cells are injured: prerenal AKI becomes ATN, which no longer responds to fluid

Note: Patients with CKD have weaker autoregulation, so a smaller fall in perfusion lowers their GFR.

Etiology

  • Too little blood volume
  • 1Fluid lossBleeding, burns, vomiting, diarrhea, high ostomy output, and overdiuresis
  • The heart and vessels
  • 2Low cardiac outputCardiogenic shock, massive PE, and acute coronary syndrome
  • 3VasodilationSeptic shock, anaphylaxis, and anesthesia
  • 4HF (cardiorenal syndrome)Low output and high venous pressure both lower renal perfusion; diuresis is used cautiously
  • 5Cirrhosis (hepatorenal syndrome)Splanchnic vasodilation underfills the arteries and the kidneys constrict their vessels intensely; triggered by bleeding, overdiuresis, large-volume paracentesis without albumin, infection, and NSAIDs (see Acute liver failure and cirrhosis)
  • The kidney's own vessels
  • 6Afferent constrictionNSAIDs remove the prostaglandins that dilate the afferent arteriole; iodinated contrast, amphotericin B, and CNIs constrict it
  • 7Efferent dilationACEi and ARBs remove the angiotensin II that holds glomerular pressure up
  • 8Renal artery stenosis and dissectionBilateral stenosis, or stenosis of a single working kidney, especially once ACEi or ARBs start; aortic dissection
  • 9Abdominal compartment syndromeIncreased intra-abdominal pressure compresses the renal veins and kidneys and lowers renal perfusion

Note: Prerenal AKI and ATN together cause about three quarters of hospital AKI; prerenal AKI alone about 21%.

Symptoms and complications

Features come from the cause, such as thirst, postural dizziness, and low output, or edema in HF and cirrhosis, and from the AKI itself, as on .

  • HypovolemiaThirst, dry mucosa, low skin turgor, tachycardia, and a postural fall in blood pressure
  • Low urine outputConcentrated urine in small volumes
  • Progression to ATNIf perfusion is not restored, tubular injury follows and recovery takes weeks

Diagnosis

The urine is bland and concentrated with little Na+, and creatinine returns toward baseline within 24–72 hours of restoring volume, the best test; the indices are compared with ATN and obstruction on .

ForObtain
Any prerenal causeUrinalysis (normal, or hyaline casts); urine Na+ below 20 mmol/L; FENa below 1%, or FEUrea below 35% with diuretics; urine osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg; UCR above 100
Fluid loss (1)History, orthostatic vital signs, and response to isotonic fluid
Heart (2, 4)ECG, troponin, BNP, and echocardiography
Sepsis (3)Cultures, lactate
Hepatorenal syndrome (5)Cirrhosis with ascites; no response to stopping diuretics and giving albumin; FENa low; bland urine
Drugs (6, 7)The drug list: NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, diuretics, CNIs, recent contrast
Renal artery stenosis (8)Creatinine rising after ACEi or ARBs; renal artery imaging
Abdominal compartment syndrome (9)Bladder pressure to measure intra-abdominal pressure

Treatment

Restore perfusion and remove what is lowering it: isotonic fluid when volume is low, treating shock or HF, and stopping NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, and diuretics, with the general care of AKI on .

CauseTreatment
Fluid loss (1)Isotonic saline or 4% albumin, both similar in outcome (the SAFE study); then maintenance fluid, watching for overload
Low output and shock (2, 3)Treat the cause; vasopressors and inotropes to restore pressure
HF (4)Cautious diuresis, which can improve renal venous congestion
Hepatorenal syndrome (5)Stop diuretics and nephrotoxins; albumin; vasoconstrictors such as terlipressin; transplant referral
Drugs (6, 7)Stop NSAIDs; hold ACEi and ARBs until volume and creatinine recover
Renal artery stenosis (8)Stop ACEi and ARBs; revascularization in selected patients
Abdominal compartment syndrome (9)Lower intra-abdominal pressure, by surgical decompression when severe

Note: Low-dose dopamine does not protect the kidney and may worsen function.

Review article

Prerenal AKI: a healthy kidney without enough perfusion

Prerenal AKI follows reduced perfusion of otherwise healthy kidneys, from fluid loss, low cardiac output, vasodilation, low effective volume in HF and cirrhosis, or drugs and lesions that act on the renal vessels. Autoregulation holds GFR until perfusion falls further, and the intact tubules conserve Na+, water, and urea, producing bland, concentrated, Na+-poor urine. Restoring perfusion reverses it, but prolonged hypoperfusion causes ATN. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider its relationships to ATN, hypovolemia, and cirrhosis.

Key points

  • Autoregulation, through efferent constriction by angiotensin II and afferent dilation by prostaglandins, holds GFR until systolic pressure falls below about 80 mmHg.
  • Causes are fluid loss; low cardiac output and vasodilation; HF and cirrhosis (cardiorenal and hepatorenal syndromes); NSAIDs, contrast, and CNIs (afferent constriction); ACEi and ARBs (efferent dilation); renal artery stenosis; and abdominal compartment syndrome.
  • The urine is bland, with urine Na+ below 20 mmol/L, FENa below 1% (FEUrea below 35% with diuretics), osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg, and a UCR above 100.
  • Creatinine returning toward baseline within 24–72 hours of restoring volume is the best confirmation.
  • Treatment restores perfusion and stops NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, and diuretics; low-dose dopamine does not help.

Pathophysiology

When perfusion falls, baroreceptors raise sympathetic tone and the afferent arteriole releases renin, and ADH rises. Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole and prostaglandins dilate the afferent, holding GFR until systolic pressure falls below about 80 mmHg; further angiotensin II and sympathetic drive then constrict the afferent arteriole too and GFR falls. The tubules still work, reabsorbing Na+ and water avidly, with urea following passively in the proximal tubule, so the UCR rises. Patients with CKD autoregulate less well, and prolonged hypoperfusion injures the tubules, turning prerenal AKI into ATN.

Etiology

Fluid loss from bleeding, burns, vomiting, diarrhea, high ostomy output, or overdiuresis lowers volume; cardiogenic shock, massive PE, and acute coronary syndrome lower output; and septic shock, anaphylaxis, and anesthesia dilate vessels. In HF, low output and high venous pressure lower renal perfusion (cardiorenal syndrome), and in cirrhosis, splanchnic vasodilation underfills the arteries and the kidneys constrict their vessels (hepatorenal syndrome), often triggered by bleeding, overdiuresis, paracentesis without albumin, infection, or NSAIDs. NSAIDs remove afferent prostaglandins and contrast, amphotericin B, and CNIs constrict the afferent arteriole, whereas ACEi and ARBs remove efferent angiotensin II; bilateral renal artery stenosis, or stenosis of a single working kidney, aortic dissection, and abdominal compartment syndrome also lower renal perfusion. Prerenal AKI causes about 21% of hospital AKI.

Presentation and diagnosis

Features come from the cause and from the AKI itself, as in the review of : thirst, dry mucosa, tachycardia, and a postural fall in pressure in hypovolemia, and edema in HF and cirrhosis, with small volumes of concentrated urine. The urinalysis is normal or shows hyaline casts, urine Na+ is below 20 mmol/L, FENa below 1%, or FEUrea below 35% in patients taking diuretics, urine osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg, and the UCR above 100; creatinine returning toward baseline within 24–72 hours of restoring volume is the best test, except in hepatorenal and cardiorenal syndromes. Cause-specific tests include orthostatic vital signs, cardiac tests, cultures and lactate, the drug list, renal artery imaging, and bladder pressure.

Management

Isotonic saline or 4% albumin, similar in outcome, restores volume, followed by maintenance fluid with care to avoid overload; shock and low output are treated by their cause with vasopressors and inotropes, and HF with cautious diuresis. Hepatorenal syndrome is treated by stopping diuretics and nephrotoxins and giving albumin and vasoconstrictors such as terlipressin, with transplant referral. NSAIDs are stopped and ACEi and ARBs held until recovery, renal artery stenosis may need revascularization, and abdominal compartment syndrome needs decompression when severe. Low-dose dopamine does not protect the kidney.

Relationships to other conditions

. Prolonged prerenal AKI becomes ATN; in prerenal AKI the tubules conserve Na+ and concentrate urine, whereas in ATN they cannot, and fluid no longer helps.

. True volume loss is the most common prerenal cause and is treated with isotonic fluid, whereas the low effective volume of HF and cirrhosis is not corrected by giving fluid.

Intrarenal AKI

Pathophysiology

The injury lies in the kidney itself, in its vessels, glomeruli, tubules, or interstitium, so the tubules cannot conserve Na+ or concentrate urine, and restoring perfusion does not reverse it; injured tubules release vasoconstrictors that lower GFR further.

  • 1Small vesselsEndothelial injury and clots in thrombotic microangiopathy; cholesterol emboli; malignant hypertension
  • 2GlomerulusImmune injury and inflammation lower filtration and let blood and protein through
  • 3TubulesIschemia or toxins kill tubular cells, effacing the brush border; casts, crystals, pigments, or light chains block the lumen
  • 4InterstitiumAn immune reaction, usually to a drug, infiltrates the interstitium with white cells

Note: ATN causes about 45% of hospital AKI, glomerulonephritis and vasculitis about 4%, AIN about 2%, and atheroemboli about 1%.

Etiology

CompartmentCausesDetails
Tubules (3): ATNIschemia from hypovolemic, cardiogenic, or septic shock; aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, and vancomycin; iodinated contrast; myoglobin and hemoglobin; crystals (urate in TLS, acyclovir, indinavir, and ethylene glycol) and light chains in myeloma, which block the lumen
Interstitium (4): AINDiuretics, NSAIDs, penicillins and cephalosporins, PPIs, rifampin, sulfonamides, and allopurinol; infection; SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, and IgG4-related disease
Glomeruli (2)Nephrotic: MCD, FSGS, MN, DKD, and amyloid; nephritic: anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, Alport syndrome, IgA nephropathy, PSGN, MPGN, and lupus nephritis
Vessels (1)Thrombotic microangiopathy (HUS, TTP), atheroemboli after vascular procedures, and malignant hypertension

Two common tubular injuries

  • Contrast-associated AKIIodinated contrast constricts renal vessels and is toxic to tubular cells; risk is highest in CKD, DM, HF, volume depletion, and with large contrast volumes; hydration beforehand lowers it
  • RhabdomyolysisMyoglobin from damaged muscle blocks and injures the tubules; CK is above 5 times the upper limit, and the urine dipstick is positive for blood with few red cells

Symptoms and complications

AKI itself is often silent, as on , so the clues come from the compartment.

CompartmentClues
Tubules (ATN)A clear insult: hypotension, sepsis, contrast, nephrotoxins, crush injury; creatinine rising steadily
Interstitium (AIN)A new drug 1–2 weeks before; fever, rash, and eosinophilia in only about 10%; polyuria from a concentrating defect
GlomeruliHematuria, protein, edema, and hypertension; systemic signs such as a butterfly rash, purpura, or hemoptysis
VesselsLivedo reticularis and digital ischemia after a vascular procedure (atheroemboli); anemia and low platelets (TMA)

Diagnosis

The urine is the key: unlike prerenal AKI, it shows FENa above 2% and osmolality below 450 mOsm/kg in ATN, and the sediment points to the compartment; biopsy is reserved for unexplained or rapidly progressive AKI, as on .

CompartmentUrine sedimentOther tests
Tubules (ATN)Muddy brown granular casts and renal tubular epithelial cells; may be normal earlyCK and urine myoglobin; urate and phosphate; SPEP and UPEP, and serum free light chains in older patients
Interstitium (AIN)White cell casts; sterile pyuria, its most specific sign; eosinophiluria, which is unreliableEosinophilia; biopsy if no improvement 3–7 days after stopping the drug
GlomeruliRed cell casts and dysmorphic red cells; proteinComplement, ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, and biopsy
VesselsOften bland; eosinophiluria in atheroemboliBlood film for schistocytes, platelets, LDH (TMA); low complement in atheroemboli

Treatment

Treat the compartment's cause and support the kidney while it recovers, which in ATN takes weeks to months; the general care of AKI, including dialysis, is on .

CauseTreatment
ATNRemove the insult; avoid further nephrotoxins; support until recovery, with dialysis if needed
RhabdomyolysisLarge volumes of IV fluid started early, aiming for urine output of 200–300 mL/h
TLSPrevention: IV fluid from 48 hours before chemotherapy, with allopurinol or rasburicase
Contrast-associated AKIPrevention: hydration, the lowest contrast dose, and avoiding repeat exposure
AINStop the drug; corticosteroids if no improvement within 3–7 days
Glomerulonephritis and vasculitisImmunosuppression (see the glomerular disease pages)
Thrombotic microangiopathyPlasma exchange or complement blockade, by type

Review article

Intrarenal AKI: injury to the vessels, glomeruli, tubules, or interstitium

Intrarenal AKI arises from injury within the kidney: to the small vessels, the glomeruli, the tubules, or the interstitium. ATN, from ischemia or toxins, is the most common cause of hospital AKI, and acute interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis, and thrombotic microangiopathy are the others. The injured tubules cannot conserve Na+ or concentrate urine, so FENa and urine osmolality separate it from prerenal AKI, and the urine sediment points to the compartment. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes by compartment, clues, diagnosis, and treatment.

Key points

  • Intrarenal AKI injures the vessels, glomeruli, tubules, or interstitium; ATN causes about 45% of hospital AKI.
  • ATN follows shock, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, vancomycin, contrast, myoglobin, or hemoglobin; crystals and light chains obstruct the tubules.
  • AIN follows diuretics, NSAIDs, penicillins and cephalosporins, PPIs, rifampin, sulfonamides, allopurinol, infection, or autoimmune disease.
  • Muddy brown casts suggest ATN, white cell casts and sterile pyuria AIN, and red cell casts glomerulonephritis.
  • FENa above 2% and osmolality below 450 mOsm/kg separate ATN from prerenal AKI; biopsy is reserved for unexplained or rapidly progressive AKI.

Pathophysiology and etiology

Injury within the kidney prevents the tubules from conserving Na+ or concentrating urine, and injured tubules release vasoconstrictors, so restoring perfusion does not reverse it. In the tubules, ischemia or toxins kill cells and efface the brush border, as in ATN from hypovolemic, cardiogenic, or septic shock, aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, vancomycin, contrast, rhabdomyolysis, and hemolysis, and crystals (urate, acyclovir, indinavir, and ethylene glycol) and light chains obstruct the lumen. In the interstitium, AIN follows diuretics, NSAIDs, penicillins and cephalosporins, PPIs, rifampin, sulfonamides, allopurinol, infection, SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, or IgG4-related disease. Glomerular causes are nephrotic (MCD, FSGS, MN, DKD, and amyloid) or nephritic (anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, Alport syndrome, IgA nephropathy, PSGN, MPGN, and lupus nephritis), and vascular causes thrombotic microangiopathy, atheroemboli, and malignant hypertension. Contrast-associated AKI is most likely in CKD, DM, HF, and volume depletion, and rhabdomyolysis gives a very high CK and a dipstick positive for blood with few red cells. ATN causes about 45% of hospital AKI, glomerulonephritis and vasculitis about 4%, AIN about 2%, and atheroemboli about 1%.

Clues and diagnosis

ATN follows a clear insult with a steadily rising creatinine; AIN follows a new drug by 1–2 weeks, sometimes with fever, rash, and eosinophilia (in about 10%) and polyuria; glomerular disease brings hematuria, protein, edema, hypertension, and systemic signs; and vascular disease brings livedo and digital ischemia after a procedure, or anemia and low platelets. FENa above 2% and urine osmolality below 450 mOsm/kg separate ATN from prerenal AKI, as in the review of . The sediment shows muddy brown casts and tubular cells in ATN, though it may be normal early; white cell casts, sterile pyuria, and unreliable eosinophiluria in AIN; and red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells in glomerulonephritis. CK, urate, SPEP, UPEP, and serum free light chains, serology, complement, a blood film, and biopsy complete the workup.

Management

The cause is treated and the kidney supported while it recovers, which in ATN takes weeks to months: the insult is removed and further nephrotoxins avoided, rhabdomyolysis is treated with large volumes of IV fluid aiming for urine output of 200–300 mL/h, TLS is prevented with fluid and allopurinol or rasburicase, and contrast-associated AKI is prevented by hydration and the lowest dose. AIN is treated by stopping the drug and with corticosteroids if it does not improve within 3–7 days, glomerulonephritis and vasculitis with immunosuppression, and thrombotic microangiopathy with plasma exchange or complement blockade, as described in , , and .

Acute Tubular Necrosis

Pathophysiology

Ischemia or a toxin kills tubular epithelial cells, which slough into the lumen and lower GFR by blocking the tubule, leaking filtrate back, and triggering afferent constriction; the surviving tubule can no longer conserve Na+ or concentrate urine.

  1. InjuryIschemia, a toxin, or both
  2. Cells die and sloughThe brush border is lost and cells detach from the basement membrane
  3. Casts formDead cells and debris bind uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) into muddy brown granular casts
  4. GFR fallsObstruction, backleak, and vasoconstriction (A–D, below)
  5. Tubular failureNa+ is lost and urine is not concentrated: urine Na+ above 40 mmol/L, FENa above 2%
  6. RepairSurviving cells divide and reline the tubule over weeks

How GFR falls

  • ATubular obstructionCasts raise the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, which opposes filtration
  • BBackleakFiltrate leaks across the bare basement membrane into the interstitium and back into the blood
  • CTubuloglomerular feedbackThe injured proximal tubule reabsorbs less Na+, so more reaches the macula densa, which constricts the afferent arteriole
  • DIntrarenal vasoconstrictionInjured endothelium makes more endothelin and less NO

Ischemic and nephrotoxic injury

FeatureIschemicNephrotoxic
Segments hitStraight proximal tubule and medullary thick ascending limb, in the outer medullaProximal convoluted tubule
Why thereHigh O2 demand from active transport, with little O2 supply in the medullaIt concentrates and takes up filtered toxins
PatternPatchy; the basement membrane can breakDiffuse; the basement membrane stays intact

Note: Ischemic ATN is prerenal AKI that has lasted too long, so the same causes lead to both, and fluid helps only before the tubules die.

Etiology

  • Ischemic: any prerenal cause that is severe or prolonged, including major surgery
  • 1Hypovolemic shockBleeding, burns, and vomiting or diarrhea
  • 2Cardiogenic shockLow cardiac output from myocardial infarction or HF
  • 3Septic shockVasodilation lowers perfusion, and cytokines and endotoxin injure tubules directly, so sepsis is often mixed
  • Nephrotoxic: direct injury to tubular cells
  • 4DrugsAminoglycosides, taken up by the proximal tubule; cisplatin; amphotericin B; vancomycin, more often with piperacillin-tazobactam
  • 5Iodinated contrastConstricts renal vessels and is toxic to tubular cells; risk is highest in CKD, DM, HF, and volume depletion
  • 6PigmentsMyoglobin from rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis: heme constricts vessels by binding NO, injures cells, and forms casts
  • Nephrotoxic: blocking the lumen
  • 7CrystalsUric acid in TLS; drugs such as acyclovir and indinavir; calcium oxalate in ethylene glycol poisoning
  • 8Light chainsMultiple myeloma: free light chains bind uromodulin into casts in the distal tubule (cast nephropathy) and injure the proximal tubule

Rhabdomyolysis (6)

  • CausesCrush injury and long immobilization, strenuous exercise, seizures, heat, electrical injury, and drugs such as statins
  • MuscleInjured cells take in Na+ and Ca2+, swell, and break down, releasing K+, phosphate, urate, CK, and myoglobin
  • KidneyRenal vasoconstriction (heme binds NO); direct heme toxicity to tubular cells; tubular obstruction by myoglobin casts, which form more readily in acidic urine
  • FeaturesMuscle pain, weakness, and dark tea-colored urine, all three in under half of patients
  • ComplicationsHyperkalemia and arrhythmias, low Ca2+ early and high Ca2+ in recovery, compartment syndrome, and DIC

Tumor lysis syndrome (7)

  • CausesChemotherapy for fast-growing cancers, especially high-grade lymphomas such as Burkitt lymphoma and acute leukemias with a high WBC count; usually within 72 hours
  • ReleaseDying cells release K+, phosphate, and nucleic acids, which are broken down to uric acid
  • KidneyUric acid crystallizes in the tubules and blocks them; calcium phosphate deposits; urate also binds NO and constricts vessels
  • FeaturesHigh urate, K+, phosphate, and LDH, with low Ca2+ (it binds phosphate): cramps, tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias

Symptoms and complications

ATN follows a clear insult, and its features are those of AKI, as on , lasting longer than in prerenal AKI because the tubules must regrow.

  • OliguriaCommon in ischemic ATN; nephrotoxic ATN, especially from aminoglycosides (4), is often non-oliguric
  • Azotemia to uremiaUrea and creatinine increase, creatinine by about 26.5–44 µmol/L a day; azotemia is the laboratory finding, and uremia follows when symptoms appear (nausea, confusion, pericarditis, and bleeding)
  • HypervolemiaFluid given into a kidney that cannot excrete it: edema and pulmonary edema
  • An AGMA, because the kidney cannot excrete acid or make new HCO3−
  • Less K+ is secreted, acidosis moves K+ out of cells, and rhabdomyolysis (6) and TLS (7) release more
  • Polyuric recoveryFiltration returns before the tubules can concentrate urine, so Na+, K+, Mg2+, and water are lost: watch for hypovolemia and hypokalemia

Note: Recovery is often incomplete: over half of patients with biopsy-proven ATN do not regain a GFR above 60 mL/min/1.73 m², and repeated injury leads to CKD.

Diagnosis

The urine shows the tubules have failed, unlike in prerenal AKI, and the cause is found from the history and a few targeted tests; the indices are compared on .

  • +Any ATNMuddy brown granular casts and tubular epithelial cells; urine Na+ above 40 mmol/L; FENa above 2% (FEUrea above 50% with diuretics); urine osmolality below 450 mOsm/kg; UCR not increased; no response to fluid; biopsy only if another cause is suspected
  • 1–3IschemicA period of shock or major surgery; lactate; cultures in sepsis
  • 4DrugsThe drug list and its timing; aminoglycoside and vancomycin trough levels; low K+ and Mg2+ with aminoglycosides, cisplatin, and amphotericin B
  • 5Iodinated contrastCreatinine rising within 48–72 hours of contrast, peaking at 2–5 days, and back to baseline by about 2 weeks; FENa can be low
  • 6PigmentsCK above 5 times the upper limit, with AKI likely above 5000 U/L; dipstick positive for blood with few red cells; red-brown casts; hemolysis: high LDH, low haptoglobin, and free hemoglobin; FENa can be low
  • 7CrystalsTLS: high urate, K+, phosphate, and LDH, and low Ca2+; ethylene glycol: an AGMA, a high osmolal gap early, and calcium oxalate crystals; the drug history for acyclovir and indinavir
  • 8Light chainsSPEP, UPEP, and serum free light chains; the dipstick misses light chains, so urine protein is higher than the dipstick suggests; hypercalcemia and anemia

Treatment

There is no treatment that repairs the tubules, so care removes the insult, prevents further injury, and supports the patient while the tubules regrow, with the shared care and dialysis on .

  • +Any ATNStop nephrotoxins and adjust drug doses for GFR; keep the patient euvolemic; treat hyperkalemia and acidosis; dialysis by the AEIOU indications
  • 1–3IschemicRestore perfusion with IV fluid and vasopressors; treat sepsis with ABX and source control; hold ACEi and ARBs
  • 4DrugsStop or replace the drug; dose aminoglycosides once daily with trough levels; use liposomal amphotericin B; replace K+ and Mg2+
  • 5Iodinated contrastPrevention: isotonic IV fluid before and after, the lowest dose, and no repeat exposure or NSAIDs
  • 6PigmentsLarge volumes of IV fluid started early, before a trapped limb is freed, aiming for urine output of 200–300 mL/h; treat hyperkalemia; fasciotomy for compartment syndrome
  • 7CrystalsTLS: IV fluid from 48 hours before chemotherapy, with allopurinol to stop new urate or rasburicase to break down existing urate; ethylene glycol: fomepizole and dialysis; acyclovir: hydration and dosing for GFR
  • 8Light chainsChemotherapy to lower light chain production; IV fluid; avoid NSAIDs and contrast

Note: Loop diuretics treat overload and may increase urine output, but turning oliguric into non-oliguric ATN does not improve recovery, the need for dialysis, or survival, and low-dose dopamine does not help.

Related: Tubular Transport Glomerular Filtration

Review article

Acute tubular necrosis: ischemic and toxic death of the tubular epithelium

Acute tubular necrosis is the most common cause of AKI in hospital. Ischemia from shock, or toxins such as aminoglycosides, contrast, heme pigments, crystals, and light chains, kill tubular epithelial cells, which slough into casts that block the tubule, while filtrate leaks back and tubuloglomerular feedback and endothelial injury constrict the afferent arteriole. The tubules lose their ability to conserve Na+ and concentrate urine, giving muddy brown casts, a FENa above 2%, and no response to fluid. Treatment is supportive, with prevention for the toxic causes, while the tubules regrow over weeks. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider its relationships to prerenal AKI, AIN, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis.

Key points

  • GFR falls through tubular obstruction by casts, which raises the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, backleak of filtrate, tubuloglomerular feedback, and intrarenal vasoconstriction.
  • Ischemic ATN injures the straight proximal tubule and medullary thick ascending limb in patches; nephrotoxic ATN injures the proximal convoluted tubule diffusely, sparing the basement membrane.
  • Causes are hypovolemic, cardiogenic, and septic shock; aminoglycosides, cisplatin, amphotericin B, vancomycin, and contrast; myoglobin and hemoglobin; crystals; and myeloma light chains.
  • Muddy brown casts, urine Na+ above 40 mmol/L, FENa above 2%, and osmolality below 450 mOsm/kg distinguish it from prerenal AKI, though contrast and pigment ATN can have a low FENa.
  • Care is supportive; rhabdomyolysis needs early large-volume IV fluid, TLS needs fluid with allopurinol or rasburicase, and diuretics and dopamine do not speed recovery.

Pathophysiology

Ischemia or a toxin kills tubular epithelial cells, which lose their brush border, detach from the basement membrane, and slough into the lumen, where they bind uromodulin (Tamm-Horsfall protein) into muddy brown granular casts. GFR falls by four routes: casts obstruct the tubule and raise the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, which opposes filtration; filtrate leaks back across the bare basement membrane into the interstitium; the injured proximal tubule reabsorbs less Na+, so more reaches the macula densa, which constricts the afferent arteriole by tubuloglomerular feedback; and injured endothelium makes more endothelin and less NO. The surviving tubule cannot conserve Na+ or concentrate urine, so urine Na+ exceeds 40 mmol/L and FENa 2%. Ischemic injury falls on the straight proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb of the outer medulla, where active transport demands much O2 and supply is poor, and is patchy, sometimes breaking the basement membrane; nephrotoxic injury falls on the proximal convoluted tubule, which concentrates and takes up filtered toxins, and is diffuse, leaving the basement membrane intact. Surviving cells divide and reline the tubule over weeks. Ischemic ATN is prerenal AKI that has lasted too long, so fluid helps only before the tubules die.

Etiology and mechanisms

Ischemic ATN follows any severe or prolonged prerenal cause, including major surgery: hypovolemic shock from bleeding, burns, vomiting, or diarrhea; cardiogenic shock from myocardial infarction or HF; and septic shock, in which vasodilation lowers perfusion and cytokines and endotoxin injure the tubules directly, so sepsis is often mixed. Nephrotoxic drugs include aminoglycosides, which the proximal tubule takes up, cisplatin, amphotericin B, and vancomycin, more often combined with piperacillin-tazobactam. Iodinated contrast constricts renal vessels and is toxic to tubular cells, especially in CKD, DM, HF, and volume depletion. Myoglobin from rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobin from intravascular hemolysis constrict vessels as heme binds NO, injure tubular cells, and form casts. Crystals block the lumen: uric acid in TLS, drugs such as acyclovir and indinavir, and calcium oxalate in ethylene glycol poisoning; in multiple myeloma, free light chains bind uromodulin into distal casts (cast nephropathy) and injure the proximal tubule.

Rhabdomyolysis follows crush injury and long immobilization, strenuous exercise, seizures, heat, electrical injury, and drugs such as statins. Injured muscle takes in Na+ and Ca2+, swells, and breaks down, releasing K+, phosphate, urate, CK, and myoglobin; the kidney is injured by vasoconstriction, direct heme toxicity, and myoglobin casts, which form more readily in acidic urine. Muscle pain, weakness, and tea-colored urine occur together in under half of patients, and hyperkalemia with arrhythmias, low Ca2+ early and high Ca2+ in recovery, compartment syndrome, and DIC complicate it. TLS follows chemotherapy for fast-growing cancers, especially high-grade lymphomas such as Burkitt lymphoma and acute leukemias with a high WBC count, usually within 72 hours; dying cells release K+, phosphate, and nucleic acids broken down to uric acid, which crystallizes in the tubules, while calcium phosphate deposits and urate constricts vessels. It gives high urate, K+, phosphate, and LDH with low Ca2+, causing cramps, tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias.

Clinical presentation and complications

ATN follows a clear insult and causes the features of AKI, lasting longer than in prerenal AKI because the tubules must regrow. Oliguria is common in ischemic ATN, whereas nephrotoxic ATN, especially from aminoglycosides, is often non-oliguric. Urea and creatinine increase, creatinine by about 26.5–44 µmol/L a day, and this azotemia becomes uremia when nausea, confusion, pericarditis, or bleeding appear. Fluid given into a kidney that cannot excrete it causes edema and pulmonary edema; an AGMA develops because the kidney cannot excrete acid or make new HCO3−; and hyperkalemia follows reduced K+ secretion, the shift of K+ out of cells in acidosis, and the release of K+ in rhabdomyolysis and TLS. In the polyuric recovery phase, filtration returns before the tubules concentrate urine, so Na+, K+, Mg2+, and water are lost, risking hypovolemia and hypokalemia. Recovery is often incomplete: over half of patients with biopsy-proven ATN do not regain a GFR above 60 mL/min/1.73 m², and repeated injury leads to CKD.

Diagnosis

The urine shows muddy brown granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, urine Na+ above 40 mmol/L, FENa above 2%, or FEUrea above 50% in patients taking diuretics, and osmolality below 450 mOsm/kg; the UCR is not increased, there is no response to fluid, and biopsy is reserved for suspicion of another cause. Ischemic ATN follows a period of shock or major surgery, with lactate and cultures guiding care. Drug-induced ATN is traced through the drug list and its timing, with aminoglycoside and vancomycin trough levels, and aminoglycosides, cisplatin, and amphotericin B also lower K+ and Mg2+. After contrast, creatinine rises within 48–72 hours, peaks at 2–5 days, and returns to baseline by about 2 weeks. Rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed by a CK above 5 times the upper limit, with AKI likely above 5000 U/L, and a dipstick positive for blood with few red cells; hemolysis gives a high LDH, low haptoglobin, and free hemoglobin; and contrast and pigment ATN can have a low FENa. TLS gives high urate, K+, phosphate, and LDH with low Ca2+, and ethylene glycol gives an AGMA, an early high osmolal gap, and calcium oxalate crystals. Myeloma is sought with SPEP, UPEP, and serum free light chains; the dipstick misses light chains, so urine protein exceeds what it suggests, and hypercalcemia and anemia support the diagnosis.

Management

No treatment repairs the tubules, so nephrotoxins are stopped, drug doses adjusted for GFR, euvolemia maintained, hyperkalemia and acidosis treated, and dialysis started by the AEIOU indications. Ischemic ATN needs perfusion restored with IV fluid and vasopressors, sepsis treated with ABX and source control, and ACEi and ARBs held. Nephrotoxic drugs are stopped or replaced, aminoglycosides dosed once daily with trough levels, liposomal amphotericin B preferred, and K+ and Mg2+ replaced. Contrast-associated AKI is prevented with isotonic IV fluid before and after, the lowest dose, and no repeat exposure or NSAIDs. Rhabdomyolysis needs large volumes of IV fluid started early, before a trapped limb is freed, aiming for urine output of 200–300 mL/h, with treatment of hyperkalemia and fasciotomy for compartment syndrome. TLS is prevented with IV fluid from 48 hours before chemotherapy and allopurinol, which stops new urate, or rasburicase, which breaks down existing urate; ethylene glycol is treated with fomepizole and dialysis, and acyclovir crystals with hydration and dosing for GFR. Cast nephropathy needs chemotherapy to lower light chain production, IV fluid, and avoidance of NSAIDs and contrast. Loop diuretics treat overload and may increase urine output, but turning oliguric into non-oliguric ATN does not improve recovery, the need for dialysis, or survival, and low-dose dopamine does not help.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both follow low perfusion, and prolonged prerenal AKI becomes ischemic ATN. In prerenal AKI the tubules conserve Na+ and concentrate urine, giving a FENa below 1%, a high UCR, bland urine, and a response to fluid; in ATN they cannot, giving a FENa above 2%, muddy brown casts, and no response.

. Both injure the tubules and follow drugs. ATN follows ischemia or a direct toxin and shows muddy brown casts, whereas AIN is an immune reaction, often days to weeks after a new drug, with white cell casts, sterile pyuria, and sometimes fever, rash, and eosinophilia; vancomycin can cause either.

and . Both follow the loss of tubular function and are most severe when rhabdomyolysis or TLS release K+ and acid from cells.

Acute Interstitial Nephritis

Pathophysiology

A drug or infection triggers a T cell–mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction in the interstitium; the inflammation and edema compress the tubules, which raises the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure and lowers GFR.

  1. Hapten formsA drug is taken up by tubular cells and binds a protein, which the immune system sees as new
  2. T cells activateDendritic cells present it in a lymph node; Th2 cells release IL-4 and IL-5
  3. Eosinophils are recruitedIL-5 increases eosinophils, which infiltrate the interstitium with T cells
  4. Interstitial edemaInflammation swells the interstitium and invades the tubule wall (tubulitis)
  5. GFR fallsCompressed tubules raise the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, and angiotensin II from the inflamed kidney constricts its vessels
  6. Tubular dysfunctionPolyuria from a concentrating defect; glucosuria and low phosphate, urate, and HCO3− from proximal injury

The interstitium in AIN

  • AHaptenThe drug binds a protein in tubular cells or their basement membrane
  • BAntigen presentationDendritic cells near the basement membrane carry it to a lymph node
  • CT cell activationActivated T cells return; Th2 cells release IL-4 and IL-5
  • DInfiltrateEosinophils and T cells fill the interstitium and invade the tubules
  • ETubular compressionEdema squeezes the tubules, so the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure increases and GFR falls

Note: If exposure continues, inflammation gives way to fibrosis and tubular atrophy, which corticosteroids cannot reverse.

Etiology

  • Drugs: the 5 Ps and others, causing most AIN
  • 1Diuretics (Pee)Loop diuretics and thiazides, which are sulfonamides
  • 2NSAIDs (Pain-free)The most common cause, in about 44%; older, long-term users; months after starting, with few allergic signs and sometimes nephrotic-range protein from minimal change disease
  • 3Penicillins and cephalosporinsThe most likely to cause fever, rash, and eosinophilia; more likely after a previous reaction
  • 4PPIsSecond most common in some series; milder AKI but less complete recovery, because exposure is often long
  • 5Rifampin (rifamPin)Antibodies against rifampin; more likely with intermittent dosing
  • 6SulfonamidesTMP-SMX and other sulfonamide antibiotics
  • 7AllopurinolOften with rash and systemic hypersensitivity
  • 8Other drugsICIs, 5-ASA, ciprofloxacin, and phenytoin
  • Infection
  • 9InfectionStreptococci, leptospirosis, CMV, EBV, and HIV; bacteria such as E. coli when there is obstruction or reflux
  • Autoimmune disease
  • 10Autoimmune diseaseSLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, and TINU

Symptoms and complications

AIN usually appears 1–2 weeks after a new drug, within days after a previous exposure, and months after starting NSAIDs (2) or PPIs (4); most patients have nonspecific symptoms and a rising creatinine.

  • Classic triadFever, rash, and eosinophilia or eosinophiluria in only about 10%; most likely with β-lactams (3), rare with NSAIDs (2)
  • Usual presentationFatigue, malaise, nausea, and arthralgia, with AKI found on bloods
  • RashMaculopapular, and highly suggestive when present
  • Urine outputUsually non-oliguric; polyuria from a concentrating defect
  • Tubular dysfunctionGlucosuria without diabetes, with low phosphate, urate, and HCO3−
  • HypertensionAngiotensin II from the inflamed kidney
  • ComplicationsAKI needing short-term dialysis; CKD from fibrosis; anemia

Note: 40–60% of patients do not regain their baseline function, more often after NSAIDs, PPIs, or AKI lasting over 3 weeks, so a drug history, including over-the-counter drugs, matters more than the triad.

Diagnosis

Suspect AIN when creatinine rises after a new drug, look for inflammation in the urine, and confirm with a biopsy when stopping the drug does not help; the shared AKI workup is on .

  • +Any AINSterile pyuria, WBC casts, microscopic hematuria, and protein usually under 1 g a day; eosinophilia and a high IgE; eosinophiluria is unreliable (sensitivity about 40%); ultrasound to exclude obstruction, which may show large, echogenic kidneys
  • +BiopsyThe only definitive test: T cells and eosinophils in an edematous interstitium, with tubulitis and spared glomeruli; fibrosis predicts a poor response to corticosteroids. Indicated if function does not improve 3–7 days after stopping the drug
  • 1–8DrugsA timeline of every new drug, including NSAIDs and PPIs bought over the counter; improvement after stopping the culprit
  • 2NSAIDsNephrotic-range protein (3 g a day or more) from minimal change disease, with few allergic signs
  • 9InfectionCultures and serology for the suspected organism; imaging for obstruction or reflux
  • 10Autoimmune diseaseANA and complement (SLE); anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies (Sjögren syndrome); serum ACE, Ca2+, and a chest x-ray (sarcoidosis); IgG4 levels; an eye examination for uveitis (TINU)

Treatment

Stopping the culprit drug is the most important treatment, with the shared care of AKI and dialysis if needed, as on .

  • +Any AINStop the drug; supportive care of the AKI; short-term dialysis if needed
  • +CorticosteroidsPrednisolone if function does not improve within 3–7 days of stopping the drug, ideally after a biopsy; starting early limits fibrosis
  • 1–8DrugsRecord the reaction as an allergy and avoid the drug; ICIs are often held and corticosteroids given, because there may be no other cancer treatment
  • 9InfectionTreat the infection and relieve obstruction
  • 10Autoimmune diseaseTreat the disease, with corticosteroids or other immunosuppression

Note: Recovery usually comes within 3 months, and corticosteroids help only while inflammation is active, not once fibrosis is established.

Review article

Acute interstitial nephritis: a delayed hypersensitivity reaction in the renal interstitium

Acute interstitial nephritis is an immune reaction in the renal interstitium, most often to a drug, and less often to infection or autoimmune disease. Drugs act as haptens that T cells recognize, and Th2 cytokines recruit eosinophils into an edematous interstitium that compresses the tubules and lowers GFR. The classic triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia is seen in only about a tenth of patients, so the diagnosis rests on a rising creatinine after a new drug, sterile pyuria and white cell casts, and, when needed, a biopsy. Stopping the drug is the main treatment, with corticosteroids when function does not recover. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider its relationships to ATN and the glomerular diseases.

Key points

  • AIN is a type IV, T cell–mediated hypersensitivity reaction: a drug forms a hapten, Th2 cells release IL-4 and IL-5, and eosinophils and T cells infiltrate the interstitium.
  • Interstitial edema compresses the tubules, raising the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure and lowering GFR; continued exposure leads to fibrosis.
  • Causes are diuretics, NSAIDs, penicillins and cephalosporins, PPIs, rifampin, sulfonamides, allopurinol, and other drugs; infection; and autoimmune disease.
  • The classic triad appears in about 10%; sterile pyuria, white cell casts, and a drug timeline are more useful, eosinophiluria is unreliable, and biopsy is definitive.
  • The drug is stopped, and corticosteroids are given if function does not improve within 3–7 days; 40–60% do not regain baseline function.

Pathophysiology

AIN is a type IV, T cell–mediated hypersensitivity reaction. A drug taken up by tubular cells binds a protein in the cell or its basement membrane, forming a hapten that the immune system sees as new; dendritic cells near the basement membrane carry it to a lymph node, and activated T cells return, with Th2 cells releasing IL-4 and IL-5. IL-5 increases eosinophils, which infiltrate the interstitium with T cells and invade the tubule wall (tubulitis). The edematous interstitium compresses the tubules, raising the Bowman space hydrostatic pressure, and angiotensin II from the inflamed kidney constricts its vessels, so GFR falls. Tubular injury impairs concentration, causing polyuria, and proximal injury causes glucosuria and low phosphate, urate, and HCO3−. If exposure continues, inflammation gives way to fibrosis and tubular atrophy, which corticosteroids cannot reverse.

Etiology and mechanisms

Drugs cause most AIN, remembered as the 5 Ps with others. Loop diuretics and thiazides, which are sulfonamides, can cause it. NSAIDs are the most common cause, in about 44%, typically in older, long-term users months after starting, with few allergic signs and sometimes nephrotic-range protein from minimal change disease. Penicillins and cephalosporins most often cause fever, rash, and eosinophilia, especially after a previous reaction. PPIs are the second most common cause in some series, with milder AKI but less complete recovery because exposure is often long. Rifampin provokes antibodies, especially with intermittent dosing; sulfonamides, including TMP-SMX, and allopurinol, often with systemic hypersensitivity, are other causes, as are ICIs, 5-ASA, ciprofloxacin, and phenytoin. Infections include streptococci, leptospirosis, CMV, EBV, and HIV, and bacteria such as E. coli with obstruction or reflux. Autoimmune causes are SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, and TINU.

Clinical presentation and complications

AIN usually appears 1–2 weeks after a new drug, within days after a previous exposure, and months after starting NSAIDs or PPIs. The classic triad of fever, rash, and eosinophilia or eosinophiluria occurs in only about 10%, most often with β-lactams and rarely with NSAIDs; most patients have fatigue, malaise, nausea, or arthralgia, with AKI found on bloods. A maculopapular rash is highly suggestive when present. Patients are usually non-oliguric and may be polyuric from a concentrating defect, with glucosuria without diabetes and low phosphate, urate, and HCO3−, and hypertension from angiotensin II. Complications are AKI needing short-term dialysis, CKD from fibrosis, and anemia; 40–60% of patients do not regain their baseline function, more often after NSAIDs, PPIs, or AKI lasting over 3 weeks, so the drug history, including over-the-counter drugs, matters more than the triad.

Diagnosis

AIN is suspected when creatinine rises after a new drug. The urine shows sterile pyuria, white cell casts, microscopic hematuria, and protein usually under 1 g a day, and the blood may show eosinophilia and a high IgE; eosinophiluria is unreliable, with a sensitivity of about 40%. Ultrasound excludes obstruction and may show large, echogenic kidneys. Biopsy is the only definitive test, showing T cells and eosinophils in an edematous interstitium with tubulitis and spared glomeruli, and fibrosis predicts a poor response to corticosteroids; it is indicated when function does not improve 3–7 days after stopping the drug. A timeline of every new drug, including those bought over the counter, and improvement after stopping the culprit identify drug-induced AIN, and NSAID-induced AIN may bring nephrotic-range protein from minimal change disease. Cultures, serology, and imaging seek infection and obstruction, and ANA and complement, anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies, serum ACE, Ca2+, a chest x-ray, IgG4 levels, and an eye examination seek SLE, Sjögren syndrome, sarcoidosis, IgG4-related disease, and TINU.

Management

Stopping the culprit drug is the most important treatment, with supportive care of the AKI and short-term dialysis if needed. Prednisolone is given if function does not improve within 3–7 days of stopping the drug, ideally after a biopsy, and starting early limits fibrosis. The reaction is recorded as an allergy and the drug avoided; ICIs are often held and corticosteroids given, because there may be no other cancer treatment. Infection is treated and obstruction relieved, and autoimmune disease is treated with corticosteroids or other immunosuppression. Recovery usually comes within 3 months, and corticosteroids help only while inflammation is active.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both injure the tubules and follow drugs. ATN follows ischemia or a direct toxin soon after the insult and shows muddy brown casts, whereas AIN is an immune reaction days to weeks after a new drug, with sterile pyuria, white cell casts, and sometimes fever, rash, and eosinophilia; AIN is treated by stopping the drug and with corticosteroids, whereas ATN is supported until the tubules regrow.

. Glomerular disease brings red cell casts, dysmorphic red cells, and heavy protein, whereas AIN spares the glomeruli and shows white cell casts with little protein; NSAIDs are the exception, causing AIN with nephrotic-range protein from minimal change disease.

Minimal Change Disease, FSGS, and Membranous Nephropathy

Pathophysiology

Injury to the podocyte, from a circulating factor in MCD and primary FSGS or from immune deposits beneath it in MN, effaces the foot processes and disrupts the slit diaphragm, so albumin leaks into the urine in nephrotic-range amounts while red cells stay out.

  1. Podocyte injuryA circulating factor (MCD, primary FSGS), podocyte loss (FSGS), or complement from subepithelial deposits (MN)
  2. Foot processes effaceThe interdigitating foot processes flatten and the slit diaphragm between them is lost
  3. The size barrier failsAlbumin crosses the filter; in MCD the loss is mostly albumin (selective proteinuria)
  4. Nephrotic syndromeProteinuria above 3.5 g a day, low albumin, edema, and high lipids, as on

Where each disease injures the wall

  • AEffacementThe common lesion of all three: foot processes flatten and the slit diaphragm is lost
  • BSclerosisIn FSGS, lost podocytes leave bare GBM that sticks to Bowman capsule, and the segment scars
  • CSubepithelial depositsIn MN, IgG4 against podocyte antigens such as PLA2R binds beneath the podocyte and activates complement (C5b-9), which injures it
  • DSpikesIn MN, the GBM grows up between the deposits, then thickens around them

Note: The podocyte and slit diaphragm, which filter by size, are now thought to be the main barrier to albumin; loss of the GBM's negative charge, the older explanation, plays at most a small part.

Etiology

  • 1Minimal change diseaseThe most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (about 80%), with a male predominance in childhood; usually primary, from a circulating factor; secondary to NSAIDs, Hodgkin lymphoma, lithium, and allergy such as bee stings
  • 2FSGSA leading cause in adults, more common in men and in Black patients, linked to APOL1 variants; primary, from a circulating permeability factor; genetic, from podocyte protein genes; or secondary to HIV (the collapsing variant), heroin, and adaptive overload from obesity, sickle cell disease, or lost nephrons
  • 3Membranous nephropathyThe most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in White adults, peaking at 50–60 years; primary in 75–80%, with antibodies against PLA2R in 70–80% and THSD7A in 1–5%; secondary to hepatitis B, SLE (lupus nephritis class V), solid tumors, NSAIDs, and penicillamine

Note: MCD can progress to FSGS, and lupus nephritis class V looks like MN on biopsy, as summarized on .

Symptoms and complications

All three cause nephrotic syndrome, with the shared complications on ; what differs is the onset and the course.

  • Minimal change disease (1)Abrupt edema, often after an upper respiratory infection or allergy; usually normal BP and GFR; relapses are common; AKI can occur in older adults
  • FSGS (2)Slower onset; hypertension and microscopic hematuria are common; about half with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria reach kidney failure within 3–8 years, and primary FSGS can recur in a transplant
  • Membranous nephropathy (3)Gradual edema; thrombosis is more common than in the other two, especially renal vein thrombosis; about a third remit with supportive care alone

Diagnosis

The shared workup is on ; a biopsy separates the three in adults, whereas children with typical MCD are treated without one.

  • +Any of the threeUPCR above 300 mg/mmol or 24-hour protein above 3.5 g; low serum albumin; a bland sediment, with few red cells
  • 1Minimal change diseaseBiopsy: light microscopy, normal; immunofluorescence, negative; electron microscopy, diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes; in a child, remission with corticosteroids is diagnosis enough
  • 2FSGSBiopsy: light microscopy, segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis in some glomeruli; immunofluorescence, negative, or IgM and C3 in sclerotic segments; electron microscopy, effacement of podocyte foot processes; effacement is diffuse (over 80%) in primary FSGS and patchy in adaptive FSGS; HIV and hepatitis B and C serology; genetic testing when familial
  • 3Membranous nephropathyAnti-PLA2R antibodies, whose level tracks activity; Biopsy: light microscopy, diffuse thickening of the GBM; spikes on silver stain; immunofluorescence, granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall; electron microscopy, subepithelial deposits; screen for secondary causes with hepatitis B and C serology, ANA, and age-appropriate cancer screening

Biopsy panels

Each panel is one capillary loop in cross-section: the lumen and endothelium inside, the GBM as the dark ring, podocyte foot processes outside, and the mesangium at the left; dots are immune deposits, and the strip on the right shows the immunofluorescence pattern.

Treatment

General nephrotic care, with ACEi or ARBs, diuretics, statins, and anticoagulation where needed, is on ; each disease adds its own treatment.

  • 1Minimal change diseasePrednisolone: in children, daily for 4–6 weeks, then on alternate days, with remission in most within 4 weeks; in adults, 1 mg/kg daily for up to 16 weeks, then tapered; CNIs, cyclophosphamide, MMF, or rituximab for frequent relapses or corticosteroid dependence
  • 2FSGSPrimary: high-dose corticosteroids, then CNIs if resistant; secondary: treat the cause, such as antiretroviral therapy for HIV or weight loss, with RAAS blockade and no immunosuppression
  • 3Membranous nephropathySupportive care for about 6 months if low risk; rituximab, or cyclophosphamide with corticosteroids, if high risk or progressing; follow anti-PLA2R levels; anticoagulation when albumin is very low

Note: Secondary FSGS does not respond to immunosuppression, which can harm, so primary and secondary FSGS are separated before treatment.

Related: Glomerular Filtration

  2. Zamora G, Hanna P, Pearson-Shaver AL. Minimal Change Disease. 2023. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing. NBK560639

Review article

Minimal change disease, FSGS, and membranous nephropathy: the primary podocytopathies

Minimal change disease, FSGS, and membranous nephropathy injure the podocyte and cause nephrotic syndrome, with heavy proteinuria and little hematuria. In MCD and primary FSGS a circulating factor effaces the foot processes, FSGS adds podocyte loss and segmental scarring, and in MN IgG4 against PLA2R forms subepithelial deposits that injure the podocyte through complement. The three differ in who they affect, their course, their biopsy, and their treatment, which ranges from corticosteroids in MCD to rituximab in MN. Here, we review their mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider their relationships to the other glomerular diseases.

Key points

  • Podocyte effacement, the loss of the size barrier at the slit diaphragm, is the common lesion; loss of GBM charge plays at most a small part.
  • MCD causes about 80% of nephrotic syndrome in children; FSGS is more common in Black adults (APOL1); MN is the most common primary cause in White adults.
  • MCD has a normal light microscopy and negative immunofluorescence; FSGS shows segmental sclerosis; MN shows granular IgG and C3 with subepithelial deposits and anti-PLA2R antibodies.
  • MCD responds to corticosteroids; primary FSGS is treated with corticosteroids and CNIs, but secondary FSGS is not; MN is treated supportively or with rituximab by risk.

Pathophysiology

The podocyte and the slit diaphragm between its foot processes form the size barrier that keeps albumin in the blood. In MCD and primary FSGS a circulating factor injures the podocyte, in FSGS lost podocytes leave bare GBM that sticks to Bowman capsule and scars segmentally, and in MN IgG4 against podocyte antigens such as PLA2R binds beneath the podocyte, where complement (C5b-9) injures it while the GBM grows up between the deposits as spikes. In all three the foot processes efface and the slit diaphragm is lost, so albumin crosses the filter, selectively in MCD, and nephrotic syndrome follows; loss of the GBM's negative charge, the older explanation, plays at most a small part.

Etiology and mechanisms

MCD causes about 80% of nephrotic syndrome in children, more often in boys, and is usually primary, but follows NSAIDs, Hodgkin lymphoma, lithium, and allergy such as bee stings. FSGS is a leading cause in adults, more common in men and in Black patients through APOL1 variants, and is primary, genetic, or secondary to HIV (the collapsing variant), heroin, or adaptive overload from obesity, sickle cell disease, or lost nephrons. MN is the most common cause of primary nephrotic syndrome in White adults, peaking at 50–60 years; 75–80% is primary, with antibodies against PLA2R in 70–80% and THSD7A in 1–5%, and the rest follows hepatitis B, SLE, solid tumors, NSAIDs, or penicillamine. MCD can progress to FSGS, and lupus nephritis class V resembles MN.

Clinical presentation and complications

MCD causes abrupt edema, often after an upper respiratory infection or allergy, with normal BP and GFR, frequent relapses, and AKI in some older adults. FSGS begins more slowly, often with hypertension and microscopic hematuria, and about half with persistent nephrotic-range proteinuria reach kidney failure within 3–8 years; primary FSGS can recur in a transplant. MN causes gradual edema and carries the highest risk of thrombosis, especially renal vein thrombosis, and about a third remit with supportive care alone.

Diagnosis

All three give a UPCR above 300 mg/mmol or more than 3.5 g of protein a day, a low albumin, and a bland sediment. Children with typical MCD are treated without a biopsy, and remission confirms it. In adults, MCD shows normal light microscopy, negative immunofluorescence, and diffuse effacement of podocyte foot processes; FSGS shows segmental sclerosis and hyalinosis in some glomeruli, negative immunofluorescence or IgM and C3 in sclerotic segments, and effacement that is diffuse in primary and patchy in adaptive disease, with HIV and hepatitis serology and genetic testing; MN shows diffuse thickening of the GBM with spikes, granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall, and subepithelial deposits, and anti-PLA2R antibodies track its activity, with a search for hepatitis, SLE, and cancer.

Management

General nephrotic care applies to all three. MCD is treated with prednisolone, daily for 4–6 weeks then on alternate days in children, who mostly remit within 4 weeks, and at 1 mg/kg daily for up to 16 weeks then tapered in adults, with CNIs, cyclophosphamide, MMF, or rituximab for frequent relapses. Primary FSGS is treated with high-dose corticosteroids and then CNIs, whereas secondary FSGS is treated by its cause and RAAS blockade, because immunosuppression does not help and can harm. MN is treated supportively for about 6 months if low risk, and with rituximab, or cyclophosphamide with corticosteroids, if high risk, guided by anti-PLA2R levels, with anticoagulation when albumin is very low.

Relationships to other conditions

. These also cause nephrotic syndrome, but follow diabetes or a plasma cell or inflammatory disease, and show mesangial expansion and nodules or amyloid fibrils rather than isolated podocyte injury.

. Class V lupus nephritis also has subepithelial deposits, but shows full-house immunofluorescence and low complement, whereas primary MN shows IgG4 and anti-PLA2R antibodies.

Diabetic Kidney Disease and Amyloid Nephropathy

Pathophysiology

Diabetes damages the glomerulus slowly, through hyperfiltration and glycation that thicken the GBM and expand the mesangium, whereas amyloidosis fills the mesangium and capillary walls with fibrils; both efface the podocytes and leak protein, and both scar the kidney over time.

  1. HyperglycemiaGlucose glycates proteins into AGEs and activates PKC and TGF-β
  2. HyperfiltrationMore Na+ is reabsorbed with glucose by SGLT2, so less reaches the macula densa and the afferent arteriole dilates; angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole
  3. Structural injuryThe GBM thickens, the mesangium expands, and podocytes are lost
  4. AlbuminuriaAlbumin leaks first in small amounts, then in nephrotic-range amounts
  5. GlomerulosclerosisNodular sclerosis and hyalinosis lower GFR toward kidney failure

Where each disease injures the wall

  • AHyperfiltrationAfferent dilation and efferent constriction raise glomerular pressure, injuring the filter
  • BThick GBMAGEs cross-link GBM proteins, and matrix builds up
  • CMesangial expansionMatrix accumulates diffusely, then as nodules (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules)
  • DArteriolar hyalinosisBoth afferent and efferent arterioles thicken with hyaline, a hallmark of diabetes
  • EAmyloid fibrilsMisfolded light chains or serum amyloid A deposit in the mesangium and capillary walls, effacing podocytes

Note: Hyperfiltration explains why ACEi, ARBs, and SGLT2 inhibitors protect the kidney: each lowers glomerular pressure.

Etiology

  • Diabetic kidney disease
  • 1Type 1 diabetesUsually 15–20 years after onset; in about 30% of patients
  • 2Type 2 diabetesAlbuminuria can be present at diagnosis, because onset is uncertain; in about 40%; risk rises with poor glucose control, hypertension, smoking, and obesity
  • Amyloid nephropathy
  • 3AL amyloidosisA clonal plasma cell disorder, with or without myeloma, makes misfolded light chains
  • 4AA amyloidosisChronic inflammation raises serum amyloid A (RA, IBD, FMF, and chronic infections such as TB)

Note: DKD is the most common cause of kidney failure and of nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults, developing in 30–40% of people with diabetes.

Symptoms and complications

Both present with proteinuria and progress to CKD, with the shared nephrotic complications on ; amyloidosis also affects other organs.

  • DKD (1, 2)No symptoms early; albuminuria increases, then nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, and a falling GFR; retinopathy is usually present; the sediment is bland
  • Amyloid nephropathy (3, 4)Nephrotic syndrome with normal-sized or large kidneys, often without hypertension
  • Other organs in amyloidosisRestrictive cardiomyopathy, neuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome, orthostatic hypotension, hepatomegaly, and macroglossia in AL amyloidosis

Note: Retinopathy with albuminuria and no hematuria supports DKD; hematuria, a rapid fall in GFR, or no retinopathy calls for a biopsy.

Diagnosis

The shared workup is on ; DKD is usually diagnosed without a biopsy, whereas amyloidosis needs tissue and typing.

  • 1, 2DKDUACR on 2 of 3 samples over 3–6 months: moderately increased at 3–30 mg/mmol, severely increased above 30 mg/mmol; screen from 5 years after diagnosis in type 1 diabetes and at diagnosis in type 2, then yearly; eGFR and HbA1c; Biopsy: light microscopy, mesangial expansion, nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules), and arteriolar hyalinosis; immunofluorescence, linear IgG along the GBM, which is nonspecific; electron microscopy, thickening of the GBM, only if atypical
  • 3AL amyloidosisSPEP, UPEP, immunofixation, and serum free light chains with the κ to λ ratio; fat pad or kidney biopsy with Congo red; Biopsy: light microscopy, mesangial and capillary wall deposits; apple-green birefringence with Congo red; immunofluorescence, κ or λ light chains in AL amyloidosis; electron microscopy, randomly arranged nonbranching fibrils of 7–12 nm; bone marrow biopsy; troponin, BNP, and echocardiography for the heart
  • 4AA amyloidosisThe underlying inflammatory disease and CRP; biopsy with Congo red and typing of the amyloid protein

Biopsy panels

Each panel is one capillary loop in cross-section: the lumen and endothelium inside, the GBM as the dark ring, podocyte foot processes outside, and the mesangium at the left; dots are immune deposits, and the strip on the right shows the immunofluorescence pattern.

Treatment

General nephrotic and CKD care is on ; DKD is slowed by controlling glucose and glomerular pressure, and amyloidosis by stopping the protein that forms the fibrils.

  • 1, 2DKDGlucose control, with an HbA1c target of about 7%, individualized; BP control with ACEi or ARBs at the highest tolerated dose; SGLT2 inhibitors; finerenone in type 2 diabetes with persistent albuminuria; GLP-1 receptor agonists; statins and stopping smoking
  • 3AL amyloidosisChemotherapy against the plasma cell clone, with autologous stem cell transplant in selected patients
  • 4AA amyloidosisTreat the inflammation, such as with TNF inhibitors in RA and colchicine in FMF

Diabetic kidney disease and amyloid nephropathy: slow glomerular injury from glucose and fibrils

Diabetic kidney disease and amyloid nephropathy cause proteinuria that progresses to chronic kidney disease. In diabetes, hyperfiltration and glycation thicken the GBM, expand the mesangium into nodules, and hyalinize the arterioles, whereas in amyloidosis misfolded light chains or serum amyloid A deposit as fibrils in the mesangium and capillary walls. Diabetic kidney disease is diagnosed by persistent albuminuria, usually with retinopathy, and slowed by glucose and pressure control with ACEi or ARBs and SGLT2 inhibitors; amyloidosis needs a biopsy with Congo red and treatment of its source. Here, we review their mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider their relationships to the other glomerular diseases.

Key points

  • Hyperfiltration from afferent dilation and efferent constriction, with AGEs, drives DKD; ACEi, ARBs, and SGLT2 inhibitors protect by lowering glomerular pressure.
  • DKD shows mesangial expansion, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, arteriolar hyalinosis, and a thick GBM, and develops in 30–40% of people with diabetes.
  • Persistent albuminuria (UACR above 3 mg/mmol) with retinopathy and a bland sediment supports DKD without a biopsy.
  • AL amyloidosis comes from a plasma cell clone and AA amyloidosis from chronic inflammation; both show apple-green birefringence with Congo red.

Pathophysiology

Hyperglycemia glycates proteins into AGEs and activates PKC and TGF-β. More Na+ is reabsorbed with glucose by SGLT2, so less reaches the macula densa, the afferent arteriole dilates, and angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, raising glomerular pressure. The GBM thickens as AGEs cross-link its proteins, the mesangium expands, diffusely and then as Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, both arterioles hyalinize, and podocytes are lost, so albumin leaks in increasing amounts until glomerulosclerosis lowers GFR. In amyloidosis, misfolded light chains or serum amyloid A deposit as fibrils in the mesangium and capillary walls and efface the podocytes. Lowering glomerular pressure with ACEi, ARBs, or SGLT2 inhibitors explains their protective effect.

Etiology and mechanisms

DKD develops in about 30% of people with type 1 diabetes, usually 15–20 years after onset, and about 40% with type 2 diabetes, in whom albuminuria can be present at diagnosis; poor glucose control, hypertension, smoking, and obesity raise the risk. It is the most common cause of kidney failure and of nephrotic-range proteinuria in adults. AL amyloidosis follows a clonal plasma cell disorder, with or without myeloma, and AA amyloidosis follows chronic inflammation (RA, IBD, FMF, and chronic infections such as TB).

Clinical presentation and complications

DKD causes no symptoms early; albuminuria increases, then nephrotic-range proteinuria, hypertension, and a falling GFR follow, usually with retinopathy and a bland sediment, and hematuria, a rapid decline, or no retinopathy suggests another disease. Amyloid nephropathy causes nephrotic syndrome with normal-sized or large kidneys, often without hypertension, and amyloidosis also causes restrictive cardiomyopathy, neuropathy and carpal tunnel syndrome, orthostatic hypotension, hepatomegaly, and, in AL amyloidosis, macroglossia.

Diagnosis

DKD is diagnosed by a UACR that is moderately (3–30 mg/mmol) or severely (above 30 mg/mmol) increased on 2 of 3 samples over 3–6 months, screened from 5 years after diagnosis in type 1 diabetes and at diagnosis in type 2, then yearly, with eGFR and HbA1c; a biopsy, kept for atypical cases, shows mesangial expansion, nodular glomerulosclerosis, and arteriolar hyalinosis, nonspecific linear IgG along the GBM, and a thick GBM. AL amyloidosis is sought with SPEP, UPEP, immunofixation, and serum free light chains, and a fat pad or kidney biopsy shows deposits with apple-green birefringence on Congo red, κ or λ light chains, and randomly arranged fibrils of 7–12 nm, with bone marrow biopsy and cardiac tests; AA amyloidosis is suggested by the inflammatory disease and confirmed by typing.

Management

DKD is slowed by glucose control, with an HbA1c target of about 7% individualized, BP control with ACEi or ARBs at the highest tolerated dose, SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone in type 2 diabetes with persistent albuminuria, GLP-1 receptor agonists, statins, and stopping smoking. AL amyloidosis is treated with chemotherapy against the plasma cell clone, with stem cell transplant in selected patients, and AA amyloidosis by treating the inflammation, such as with TNF inhibitors or colchicine in FMF.

Relationships to other conditions

. These are primary podocytopathies with normal or near-normal light microscopy or subepithelial deposits, whereas DKD and amyloidosis expand the mesangium and follow a systemic disease; diabetes can coexist with them, which is why atypical features call for a biopsy.

. DKD is the leading cause of CKD and kidney failure, and its treatment with RAAS blockade and SGLT2 inhibitors is the model for slowing CKD from any cause.

Anti-GBM Disease, ANCA-Associated Vasculitis, and Alport Syndrome

Pathophysiology

Antibodies bind the GBM itself in anti-GBM disease, activated neutrophils destroy capillary walls without immune deposits in ANCA vasculitis, and the GBM is built wrongly in Alport syndrome; in each, breaks in the capillary wall let red cells and protein into the urine, and severe injury fills Bowman space with crescents.

  1. Capillary wall injuryAntibodies against the GBM, ANCA-activated neutrophils, or abnormal type IV collagen
  2. The GBM breaksRed cells squeeze through and are deformed (dysmorphic), and protein leaks
  3. Bowman space fillsFibrin, macrophages, and proliferating parietal cells form crescents
  4. GFR fallsOver days to weeks in anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis (RPGN), or over years in Alport syndrome
  5. Na+ is retainedHypertension and edema, as in any nephritic syndrome

Where each disease injures the wall

  • AAnti-GBM antibodiesIgG binds the α3 chain of type IV collagen in the GBM and alveoli, and complement injures the wall
  • BANCA and neutrophilsANCA bind PR3 or MPO on primed neutrophils, which release enzymes and oxygen radicals that necrose the capillary
  • CBreaks in the wallRed cells and protein leak through the ruptured GBM
  • DCrescentsFibrin and cells fill Bowman space; cellular crescents can recover, but fibrous ones cannot
  • EAbnormal type IV collagenIn Alport syndrome, the α3α4α5 network is missing, so the GBM thins, splits, and fails

Note: RPGN has 3 immunofluorescence patterns: type I, linear (anti-GBM disease); type II, granular (immune complex disease); and type III, pauci-immune (ANCA vasculitis), as compared on .

Etiology

  • Antibodies against the GBM
  • 1Anti-GBM diseaseAutoantibodies against the α3 chain of type IV collagen; with pulmonary hemorrhage in 40–60% (Goodpasture syndrome); linked to HLA-DR2 and triggered by smoking, inhaled hydrocarbons, and infection
  • ANCA-associated vasculitis
  • 2GPAMostly PR3-ANCA (c-ANCA); necrotizing granulomas of the upper and lower airways
  • 3MPAMostly MPO-ANCA (p-ANCA); no granulomas
  • 4EGPAAsthma and eosinophilia; ANCA in about 30%; the kidney is involved less often
  • Genetic
  • 5Alport syndromeMutations in type IV collagen: X-linked COL4A5 in about 85%, and COL4A3 or COL4A4 in autosomal recessive and dominant forms

Note: Drugs such as hydralazine, propylthiouracil, and levamisole-adulterated cocaine can trigger ANCA vasculitis.

Symptoms and complications

All five cause a nephritic syndrome, as on ; anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis usually present as RPGN, often with the lungs involved, whereas Alport syndrome progresses slowly from childhood.

  • Anti-GBM disease (1)RPGN over days to weeks; hemoptysis and pulmonary hemorrhage in Goodpasture syndrome
  • GPA (2)Sinusitis, nasal crusting, and a saddle nose; lung nodules and cavities; RPGN; fever and weight loss
  • MPA (3)RPGN, pulmonary hemorrhage, purpura, and mononeuritis multiplex
  • EGPA (4)Asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy, and heart involvement; milder kidney disease
  • Alport syndrome (5)Microscopic hematuria in childhood, then proteinuria, hypertension, and kidney failure; sensorineural hearing loss in about 80% of males with the X-linked form by their teens; anterior lenticonus; female carriers are affected less
  • ComplicationsPulmonary-renal syndrome, kidney failure, and relapse in ANCA vasculitis

Diagnosis

The shared workup is on ; anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA are tested urgently in any RPGN, and treatment does not wait for the biopsy when suspicion is high.

  • +Any of the fiveDysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; normal C3; chest imaging for hemorrhage, nodules, or cavities; biopsy, in which the share of crescents predicts recovery
  • 1Anti-GBM diseaseAnti-GBM antibodies; Biopsy: light microscopy, crescents; immunofluorescence, linear IgG and C3 along the GBM; electron microscopy, no deposits; breaks in the GBM
  • 2–4ANCA vasculitisPR3-ANCA or MPO-ANCA; Biopsy: light microscopy, crescents and necrosis; immunofluorescence, negative or scant (pauci-immune); electron microscopy, no deposits; nasal or lung biopsy for granulomas in GPA; eosinophil count and IgE in EGPA
  • 5Alport syndromeFamily history, hearing test, and eye examination; genetic testing of COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5; Biopsy: light microscopy, normal early; segmental sclerosis later; immunofluorescence, negative; type IV collagen α5 chain absent; electron microscopy, splitting and thickening of the GBM (basket-weave)

Biopsy panels

Each panel is one capillary loop in cross-section: the lumen and endothelium inside, the GBM as the dark ring, podocyte foot processes outside, and the mesangium at the left; dots are immune deposits, and the strip on the right shows the immunofluorescence pattern.

Treatment

General nephritic care is on ; anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis need urgent immunosuppression, whereas Alport syndrome has no specific treatment.

  • 1Anti-GBM diseasePlasma exchange to remove the antibodies, with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide, started at once; dialysis and ventilation as needed
  • 2–4ANCA vasculitisInduction with corticosteroids and rituximab or cyclophosphamide; avacopan, a C5a receptor antagonist, to spare corticosteroids; plasma exchange in selected severe cases; maintenance with rituximab or azathioprine
  • 5Alport syndromeACEi or ARBs started early, which delay kidney failure; hearing aids; dialysis or a transplant, after which a few develop anti-GBM disease against the collagen they lacked
