Review article

Anti-GBM disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and Alport syndrome: disease of the glomerular basement membrane and capillary wall

Anti-GBM disease, ANCA-associated vasculitis, and Alport syndrome cause nephritic syndrome by breaking the glomerular capillary wall. In anti-GBM disease, antibodies against type IV collagen bind the GBM in a linear pattern; in ANCA vasculitis, antibodies against PR3 or MPO activate neutrophils that necrose capillaries without immune deposits; and in Alport syndrome, inherited defects in type IV collagen leave a thin, split GBM. The first two present as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, often with lung involvement, and need urgent immunosuppression and plasma exchange, whereas Alport syndrome progresses slowly with hearing loss and is treated with RAAS blockade. Here, we review their mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider their relationships to the other glomerular diseases.

Key points

  • Breaks in the capillary wall let dysmorphic red cells and protein into the urine, and severe injury fills Bowman space with crescents (RPGN).
  • Anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG along the GBM, with pulmonary hemorrhage in 40–60%; ANCA vasculitis is pauci-immune, with PR3-ANCA in GPA and MPO-ANCA in MPA.
  • Alport syndrome, mostly X-linked (COL4A5), causes hematuria in childhood, sensorineural hearing loss, and a split, basket-weave GBM.
  • Anti-GBM disease is treated with plasma exchange, corticosteroids, and cyclophosphamide; ANCA vasculitis with corticosteroids and rituximab or cyclophosphamide; Alport syndrome with early ACEi or ARBs.

Pathophysiology

In anti-GBM disease, IgG binds the α3 chain of type IV collagen in the GBM and alveoli, and complement injures the wall. In ANCA vasculitis, ANCA bind PR3 or MPO on primed neutrophils, which release enzymes and oxygen radicals that necrose the capillary, leaving few immune deposits. In Alport syndrome, the α3α4α5 collagen network is missing, so the GBM thins, splits, and fails. Breaks in the wall let red cells through, deformed, with protein, and severe injury fills Bowman space with fibrin, macrophages, and proliferating parietal cells as crescents, which can recover while cellular but not once fibrous. GFR falls over days to weeks in anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis, as RPGN, and over years in Alport syndrome, and Na+ retention causes hypertension and edema. RPGN shows a linear pattern in anti-GBM disease (type I), a granular pattern in immune complex disease (type II), and a pauci-immune pattern in ANCA vasculitis (type III).

Etiology and mechanisms

Anti-GBM disease is linked to HLA-DR2 and triggered by smoking, inhaled hydrocarbons, and infection, with pulmonary hemorrhage in 40–60% (Goodpasture syndrome). GPA is mostly PR3-ANCA positive, with necrotizing granulomas of the airways; MPA is mostly MPO-ANCA positive, without granulomas; and EGPA combines asthma and eosinophilia, with ANCA in about 30% and less kidney involvement. Drugs such as hydralazine, propylthiouracil, and levamisole-adulterated cocaine can trigger ANCA vasculitis. Alport syndrome is X-linked through COL4A5 in about 85%, and autosomal through COL4A3 or COL4A4 in the rest.

Clinical presentation and complications

Anti-GBM disease causes RPGN over days to weeks, with hemoptysis and pulmonary hemorrhage in Goodpasture syndrome. GPA causes sinusitis, nasal crusting, a saddle nose, lung nodules and cavities, RPGN, and constitutional symptoms; MPA causes RPGN, pulmonary hemorrhage, purpura, and mononeuritis multiplex; and EGPA causes asthma, eosinophilia, neuropathy, and heart involvement with milder kidney disease. Alport syndrome causes microscopic hematuria in childhood, then proteinuria, hypertension, and kidney failure, with sensorineural hearing loss in about 80% of males with the X-linked form by their teens and anterior lenticonus; female carriers are affected less. Complications are pulmonary-renal syndrome, kidney failure, and, in ANCA vasculitis, relapse.

Diagnosis

All five give dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts with a normal C3, and chest imaging looks for hemorrhage, nodules, or cavities; anti-GBM antibodies and ANCA are tested urgently, and treatment does not wait for a biopsy when suspicion is high. Anti-GBM disease shows crescents, linear IgG and C3 along the GBM, and breaks in the GBM without deposits. ANCA vasculitis shows PR3-ANCA or MPO-ANCA and crescents with necrosis, with negative or scant immunofluorescence and no deposits; nasal or lung tissue shows granulomas in GPA, and EGPA raises eosinophils and IgE. Alport syndrome is suggested by the family history, hearing test, and eye examination and confirmed by genetic testing of COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5; its biopsy is normal early, with negative immunofluorescence, absent type IV collagen α5 chain, and splitting and thickening of the GBM in a basket-weave pattern.

Management

Anti-GBM disease is treated at once with plasma exchange to remove the antibodies, corticosteroids, and cyclophosphamide, with dialysis and ventilation as needed. ANCA vasculitis is induced with corticosteroids and rituximab or cyclophosphamide, with avacopan, a C5a receptor antagonist, to spare corticosteroids and plasma exchange in selected severe cases, then maintained with rituximab or azathioprine. Alport syndrome is treated with ACEi or ARBs started early, which delay kidney failure, hearing aids, and dialysis or a transplant, after which a few develop anti-GBM disease against the collagen they lacked.

Relationships to other conditions

. These immune complex diseases also cause nephritic syndrome and can form crescents (RPGN type II), but show granular immunofluorescence, and PSGN and MPGN lower C3, whereas anti-GBM disease is linear and ANCA vasculitis pauci-immune with a normal C3.

. Late Alport syndrome can scar segmentally like FSGS, but begins with hematuria and hearing loss rather than nephrotic syndrome.

IgA Nephropathy, PSGN, and MPGN

Pathophysiology

Immune complexes lodge in the glomerulus, in the mesangium in IgA nephropathy, beneath the epithelium in PSGN, and beneath the endothelium in MPGN, and activate complement and inflammation, so red cells and protein leak into the urine.

  1. An antigenGalactose-deficient IgA1, a streptococcal antigen, a chronic infection, or uncontrolled complement
  2. Immune complexes depositFrom the blood or formed in place; where they lodge sets the pattern
  3. Complement activatesC3 is consumed in PSGN and MPGN, so serum C3 is low
  4. Inflammation and proliferationNeutrophils arrive and mesangial and endothelial cells multiply
  5. Nephritic syndromeHematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and a falling GFR, as on

Where each disease injures the wall

  • AMesangial depositsIgA nephropathy: complexes of galactose-deficient IgA1 and IgG against it lodge in the mesangium
  • BSubepithelial humpsPSGN: streptococcal antigens and antibodies form large deposits beneath the podocyte
  • CSubendothelial depositsMPGN: complexes beneath the endothelium face the blood and draw inflammatory cells
  • DComplement activationC3 is consumed, by immune complexes in PSGN and immune complex MPGN, or by an overactive alternative pathway in C3 glomerulopathy
  • ETram-track GBMMesangial cells grow into the capillary wall and lay down new basement membrane, splitting the GBM

Note: Mesangial and subendothelial deposits face the blood and draw inflammatory cells, so they cause nephritic disease, whereas subepithelial deposits in MN mainly injure podocytes; PSGN, with subepithelial humps and intense inflammation, is the exception.

Etiology

  • 1IgA nephropathyThe most common primary GN worldwide, most often in young men and East Asian people; galactose-deficient IgA1 is inherited, and mucosal infections trigger flares; secondary to cirrhosis, celiac disease, IBD, and HIV; IgA vasculitis is its systemic form, mostly in children
  • 2PSGNThe most common cause of acute GN in children, after nephritogenic group A β-hemolytic streptococci: 7–10 days after pharyngitis or 2–3 weeks after impetigo; other infections cause infection-related GN in adults
  • 3Immune complex MPGNChronic antigen in the blood: hepatitis C with cryoglobulinemia, hepatitis B, chronic infections such as endocarditis, autoimmune disease, and monoclonal gammopathy
  • 4C3 glomerulopathyUncontrolled alternative complement: C3 nephritic factor, an autoantibody that stabilizes C3 convertase, or mutations in factors H, I, or B; includes dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis

Symptoms and complications

All four cause a nephritic syndrome, as on , but they differ in timing: IgA nephropathy flares with an infection, PSGN follows one by weeks, and MPGN is chronic.

  • IgA nephropathy (1)Visible hematuria within 1–2 days of a mucosal infection, often recurrent; or persistent microscopic hematuria and proteinuria found by chance; slow progression in many; IgA vasculitis adds purpura on the legs and buttocks, arthritis, and abdominal pain
  • PSGN (2)Cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, and oliguria weeks after the infection; most children recover fully, and adults less often
  • MPGN (3, 4)Mixed nephrotic and nephritic features with progressive loss of GFR; purpura, arthralgia, and neuropathy with cryoglobulinemia

Note: MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy often present with nephrotic-range proteinuria, and IgA nephropathy occasionally does, so a nephrotic picture does not exclude them.

Diagnosis

The shared workup is on ; complement and the timing of an infection point to the cause, and a biopsy confirms it.

  • +Any of the fourDysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; UPCR; C3 and C4
  • 1IgA nephropathyNormal C3; Biopsy: light microscopy, mesangial proliferation; immunofluorescence, granular IgA and C3 in the mesangium; electron microscopy, mesangial deposits
  • 2PSGNASO after pharyngitis and anti-DNase B after skin infection; low C3 and normal C4, with C3 back to normal within about 8 weeks; Biopsy: light microscopy, diffuse endocapillary proliferation with neutrophils; immunofluorescence, granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall (starry sky); electron microscopy, subepithelial deposits (humps), only if atypical
  • 3Immune complex MPGNLow C3, often with low C4; hepatitis B and C serology, cryoglobulins, ANA, SPEP, and serum free light chains; Biopsy: light microscopy, mesangial proliferation and a split GBM (tram-track); immunofluorescence, granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall; electron microscopy, subendothelial deposits
  • 4C3 glomerulopathyLow C3 and normal C4; C3 nephritic factor and complement factor testing; Biopsy: light microscopy, mesangial proliferation and a split GBM (tram-track); immunofluorescence, granular C3 without IgG; electron microscopy, dense deposits within the GBM, or mesangial and subendothelial deposits

Biopsy panels

Each panel is one capillary loop in cross-section: the lumen and endothelium inside, the GBM as the dark ring, podocyte foot processes outside, and the mesangium at the left; dots are immune deposits, and the strip on the right shows the immunofluorescence pattern.

Treatment

General nephritic care, with BP control, ACEi or ARBs, and salt restriction, is on ; specific treatment depends on the cause and severity.

  • 1IgA nephropathyACEi or ARBs with a BP target below 130/80; SGLT2 inhibitors; corticosteroids if proteinuria stays above 1 g a day after 3 months of supportive care; immunosuppression for crescentic disease
  • 2PSGNSupportive: salt and fluid restriction, loop diuretics, and antihypertensives; penicillin to clear the streptococci, which does not change the nephritis; dialysis rarely
  • 3Immune complex MPGNTreat the cause, such as antivirals for hepatitis C or B; immunosuppression if idiopathic and progressive
  • 4C3 glomerulopathySupportive care if mild; MMF with corticosteroids if moderate or severe; complement inhibitors in selected patients

Note: C3 that stays low beyond about 8 weeks after presumed PSGN suggests C3 glomerulopathy or MPGN and calls for a biopsy.

  2. Hashmi MS, Pandey J. Nephritic Syndrome (Archived). 2023. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing. NBK562240

IgA nephropathy, PSGN, and MPGN: immune complex glomerulonephritis

IgA nephropathy, poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis cause nephritic syndrome through immune complexes and complement. Where the deposits lodge sets the pattern: in the mesangium in IgA nephropathy, beneath the epithelium in PSGN, and beneath the endothelium in MPGN, with C3 glomerulopathy driven by an overactive alternative pathway. IgA nephropathy flares within days of a mucosal infection with a normal C3, PSGN follows a streptococcal infection by weeks with a low C3 that recovers, and MPGN is chronic, often with mixed nephrotic features and a persistently low C3. Here, we review their mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider their relationships to the other glomerular diseases.

Key points

  • Mesangial and subendothelial deposits face the blood and inflame; PSGN is the exception, with subepithelial humps and intense inflammation.
  • IgA nephropathy, the most common primary GN worldwide, gives visible hematuria within 1–2 days of a mucosal infection, with mesangial IgA and a normal C3.
  • PSGN follows pharyngitis by 7–10 days or impetigo by 2–3 weeks, with a low C3 and normal C4 that recover within about 8 weeks.
  • MPGN follows chronic antigenemia such as hepatitis C or uncontrolled complement (C3 glomerulopathy), with a split GBM and a persistently low C3.

Pathophysiology

Immune complexes, from the blood or formed in place, lodge in the glomerulus, activate complement, and draw neutrophils while mesangial and endothelial cells multiply, causing hematuria, proteinuria, hypertension, and a falling GFR. In IgA nephropathy, complexes of galactose-deficient IgA1 and IgG against it lodge in the mesangium; in PSGN, streptococcal antigens and antibodies form subepithelial humps; and in MPGN, subendothelial complexes face the blood, while mesangial cells grow into the capillary wall and split the GBM. C3 is consumed by immune complexes in PSGN and immune complex MPGN, and by an overactive alternative pathway in C3 glomerulopathy. Mesangial and subendothelial deposits cause nephritic disease, whereas subepithelial deposits in MN mainly injure podocytes; PSGN is the exception.

Etiology and mechanisms

IgA nephropathy is the most common primary GN worldwide, most often in young men and East Asian people; galactose-deficient IgA1 is inherited, mucosal infections trigger flares, cirrhosis, celiac disease, IBD, and HIV cause secondary forms, and IgA vasculitis is its systemic form in children. PSGN is the most common cause of acute GN in children, following nephritogenic group A β-hemolytic streptococci by 7–10 days after pharyngitis or 2–3 weeks after impetigo, and other infections cause infection-related GN in adults. Immune complex MPGN follows chronic antigenemia: hepatitis C with cryoglobulinemia, hepatitis B, chronic infections such as endocarditis, autoimmune disease, and monoclonal gammopathy. C3 glomerulopathy follows C3 nephritic factor or mutations in factors H, I, or B, and includes dense deposit disease and C3 glomerulonephritis.

Clinical presentation and complications

IgA nephropathy causes visible hematuria within 1–2 days of a mucosal infection, often recurrent, or persistent microscopic hematuria and proteinuria found by chance, progressing slowly in many; IgA vasculitis adds purpura on the legs and buttocks, arthritis, and abdominal pain. PSGN causes cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, hypertension, and oliguria weeks after the infection, and most children recover fully. MPGN causes mixed nephrotic and nephritic features with progressive loss of GFR, with purpura, arthralgia, and neuropathy when cryoglobulins are present. MPGN and C3 glomerulopathy often reach nephrotic-range proteinuria, and IgA nephropathy occasionally does.

Diagnosis

All four give dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, and C3 and C4 separate them. IgA nephropathy has a normal C3, with mesangial proliferation, granular IgA and C3 in the mesangium, and mesangial deposits. PSGN is supported by ASO after pharyngitis or anti-DNase B after skin infection and a low C3 with a normal C4 that recovers within about 8 weeks; a biopsy, kept for atypical cases, shows diffuse endocapillary proliferation with neutrophils, granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall in a starry sky pattern, and subepithelial humps. Immune complex MPGN lowers C3, often with C4, prompting hepatitis B and C serology, cryoglobulins, ANA, SPEP, and serum free light chains, and shows mesangial proliferation and a tram-track GBM, granular IgG and C3 along the capillary wall, and subendothelial deposits. C3 glomerulopathy lowers C3 with a normal C4, prompting C3 nephritic factor and complement factor testing, and shows granular C3 without IgG, with dense deposits within the GBM or mesangial and subendothelial deposits.

Management

All are given BP control, ACEi or ARBs, and salt restriction. IgA nephropathy is treated with ACEi or ARBs to a BP below 130/80 and SGLT2 inhibitors, with corticosteroids if proteinuria stays above 1 g a day after 3 months of supportive care and immunosuppression for crescentic disease. PSGN is treated supportively with salt and fluid restriction, loop diuretics, and antihypertensives, and penicillin clears the streptococci without changing the nephritis. Immune complex MPGN is treated by its cause, such as antivirals for hepatitis C or B, and C3 glomerulopathy with supportive care, then MMF with corticosteroids or complement inhibitors if more severe. A C3 that stays low beyond about 8 weeks after presumed PSGN suggests C3 glomerulopathy or MPGN.

Relationships to other conditions

. These also cause nephritic syndrome, but anti-GBM disease is linear, ANCA vasculitis pauci-immune, and Alport syndrome genetic, all with a normal C3.

. Class IV lupus nephritis also has subendothelial deposits and a low C3, but with a low C4, anti-dsDNA, and full-house immunofluorescence.

Glomerular Disease: Comparison and Workup

Nephrotic syndrome

Podocyte injury lets albumin through the filter, so the urine carries heavy protein but few red cells, and the loss of albumin and other proteins drives edema, high lipids, clots, and infection.

  1. Podocyte injuryFoot processes efface and the slit diaphragm, the size barrier, is lost
  2. ProteinuriaAbove 3.5 g a day, or a UPCR above 300 mg/mmol
  3. Low albuminBelow 30 g/L, because the liver cannot replace what is lost
  4. EdemaLow oncotic pressure (underfill) and Na+ retained by the collecting duct, where filtered plasmin activates ENaC (overfill)
  5. Downstream effectsHigh lipids, clots, infection, and CKD

Complications

ProblemMechanismWhat is seen
EdemaLow oncotic pressure and primary Na+ retentionPeriorbital edema in children, leg and genital edema, ascites, and effusions
HyperlipidemiaThe liver makes more lipoproteins and clears fewerHigh cholesterol and triglycerides; lipiduria
ClotsAntithrombin III is lost in the urine while the liver makes more clotting factorsRenal vein thrombosis (most often in MN), DVT, and PE
InfectionIgG and complement are lostCellulitis and, in children, peritonitis from encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae
Other lossesVitamin D-binding and thyroxine-binding proteins are lostLow vitamin D, abnormal thyroid tests, and altered drug binding
KidneyOngoing injury and scarringAKI and CKD

Typical tests

  • UrineDipstick protein 3+ or more, with little blood; oval fat bodies, fatty casts, and Maltese crosses under polarized light
  • QuantityUPCR above 300 mg/mmol, or more than 3.5 g in 24 hours
  • BloodsLow albumin; high cholesterol and triglycerides; urea and creatinine normal or high

Note: The size barrier at the podocyte and slit diaphragm, not loss of the GBM's negative charge, is now thought to be the main defense against albuminuria.

Nephritic syndrome

Inflammation breaks the glomerular capillary wall, so red cells and protein leak into the urine, GFR falls, and the kidney retains Na+ and water, causing hypertension and edema.

  1. Glomerular injuryImmune complexes, antibodies against the GBM, ANCA, or an abnormal GBM
  2. A porous glomerulusBreaks in the GBM let red cells and protein through
  3. Hematuria and proteinuriaDysmorphic red cells and red cell casts; protein usually below 3.5 g a day
  4. GFR fallsInflamed, crowded capillaries filter less
  5. Na+ and water retainedHypertension, edema, and oliguria

RPGN and DPGN

  • RPGNA clinical syndrome: GFR lost over days to weeks, with crescents in more than half of glomeruli; any nephritic cause can reach it
  • Type I: linearAnti-GBM disease, on
  • Type II: granularImmune complex disease: lupus nephritis, PSGN, IgA nephropathy, and MPGN
  • Type III: pauci-immuneANCA vasculitis: GPA, MPA, and EGPA
  • DPGNA biopsy pattern, not a syndrome: endocapillary proliferation in more than half of glomeruli, typical of lupus nephritis class IV, and also seen in PSGN and MPGN

Complications

ProblemMechanismWhat is seen
HypertensionNa+ and water retention, with renin from ischemic glomeruliHypertension that can be hard to control; hypertensive encephalopathy in children with PSGN
Volume overloadLow GFR with Na+ retentionEdema and pulmonary edema
Falling kidney functionInflammation, then crescents and scarringAKI, often oliguric in RPGN, then CKD
LungsThe same antibodies attack alveolar capillariesPulmonary hemorrhage in anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis

Typical tests

  • UrineVisible (cola-colored) or microscopic hematuria with dysmorphic red cells, at least 1 in 20 being an acanthocyte; red cell casts; protein, usually below 3.5 g a day
  • BloodsUrea and creatinine increased; K+ may be high; C3 low or normal by cause

Note: Proteinuria can exceed 3.5 g a day in nephritic disease, especially in MPGN, lupus nephritis, and some IgA nephropathy, so the 3.5 g threshold separates the syndromes only roughly.

Comparison

The nephrotic syndromes injure the podocyte and leak protein, whereas the nephritic syndromes inflame the capillary wall and leak blood; complement then narrows the nephritic causes.

FeatureNephroticNephritic
ProteinuriaHigh above 3.5 g a dayVariable usually below 3.5 g a day
HematuriaNormal little or noneHigh dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts
SedimentOval fat bodies and fatty castsRed cell casts
AlbuminLow below 30 g/LVariable mildly low
LipidsHighNormal
EdemaMarkedMild, periorbital
BPNormal oftenHigh
GFRNormal at firstLow
Main sitePodocyteCapillary wall, mesangium, and GBM
Causes; ; lupus nephritis class V; ; lupus nephritis classes III and IV

Complement in nephritic syndrome

C3C4Causes
LowLowLupus nephritis, immune complex MPGN, and cryoglobulinemia
LowNormalPSGN, which recovers within about 8 weeks, and C3 glomerulopathy, which does not
NormalNormalIgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, and Alport syndrome

Diagnosis

  1. 1. Confirm and quantifyUACR or UPCR on a spot sample, repeated to exclude transient or orthostatic proteinuria; 24-hour protein if needed
  2. 2. Urine microscopyDysmorphic red cells and red cell casts (nephritic), or fatty casts and oval fat bodies (nephrotic)
  3. 3. BloodsElectrolytes, urea, and creatinine; albumin; lipid panel; FBC; HbA1c
  4. 4. Serology by syndromeChosen from the table below
  5. 5. LungsChest imaging and oxygen saturation if anti-GBM disease or ANCA vasculitis is possible
  6. 6. BiopsyKidney ultrasound first; then light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy

Is the proteinuria persistent?

  • Fever, heavy exercise, or emotional stressTransient proteinuria, which clears on a repeat sample and needs no workup
  • Protein in a teenager or young adult, absent in first-morning urineOrthostatic (postural) proteinuria: high when upright and normal when lying down; affects 2–5% of adolescents and is uncommon after 30
  • Confirming orthostatic proteinuriaA first-morning UPCR, which is normal (below about 20 mg/mmol), and a daytime UPCR, which is high; a normal first-morning sample needs no further renal workup
  • Its courseBenign, with yearly review and no biopsy or treatment; left renal vein entrapment when upright is one proposed mechanism
  • Hematuria, an active sediment, hypertension, a low GFR, low complement, or signs of vasculitisThe full workup above, whatever the posture

Serology

If there isObtain
Nephrotic syndrome in an adultAnti-PLA2R antibodies; HbA1c; SPEP, UPEP, and serum free light chains; hepatitis B and C and HIV serology; ANA
Nephritic syndromeC3 and C4; ANA and anti-dsDNA; ANCA (PR3 and MPO); anti-GBM antibodies; hepatitis B and C serology; cryoglobulins
A recent sore throat or skin infectionASO and anti-DNase B
RPGN or hemoptysisAnti-GBM antibodies and ANCA urgently, with chest imaging

Each panel is one capillary loop in cross-section: the lumen and endothelium inside, the GBM as the dark ring, podocyte foot processes outside, and the mesangium at the left; dots are immune deposits, and the strip on the right shows the immunofluorescence pattern.

Note: Deposits are named by where they sit (subepithelial, subendothelial, or mesangial), and immunofluorescence by its pattern (granular or linear), its content, and its site, so the same finding is always described the same way.

Lupus nephritis

Lupus nephritis affects about 40% of people with SLE, usually within 5 years of diagnosis: anti-dsDNA immune complexes deposit in the mesangium, beneath the endothelium, or beneath the epithelium, and where they lodge sets the class and whether it is nephritic or nephrotic.

ClassPatternPresentationTreatment
I and IIMinimal or proliferative mesangial depositsMild hematuria or proteinuriaHydroxychloroquine; usually no immunosuppression
IIIFocal proliferative: endocapillary proliferation in fewer than 50% of glomeruli; subendothelial depositsNephriticCorticosteroids with MMF or cyclophosphamide
IVDiffuse proliferative (DPGN): 50% or more of glomeruli; subendothelial deposits and wire loopsNephritic; the most common and severe classCorticosteroids with MMF or cyclophosphamide
VMembranous: subepithelial depositsNephroticMMF with corticosteroids; ACEi or ARBs
VIAdvanced sclerosis of more than 90% of glomeruliCKDDialysis or a transplant
  • TestsLow C3 and C4; anti-dsDNA; granular IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q on immunofluorescence (full house)
  • Every classHydroxychloroquine, which reduces flares, with yearly eye examinations
  • Biopsy whenProtein above 0.5 g a day, an active sediment, or a rising creatinine in SLE

Note: Classes can overlap or change, and class V can coexist with class III or IV, so a lupus biopsy can show both nephrotic and nephritic features.

Treatment

Every glomerular disease is treated by slowing protein loss and controlling pressure and volume, with immunosuppression only where the disease calls for it, as on its own page.

Prevent infectionPneumococcal and influenza vaccination, particularly with immunosuppression
Treat the causeImmunosuppression, antivirals, or chemotherapy, as on each disease page

Review article

Glomerular disease: nephrotic and nephritic syndromes, their workup, and shared treatment

Glomerular diseases present as one of two syndromes. In nephrotic syndrome, podocyte injury lets albumin through the size barrier, causing proteinuria above 3.5 g a day, low albumin, edema, high lipids, clots, and infection; in nephritic syndrome, inflammation breaks the capillary wall, causing dysmorphic hematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, and a falling GFR, sometimes as rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with crescents. Urine microscopy, complement, and targeted serology narrow the cause, and a biopsy read by light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy confirms it. Treatment slows protein loss and controls pressure and volume, adding immunosuppression where needed. Here, we review both syndromes, their comparison, the workup and biopsy findings, lupus nephritis, and shared treatment.

Key points

  • Nephrotic syndrome comes from podocyte injury (proteinuria above 3.5 g a day, albumin below 30 g/L, edema, and hyperlipidemia), and nephritic syndrome from inflammation of the capillary wall (dysmorphic hematuria, red cell casts, hypertension, and a falling GFR).
  • Loss of antithrombin III causes clots, especially renal vein thrombosis in MN, and loss of IgG causes infection.
  • RPGN is linear (anti-GBM disease), granular (immune complex disease), or pauci-immune (ANCA vasculitis); DPGN is a biopsy pattern, typical of lupus class IV.
  • Low C3 with low C4 suggests lupus nephritis, immune complex MPGN, or cryoglobulinemia; low C3 with normal C4 suggests PSGN or C3 glomerulopathy.
  • ACEi or ARBs, SGLT2 inhibitors, BP below 130/80, salt restriction, diuretics, and statins treat every glomerular disease.

Nephrotic syndrome

Podocyte injury effaces the foot processes and removes the slit diaphragm, the size barrier that is now thought to be the main defense against albuminuria, so protein above 3.5 g a day, or a UPCR above 300 mg/mmol, leaks with few red cells, and albumin falls below 30 g/L. Edema follows low oncotic pressure and primary Na+ retention in the collecting duct, where filtered plasmin activates ENaC. The liver makes more lipoproteins and clears fewer, causing high cholesterol and triglycerides with lipiduria; antithrombin III is lost while clotting factors increase, causing renal vein thrombosis, most often in MN, DVT, and PE; IgG and complement are lost, causing cellulitis and, in children, peritonitis from encapsulated bacteria; and the loss of vitamin D-binding and thyroxine-binding proteins lowers vitamin D and alters thyroid tests and drug binding, with AKI and CKD over time. The urine shows heavy dipstick protein with little blood, oval fat bodies, fatty casts, and Maltese crosses.

Nephritic syndrome

Immune complexes, antibodies against the GBM, ANCA, or an abnormal GBM break the capillary wall, so dysmorphic red cells, at least 1 in 20 being an acanthocyte, red cell casts, and protein, usually below 3.5 g a day, enter the urine, GFR falls, and Na+ and water retention causes hypertension, edema, and oliguria. Hypertension can be hard to control and causes encephalopathy in some children with PSGN, and pulmonary hemorrhage accompanies anti-GBM disease and ANCA vasculitis. RPGN, the loss of GFR over days to weeks with crescents in more than half of glomeruli, is linear in anti-GBM disease (type I), granular in immune complex disease (type II), and pauci-immune in ANCA vasculitis (type III), whereas DPGN is a biopsy pattern of endocapillary proliferation in more than half of glomeruli, typical of lupus class IV. Proteinuria can exceed 3.5 g a day in MPGN, lupus nephritis, and some IgA nephropathy.

Comparison

Nephrotic syndrome has heavy proteinuria with fatty casts, low albumin, high lipids, marked edema, and often normal BP and GFR, whereas nephritic syndrome has dysmorphic hematuria and red cell casts, hypertension, mild periorbital edema, and a low GFR. In nephritic syndrome, low C3 and C4 suggest lupus nephritis, immune complex MPGN, or cryoglobulinemia; a low C3 with a normal C4 suggests PSGN, which recovers within about 8 weeks, or C3 glomerulopathy; and a normal C3 suggests IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease, ANCA vasculitis, or Alport syndrome.

Diagnosis

Proteinuria is first shown to be persistent. Transient proteinuria accompanies fever, heavy exercise, or emotional stress and clears on a repeat sample. Orthostatic, or postural, proteinuria is high when the patient is upright and normal when lying down; it affects 2–5% of adolescents, is uncommon after 30, and is confirmed by a normal first-morning UPCR, below about 20 mg/mmol, with a high daytime UPCR. It is benign, needs only yearly review, and calls for no biopsy or treatment; left renal vein entrapment in the upright position is one proposed mechanism. Hematuria, an active sediment, hypertension, a low GFR, low complement, or signs of vasculitis call for the full workup whatever the posture.

The workup then quantifies protein with a UACR or UPCR, examines the urine sediment, checks electrolytes, urea, creatinine, albumin, lipids, FBC, and HbA1c, and then chooses serology by syndrome: anti-PLA2R antibodies, HbA1c, SPEP, UPEP, serum free light chains, hepatitis B and C and HIV serology, and ANA in adult nephrotic syndrome; C3 and C4, ANA and anti-dsDNA, ANCA, anti-GBM antibodies, hepatitis serology, and cryoglobulins in nephritic syndrome; ASO and anti-DNase B after a streptococcal infection; and urgent anti-GBM antibodies, ANCA, and chest imaging in RPGN. A kidney ultrasound precedes the biopsy, which is described consistently, with deposits named by where they sit and immunofluorescence by its pattern, content, and site.

Lupus nephritis

Lupus nephritis affects about 40% of people with SLE, usually within 5 years, as anti-dsDNA immune complexes deposit in the glomerulus, with low C3 and C4, anti-dsDNA, and full-house immunofluorescence. Classes I and II are mesangial and mild; class III is focal and class IV diffuse proliferative, with subendothelial deposits and wire loops, presenting as nephritic disease and treated with corticosteroids and MMF or cyclophosphamide; class V is membranous and nephrotic, treated with MMF, corticosteroids, and RAAS blockade; and class VI is sclerosed, needing dialysis or a transplant. Every class receives hydroxychloroquine, and classes can overlap or change.

Management

Every glomerular disease is treated with ACEi or ARBs at the highest tolerated dose and SGLT2 inhibitors to lower proteinuria and glomerular pressure, a BP target below 130/80, salt restriction and loop diuretics for edema, and statins, with anticoagulation after a clot or in MN with a very low albumin and vaccination against pneumococcus and influenza. Immunosuppression, antivirals, or chemotherapy treat the cause, and dialysis or a transplant replaces kidney function, though FSGS, IgA nephropathy, C3 glomerulopathy, and MN can recur.

Relationships to other conditions

and . Each disease review covers its own mechanism, causes, biopsy, and treatment; this review holds what they share.

. Glomerular disease is one of the four compartments of intrarenal AKI, recognized by red cell casts and protein, and RPGN is among its most urgent causes.

Thrombotic Microangiopathy

Pathophysiology

Injury to the endothelium of small vessels lets platelets and fibrin build thrombi on the wall, which use up platelets, shear passing red cells into schistocytes, and starve the kidney, brain, and other organs of blood.

  1. Endothelial injuryUncleaved von Willebrand factor strings, Shiga toxin, uncontrolled complement, or pressure and drugs
  2. Platelet thrombiPlatelets stick to the exposed wall and to VWF; fibrin joins them
  3. ThrombocytopeniaPlatelets are used up in the thrombi
  4. HemolysisRed cells are sheared on the strands: schistocytes, high LDH, low haptoglobin, and a negative direct Coombs test
  5. IschemiaGlomerular capillaries and arterioles block, causing AKI, and the brain, heart, and gut suffer too

What happens in the small vessels

  • ASwollen endotheliumInjured endothelial cells swell and detach, narrowing the capillary
  • BPlatelet-fibrin thrombiThrombi form on the exposed wall and block the lumen
  • CSchistocytesRed cells forced past the strands are cut into fragments
  • DOnion-skin arteriolesThe arteriolar wall thickens in layers around a narrow lumen, especially in malignant hypertension and scleroderma
  • EDouble contoursNew basement membrane forms beneath the swollen endothelium, so the GBM looks doubled

Note: Unlike DIC, TMA leaves PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen normal, because the clots are made of platelets and are not consuming clotting factors.

Etiology

  • 1TTPADAMTS13 activity below 10%, so ultra-large VWF multimers stay uncleaved and trap platelets; acquired through an autoantibody, triggered by HIV, pregnancy, estrogen, and some drugs, or congenital, which waits for a trigger; the brain is affected more than the kidney
  • 2STEC-HUSShiga toxin from E. coli (O157:H7 and other serotypes), rarely Shigella dysenteriae, binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelium; mostly children under 5, after bloody diarrhea from undercooked beef or contaminated food
  • 3Complement-mediated HUSMutations in factor H, I, or B, or anti-factor H antibodies, leave the alternative pathway uncontrolled on the endothelium, often after a trigger such as infection or pregnancy; the vascular counterpart of C3 glomerulopathy, on
  • 4Secondary TMAMalignant hypertension; pregnancy, as in preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome; drugs (gemcitabine, mitomycin C, CNIs, VEGF inhibitors, and quinine); scleroderma renal crisis; and APS
  • 5Atheroembolic diseaseNot a true TMA, but in the same vessels: cholesterol crystals break off aortic plaque after angiography, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation and lodge in small renal arteries

Note: HELLP syndrome is a pregnancy TMA in which the liver bears much of the injury, as on Liver Disease in Pregnancy.

Symptoms and complications

Every TMA combines microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury; which organ suffers most points to the cause.

  • TTP (1)Neurologic signs (headache, confusion, focal deficits, and seizures) and abdominal pain; fever; petechiae; the kidney is involved less often; a high troponin predicts a worse outcome
  • STEC-HUS (2)Painful bloody diarrhea, then AKI about 5–13 days later, with oliguria and fluid overload; about half need dialysis; the gut side is on Acute Diarrhea
  • Complement-mediated HUS (3)Fatigue and pallor, then AKI; relapses, and about half reach dialysis dependence if untreated
  • Malignant hypertension (4)Very high BP with headache, retinal hemorrhages and papilledema, and encephalopathy
  • Scleroderma renal crisis (4)Sudden hypertension and AKI in systemic sclerosis, often after high-dose corticosteroids
  • Atheroembolic disease (5)AKI days to weeks after a procedure, with livedo reticularis and blue toes

Note: The classic TTP pentad of fever, neurologic signs, AKI, anemia, and thrombocytopenia is complete in under 10%, so waiting for all five delays treatment.

Diagnosis

Hemolysis with schistocytes and low platelets, a negative direct Coombs test, and normal clotting tests establish TMA; ADAMTS13, stool tests, and complement then separate the causes, and the AKI workup is on .

  1. Confirm TMAFBC and blood film for schistocytes; LDH, haptoglobin, unconjugated bilirubin, and reticulocytes
  2. Exclude look-alikesNegative direct Coombs test; normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen (not DIC)
  3. Organ injuryCreatinine, urinalysis for blood and protein, and troponin
  4. Find the causeADAMTS13 activity, sent before plasma is given
  • 1TTPADAMTS13 activity below 10%, with an inhibitor in acquired TTP; the PLASMIC score estimates the risk before the result returns, giving 1 point each for platelets below 30 × 10⁹/L, hemolysis (reticulocytes above 2.5%, undetectable haptoglobin, or unconjugated bilirubin above 34 µmol/L), no cancer treated in the past 12 months, no transplant, MCV below 90 fL, INR below 1.5, and creatinine below 177 µmol/L; 6–7 points is high risk, 5 intermediate, and 0–4 low
  • 2STEC-HUSStool culture and Shiga toxin testing whenever there is diarrhea, which can be negative once the toxin is cleared
  • 3Complement-mediated HUSADAMTS13 above 10%, no Shiga toxin, and no secondary cause; C3 is low in some; complement genetics and anti-factor H antibodies
  • 4Secondary TMABP and fundoscopy; pregnancy test and liver tests; the drug list; antiphospholipid antibodies; scleroderma antibodies
  • 5Atheroembolic diseaseEosinophilia, eosinophiluria, and low complement; biopsy shows cholesterol clefts in small arteries

Biopsy

Biopsy: light microscopy, thrombi in glomerular capillaries and arterioles, swollen endothelium, mesangiolysis, and onion-skin arterioles; immunofluorescence, negative, or fibrin in thrombi; electron microscopy, a widened subendothelial space without deposits, and double contours of the GBM. A biopsy is often unsafe while platelets are low, so the diagnosis usually rests on the blood.

Each panel is one capillary loop in cross-section: the lumen and endothelium inside, the GBM as the dark ring, podocyte foot processes outside, and the mesangium at the left; dots are immune deposits, and the strip on the right shows the immunofluorescence pattern.

Treatment

TMA is treated by its cause, but plasma exchange starts as soon as TTP is possible, without waiting for ADAMTS13, because untreated TTP is often fatal.

  • 1TTPDaily plasma exchange, which removes the autoantibody and VWF multimers and replaces ADAMTS13; corticosteroids; caplacizumab, which blocks VWF binding to platelets; rituximab; platelet transfusion only for bleeding
  • 2STEC-HUSSupportive: fluids, red cell transfusion as needed, and dialysis; avoid ABX and antimotility drugs, which increase toxin exposure; ABX if Shigella dysenteriae or Streptococcus pneumoniae is the cause
  • 3Complement-mediated HUSComplement inhibition with eculizumab, or ravulizumab, which lasts longer and is given every 4–8 weeks, after meningococcal vaccination; plasma exchange only as a second-line or bridging treatment
  • 4Secondary TMALower BP in a controlled way in malignant hypertension; deliver the baby in preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome; stop the drug; give ACEi in scleroderma renal crisis and keep them going even if creatinine rises or dialysis is needed, though they are not given beforehand to prevent it; anticoagulate in APS
  • 5Atheroembolic diseaseNo specific treatment: statins, BP control, avoiding further procedures and, where possible, anticoagulation

Note: Platelet transfusion in TTP can add fuel to the thrombi, so it is kept for bleeding or procedures.

Review article

Thrombotic microangiopathy: endothelial injury, platelet thrombi, and mechanical hemolysis

Thrombotic microangiopathy is endothelial injury in small vessels that builds platelet and fibrin thrombi, causing thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, and ischemia of the kidney, brain, and other organs, with normal clotting tests that separate it from DIC. TTP follows ADAMTS13 deficiency and affects mainly the brain; STEC-HUS follows Shiga toxin and affects children after bloody diarrhea; complement-mediated HUS follows uncontrolled alternative complement; and secondary TMA follows malignant hypertension, pregnancy, drugs, scleroderma, or antiphospholipid antibodies. Plasma exchange treats TTP, supportive care STEC-HUS, and complement inhibition complement-mediated HUS. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider its relationships to other conditions.

Key points

  • Endothelial injury builds platelet-fibrin thrombi that consume platelets, shear red cells into schistocytes, and block glomerular capillaries and arterioles, with normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen.
  • TTP follows ADAMTS13 activity below 10%, STEC-HUS follows Shiga toxin binding Gb3, and complement-mediated HUS follows uncontrolled alternative complement.
  • The TTP pentad is complete in under 10%; the PLASMIC score estimates severe ADAMTS13 deficiency before the result returns.
  • Plasma exchange with corticosteroids, caplacizumab, and rituximab treats TTP; STEC-HUS is supportive, without ABX or antimotility drugs; eculizumab treats complement-mediated HUS.

Pathophysiology

Endothelial injury in small vessels, from uncleaved von Willebrand factor strings, Shiga toxin, uncontrolled complement, or pressure and drugs, lets platelets adhere and fibrin join them, forming thrombi on swollen, detaching endothelium. Platelets are consumed, red cells forced past the strands are cut into schistocytes, raising LDH and lowering haptoglobin with a negative direct Coombs test, and blocked glomerular capillaries and arterioles cause AKI, while the brain, heart, and gut also suffer. Arterioles thicken in layers (onion-skin), especially in malignant hypertension and scleroderma, and new basement membrane beneath the swollen endothelium doubles the contour of the GBM. Unlike DIC, TMA leaves PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen normal.

Etiology and mechanisms

In TTP, ADAMTS13 activity below 10% leaves ultra-large VWF multimers uncleaved; it is acquired through an autoantibody, triggered by HIV, pregnancy, estrogen, or drugs, or congenital and unmasked by a trigger, and it affects the brain more than the kidney. In STEC-HUS, Shiga toxin from E. coli, rarely Shigella dysenteriae, binds Gb3 on glomerular endothelium, mostly in children under 5 after bloody diarrhea from contaminated food. In complement-mediated HUS, mutations in factor H, I, or B, or anti-factor H antibodies, leave the alternative pathway uncontrolled, often after infection or pregnancy, making it the vascular counterpart of C3 glomerulopathy. Secondary TMA follows malignant hypertension, preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome, drugs (gemcitabine, mitomycin C, CNIs, VEGF inhibitors, and quinine), scleroderma renal crisis, and APS. Atheroembolic disease, not a true TMA, follows cholesterol crystals released from aortic plaque after angiography, vascular surgery, or anticoagulation; HELLP syndrome is a pregnancy TMA in which the liver bears much of the injury.

Clinical presentation and complications

Every TMA combines microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and organ injury. TTP causes neurologic signs, abdominal pain, fever, and petechiae, involves the kidney less often, and carries a worse outcome with a high troponin; its classic pentad is complete in under 10%. STEC-HUS causes painful bloody diarrhea, then AKI about 5–13 days later with oliguria and fluid overload, and about half need dialysis. Complement-mediated HUS causes fatigue and pallor, then AKI, relapses, and dialysis dependence in about half if untreated. Malignant hypertension causes headache, retinal hemorrhages, papilledema, and encephalopathy; scleroderma renal crisis causes sudden hypertension and AKI, often after high-dose corticosteroids; and atheroemboli cause AKI days to weeks after a procedure, with livedo reticularis and blue toes.

Diagnosis

A blood film with schistocytes, high LDH and unconjugated bilirubin, low haptoglobin, a high reticulocyte count, low platelets, a negative direct Coombs test, and normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen establish TMA, with creatinine, urinalysis, and troponin for organ injury. ADAMTS13 activity, sent before plasma, is below 10% in TTP, and the PLASMIC score estimates that risk from platelets below 30 × 10⁹/L, hemolysis, no cancer treated in the past 12 months, no transplant, MCV below 90 fL, INR below 1.5, and creatinine below 177 µmol/L, with 6–7 points high risk. Stool culture and Shiga toxin testing identify STEC-HUS; complement-mediated HUS is diagnosed when ADAMTS13 is above 10% without Shiga toxin or a secondary cause, sometimes with a low C3, supported by complement genetics and anti-factor H antibodies; and BP, fundoscopy, pregnancy and liver tests, the drug list, and antiphospholipid and scleroderma antibodies find secondary causes. Atheroemboli give eosinophilia, eosinophiluria, low complement, and cholesterol clefts. A biopsy, often unsafe with low platelets, shows thrombi in capillaries and arterioles, swollen endothelium, mesangiolysis, and onion-skin arterioles, negative immunofluorescence or fibrin, and a widened subendothelial space without deposits with double contours of the GBM.

Management

Plasma exchange starts as soon as TTP is possible, removing the autoantibody and VWF multimers and replacing ADAMTS13, with corticosteroids, caplacizumab, which blocks VWF binding to platelets, and rituximab, and platelets are transfused only for bleeding. STEC-HUS is managed supportively with fluids, transfusion, and dialysis, avoiding ABX and antimotility drugs, which increase toxin exposure, except when Shigella dysenteriae or Streptococcus pneumoniae is the cause. Complement-mediated HUS is treated with eculizumab or ravulizumab after meningococcal vaccination, with plasma exchange as a second-line or bridging treatment. Secondary TMA is treated by controlled lowering of BP, delivery, stopping the drug, ACEi in scleroderma renal crisis continued even if creatinine rises or dialysis is needed, or anticoagulation in APS, and atheroembolic disease with statins, BP control, and avoiding further procedures.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both follow uncontrolled alternative complement, but complement-mediated HUS injures the endothelium and forms thrombi, whereas C3 glomerulopathy deposits C3 in the glomerulus.

. Both cause hypertension and AKI from the kidney's vessels, but TMA blocks the smallest vessels with thrombi and hemolysis, whereas renal artery disease narrows or blocks the main artery.

Renal Artery Disease

Pathophysiology

A narrowed or blocked renal artery lowers the pressure reaching the kidney, which answers with renin: angiotensin II holds GFR up by constricting the efferent arteriole and raises systemic BP, so the kidney's filtration comes to depend on angiotensin II.

  1. Low perfusion pressureBeyond a stenosis or occlusion
  2. Renin risesThe juxtaglomerular cells sense low pressure
  3. Angiotensin IIConstricts the efferent arteriole, holding GFR; constricts vessels and releases aldosterone, raising BP
  4. Renovascular hypertensionRenin-dependent when one kidney is narrowed, volume-dependent when both are or the only kidney is
  5. Ischemic nephropathyLong-standing low flow shrinks and scars the kidney

How a stenosis raises BP

  • AStenosisPressure falls beyond a narrowing of about 70% or more, or a pressure gradient of 20 mmHg or more across it
  • BReninThe kidney beyond the stenosis releases renin
  • CEfferent constrictionAngiotensin II holds GFR up, so blocking it with ACEi or ARBs drops GFR in that kidney
  • DSystemic effectsVasoconstriction and aldosterone raise BP and retain Na+ (and lose K+)
  • EPressure natriuresisWith one kidney narrowed (two-kidney, one-clip), the other excretes the extra Na+, so the hypertension is renin-dependent; with both narrowed, or a single kidney (one-kidney, one-clip), Na+ is retained and the hypertension is volume-dependent

Note: Volume-dependent hypertension from bilateral stenosis explains flash pulmonary edema and the sharp fall in GFR when ACEi or ARBs are started.

Etiology

  • Stenosis
  • 1Atherosclerotic RASAbout 90% of RAS: at the ostium and proximal 2 cm, often extending from aortic plaque; older adults with smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, and other vascular disease
  • 2FMDA nonatherosclerotic disease of the arterial wall in the mid and distal artery, with a string-of-beads appearance; about 90% are women, often young; can also cause aneurysms, dissection, and carotid disease
  • Acute occlusion (renal infarction)
  • 3EmbolismUp to 55% of renal infarction, mostly from the heart, with A-fib in 64–75%; segmental arteries are end-arteries, so a wedge of kidney dies
  • 4ThrombosisOn an atherosclerotic plaque, after trauma, or in a hypercoagulable state
  • 5DissectionSpontaneous, with FMD, or extending from an aortic dissection

Note: RAS is found in under 1% of mild hypertension but 10–40% of acute, severe, or resistant hypertension, and about 75% is unilateral.

Symptoms and complications

Stenosis causes hypertension and slowly declining function, often without symptoms, whereas acute occlusion causes sudden flank pain that is easily mistaken for a stone.

  • Clues to RAS (1, 2)Hypertension that is resistant to 3 or more drugs, begins before 30 (FMD) or after 55 (atherosclerosis), or worsens suddenly; an abdominal bruit; creatinine rising by more than 30% after starting ACEi or ARBs; recurrent flash pulmonary edema; kidneys of unequal size; low K+ from secondary hyperaldosteronism
  • Ischemic nephropathy (1)Progressive CKD with a bland sediment and little protein
  • FMD beyond the kidney (2)Headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and stroke or dissection from carotid disease
  • Renal infarction (3–5)Sudden flank or abdominal pain, nausea, hematuria, and fever; livedo or blue toes in some; under half are diagnosed within 2 days

Diagnosis

Imaging finds the lesion; the AKI workup is on , and a stenosis is treated only if it is likely causing the problem.

  • +Any renal artery diseaseCreatinine and eGFR; urinalysis, which is bland or shows mild protein, with no red cell casts; renin and aldosterone, often high
  • 1, 2StenosisDuplex ultrasound first, which measures velocity and is operator-dependent; CT angiography or MRA; catheter angiography as the gold standard and before intervention
  • 2FMDString of beads in the mid and distal artery on CT angiography; image the carotid and other arteries once found
  • 3–5Renal infarctionLDH 4–5 times normal with normal AST and ALT; leukocytosis and high CRP; hematuria; contrast CT shows wedge-shaped infarcts; ECG and echocardiography for an embolic source, and thrombophilia testing if none is found

Treatment

Medical therapy is the foundation; revascularization is kept for FMD and for selected atherosclerotic disease.

  • 1Atherosclerotic RASACEi or ARBs, watching creatinine, or CCBs if they cannot be used; statins, antiplatelet therapy, and stopping smoking; stenting did not improve outcomes over medical therapy in trials (CORAL), so it is kept for recurrent flash pulmonary edema, rapidly declining function, or truly resistant hypertension
  • 2FMDAngioplasty without a stent, which cures hypertension in about 36–46%, best when younger and with a shorter history; antiplatelet therapy; BP control
  • 3EmbolismAnticoagulation; catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy in selected patients if the kidney is still viable; treat the source, such as A-fib
  • 4ThrombosisAnticoagulation, with revascularization in selected patients
  • 5DissectionAnticoagulation for 3–6 months once hemorrhage is excluded; stenting if flow is threatened

Note: ACEi and ARBs are still used in unilateral RAS, but creatinine is checked after starting them, and a rise of more than 30% suggests bilateral disease or a single kidney.

Review article

Renal artery disease: renovascular hypertension, ischemic nephropathy, and renal infarction

Renal artery disease lowers the pressure reaching the kidney, which releases renin; angiotensin II then holds GFR up by constricting the efferent arteriole and raises systemic blood pressure. Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis, at the ostium in older adults, and fibromuscular dysplasia, beaded in the mid artery of younger women, cause renovascular hypertension and ischemic nephropathy, whereas embolism, thrombosis, and dissection cause renal infarction with sudden flank pain and a very high LDH. Imaging finds the lesion; medical therapy treats atherosclerotic stenosis, angioplasty treats fibromuscular dysplasia, and anticoagulation treats infarction. Here, we review their mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider their relationships to other conditions.

Key points

  • Low perfusion raises renin; angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole to hold GFR, so ACEi and ARBs drop GFR beyond a stenosis.
  • Unilateral stenosis causes renin-dependent hypertension (two-kidney, one-clip); bilateral stenosis or a single kidney causes volume-dependent hypertension and flash pulmonary edema.
  • Atherosclerosis causes about 90% of RAS, at the ostium; FMD affects mostly young women, with a string of beads in the mid and distal artery.
  • Renal infarction, mostly embolic from A-fib, gives sudden flank pain, hematuria, and an LDH 4–5 times normal with normal transaminases.
  • Medical therapy is first for atherosclerotic RAS, as stenting did not improve outcomes in CORAL; angioplasty without a stent treats FMD.

Pathophysiology

Beyond a narrowing of about 70% or more, or an occlusion, perfusion pressure falls and the juxtaglomerular cells release renin. Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole, holding GFR up, so ACEi or ARBs drop GFR in that kidney, and it constricts vessels and releases aldosterone, raising BP, retaining Na+, and losing K+. With one kidney narrowed (two-kidney, one-clip), the other excretes the extra Na+ by pressure natriuresis and the hypertension is renin-dependent; with both narrowed, or a single kidney (one-kidney, one-clip), Na+ is retained and the hypertension is volume-dependent, which explains flash pulmonary edema. Long-standing low flow shrinks and scars the kidney as ischemic nephropathy.

Etiology and mechanisms

Atherosclerosis causes about 90% of RAS, at the ostium and proximal 2 cm, in older adults with smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, and other vascular disease. FMD, a nonatherosclerotic disease of the arterial wall, affects the mid and distal artery with a string-of-beads appearance, about 90% of patients being women, and can also cause aneurysms, dissection, and carotid disease. RAS is found in under 1% of mild hypertension but 10–40% of acute, severe, or resistant hypertension, and about 75% is unilateral. Renal infarction follows embolism, up to 55% of cases, mostly from the heart with A-fib in 64–75%, thrombosis on plaque, after trauma, or in a hypercoagulable state, and dissection, spontaneous, with FMD, or from the aorta; segmental arteries are end-arteries, so a wedge of kidney dies.

Clinical presentation and complications

RAS is suggested by hypertension resistant to 3 or more drugs, beginning before 30 (FMD) or after 55 (atherosclerosis), or worsening suddenly, an abdominal bruit, creatinine rising by more than 30% after starting ACEi or ARBs, recurrent flash pulmonary edema, kidneys of unequal size, and low K+. Ischemic nephropathy causes progressive CKD with a bland sediment and little protein, and FMD can cause headache, pulsatile tinnitus, and stroke from carotid disease. Renal infarction causes sudden flank or abdominal pain, nausea, hematuria, and fever, with livedo or blue toes in some, and fewer than half are diagnosed within 2 days.

Diagnosis

Creatinine, eGFR, and a bland urinalysis with mild protein are accompanied by often high renin and aldosterone. Stenosis is found by duplex ultrasound, which is operator-dependent, then CT angiography or MRA, with catheter angiography as the gold standard and before intervention; FMD shows a string of beads and prompts imaging of the carotid and other arteries. Renal infarction raises LDH 4–5 times with normal transaminases, with leukocytosis, a high CRP, and hematuria, and contrast CT shows wedge-shaped infarcts, with ECG and echocardiography for an embolic source and thrombophilia testing if none is found.

Management

Atherosclerotic RAS is treated with ACEi or ARBs, watching creatinine, or CCBs, with statins, antiplatelet therapy, and stopping smoking; stenting did not improve outcomes over medical therapy in CORAL, so it is kept for recurrent flash pulmonary edema, rapidly declining function, or truly resistant hypertension. FMD is treated by angioplasty without a stent, which cures hypertension in about 36–46%, best when younger and with a shorter history, with antiplatelet therapy and BP control. Embolism is treated with anticoagulation, catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy in selected patients with a viable kidney, and treatment of the source; thrombosis with anticoagulation and selected revascularization; and dissection with anticoagulation for 3–6 months once hemorrhage is excluded, or stenting if flow is threatened.

Relationships to other conditions

. RAS is a prerenal cause: the tubules work and the urine is bland, and the AKI that follows ACEi or ARBs reverses when they are stopped.

. RAS causes secondary hyperaldosteronism with high renin, whereas primary hyperaldosteronism suppresses renin; both cause hypertension with low K+.

Renal Vein Thrombosis

Pathophysiology

A clot in the renal vein, formed by one or more parts of Virchow triad, blocks outflow from the kidney, which swells and can infarct; a sudden clot causes pain and AKI, whereas a slow one is often silent as collateral veins open.

  1. Virchow triadHypercoagulability (most often nephrotic syndrome), endothelial injury, or stasis
  2. Clot in the renal veinLeft more often than right, because the left vein is longer
  3. Venous congestionThe kidney swells and its glomeruli leak more protein
  4. InfarctionSudden, complete occlusion causes hemorrhagic infarction and AKI
  5. ExtensionThe clot can grow into the IVC and embolize to the lungs

What a renal vein clot does

  • AClotThrombus forms in the renal vein, often the left
  • BSwellingOutflow is blocked, so the kidney enlarges and becomes echogenic
  • CInfarctionSudden occlusion causes hemorrhagic infarction, with flank pain and hematuria
  • DMore proteinuriaCongested glomeruli leak more protein
  • EEmbolismClot extending into the IVC can travel to the lungs as a PE
  • FVaricoceleThe left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein, so a left clot can cause a left varicocele

Note: A nephrotic patient loses antithrombin III in the urine while the liver makes more fibrinogen, which is why nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause.

Etiology

  • Hypercoagulability
  • 1Nephrotic syndromeThe most common cause: MN most often (in 5–60%), then MCD and MPGN, as on
  • 2Other hypercoagulable statesInherited thrombophilia (antithrombin III, protein C, or protein S deficiency, factor V Leiden, and the prothrombin gene variant), APS, pregnancy and estrogen, and cancer
  • Endothelial injury
  • 3Tumor invasionRCC growing into the renal vein and IVC
  • 4Trauma and surgeryIncluding a kidney transplant, usually within 48 hours
  • Stasis
  • 5Dehydration in neonatesSevere dehydration or prolonged hypotension; one of the most common venous clots in newborns

Symptoms and complications

The speed of the occlusion decides the picture: acute RVT resembles renal infarction, whereas chronic RVT is usually found by chance.

  • Acute RVTFlank pain and tenderness, visible or microscopic hematuria, worsening proteinuria, and a rapid fall in GFR; nausea, vomiting, or fever
  • Chronic RVTUsually no symptoms, as collateral veins open; sometimes leg edema
  • Transplant (4)Sudden anuria and a tender graft within 48 hours of surgery
  • Neonates (5)Visible hematuria, a flank mass, and signs of dehydration or shock
  • ComplicationsPE, AKI, a left varicocele, and loss of the kidney

Diagnosis

CT angiography confirms the clot; the AKI and nephrotic workups are on and .

  • +Any RVTCT angiography, the test of choice, showing the clot and a swollen kidney; Doppler ultrasound, which shows an enlarged, echogenic kidney but can miss the clot; MR venography; catheter venography, the gold standard, now rarely needed
  • 1Nephrotic syndromeUPCR and serum albumin; anti-PLA2R antibodies and a biopsy to find the glomerular disease
  • 2Other hypercoagulable statesThrombophilia testing and antiphospholipid antibodies when there is no nephrotic syndrome
  • 3Tumor invasionA kidney mass on CT, with tumor extending into the vein

Treatment

RVT is treated as a complication of its cause, with anticoagulation to stop the clot growing or embolizing.

  • +Any RVTAnticoagulation as for DVT or PE: LMWH or heparin, then warfarin to an INR of 2–3, or DOACs, for 3–6 months if the cause has resolved, 6–12 months if unprovoked, and for as long as nephrotic syndrome or cancer persists; catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy for acute bilateral RVT with AKI, RVT in a single kidney or transplant, extension into the IVC or PE despite anticoagulation, or severe symptoms that do not settle
  • 1Nephrotic syndromeTreat the glomerular disease, which ends the hypercoagulable state; prophylactic anticoagulation is considered in MN with a very low albumin, as on
  • 3Tumor invasionNephrectomy with removal of the tumor thrombus
  • 5Dehydration in neonatesFluids and supportive care, with anticoagulation in selected infants

Note: RVT is usually a result of kidney disease rather than its cause, so anticoagulation alone is not enough without treating the nephrotic syndrome or other source.

Review article

Renal vein thrombosis: a clot that blocks the kidney's outflow

Renal vein thrombosis forms through Virchow triad, most often from the hypercoagulability of nephrotic syndrome, in which antithrombin III is lost in the urine, and particularly in membranous nephropathy. A sudden clot congests and infarcts the kidney, causing flank pain, hematuria, worsening proteinuria, and acute kidney injury, whereas a slow clot is often silent as collateral veins open, and either can extend into the inferior vena cava and embolize to the lungs. CT angiography confirms it, and anticoagulation, with treatment of the underlying disease, is the mainstay. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and management, and consider its relationships to other conditions.

Key points

  • Nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause, through loss of antithrombin III and increased fibrinogen; MN is the glomerular disease most often involved.
  • Acute RVT causes flank pain, hematuria, worsening proteinuria, and AKI; chronic RVT is usually silent.
  • The left renal vein is longer and receives the left gonadal vein, so left RVT is more common and can cause a left varicocele.
  • CT angiography is the test of choice; anticoagulation as for DVT, with treatment of the cause, is the mainstay.

Pathophysiology

A clot forms in the renal vein through hypercoagulability, most often from nephrotic syndrome, in which antithrombin III is lost in the urine while the liver makes more fibrinogen, through endothelial injury, or through stasis. It forms more often on the left, where the vein is longer and receives the left gonadal vein, so a left clot can cause a left varicocele. Blocked outflow swells the kidney, which becomes echogenic, congested glomeruli leak more protein, and sudden occlusion causes hemorrhagic infarction with pain, hematuria, and AKI, whereas slow occlusion is often silent as collaterals open. The clot can extend into the IVC and embolize to the lungs.

Etiology and mechanisms

Nephrotic syndrome is the most common cause, especially MN, in which RVT is reported in 5–60%, then MCD and MPGN. Other hypercoagulable states include inherited thrombophilia (antithrombin III, protein C, or protein S deficiency, factor V Leiden, and the prothrombin gene variant), APS, pregnancy and estrogen, and cancer. RCC can grow into the renal vein and IVC, trauma and surgery injure the vein, including a kidney transplant within 48 hours, and severe dehydration or hypotension makes RVT one of the most common venous clots in newborns.

Clinical presentation and complications

Acute RVT causes flank pain and tenderness, hematuria, worsening proteinuria, a rapid fall in GFR, and sometimes nausea, vomiting, or fever; chronic RVT is usually silent, sometimes with leg edema. After a transplant, it causes sudden anuria and a tender graft, and in neonates, visible hematuria, a flank mass, and dehydration or shock. Complications are PE, AKI, a left varicocele, and loss of the kidney.

Diagnosis

CT angiography, the test of choice, shows the clot and a swollen kidney; Doppler ultrasound shows an enlarged, echogenic kidney but can miss the clot; and catheter venography, the gold standard, is now rarely needed. The cause is sought with the UPCR, albumin, anti-PLA2R antibodies, and a biopsy in nephrotic syndrome, thrombophilia and antiphospholipid testing otherwise, and CT for a kidney tumor extending into the vein.

Management

RVT is anticoagulated as DVT or PE, with LMWH or heparin then warfarin to an INR of 2–3, or DOACs, for 3–6 months if the cause has resolved, 6–12 months if unprovoked, and for as long as nephrotic syndrome or cancer persists, with catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy for acute bilateral RVT with AKI, RVT in a single kidney or transplant, extension into the IVC or PE despite anticoagulation, or refractory symptoms. The glomerular disease is treated to end the hypercoagulable state, and prophylactic anticoagulation is considered in MN with a very low albumin; a tumor thrombus is removed with the kidney, and neonates receive fluids and supportive care. Because RVT is usually a result of kidney disease, treating the source matters as much as anticoagulation.

Relationships to other conditions

. MN carries the highest risk of RVT among the nephrotic diseases, so a sudden rise in proteinuria or flank pain in MN calls for imaging of the renal veins.

. Both cause sudden flank pain, hematuria, and AKI, but arterial infarction raises LDH sharply and shows wedge-shaped defects, whereas RVT swells the whole kidney and shows a clot in the vein.

Postrenal AKI

Pathophysiology

Obstruction to urine flow raises the pressure in the tubules and Bowman space, so GFR falls; it causes AKI only when both kidneys, or a single working kidney, are blocked, and it reverses if relieved early but scars the kidney if it lasts.

  1. Urine cannot drainPressure rises up the urinary tract
  2. Bowman space pressure risesWithin hours, opposing filtration, so GFR falls
  3. The kidney is injuredRenal vasoconstriction, inflammation, tubular atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis
  4. Weeks to monthsBladder atony, chronic interstitial nephritis, secondary FSGS, and ESRD
  5. After reliefPost-obstructive diuresis in up to 50%

Note: A gradual blockage of one ureter may cause no AKI, because the other kidney compensates.

Etiology

  • Below the bladder
  • 1Urethra and prostateBPH, the most common cause in older men; urethral stricture, phimosis, and posterior urethral valves; prostate cancer
  • The bladder
  • 2Bladder outlet and functionNeurogenic bladder, clots from bladder or urinary tract cancer, bladder tumors, fecal impaction, and pelvic organ prolapse
  • Both ureters, or a single kidney
  • 3StonesThe most common cause in younger patients; struvite and cystine stones grow fast
  • 4Masses and fibrosisPelvic masses and cancers, the most common cause in older women; retroperitoneal fibrosis or lymph nodes
  • 5Pregnancy and pelvic diseaseThe gravid uterus and endometriosis compress the ureters

Symptoms and complications

  • Lower tractDifficulty starting to void, a weak stream, urinary retention, and a distended, tender bladder
  • Urine outputSudden anuria suggests complete obstruction; alternating polyuria and low output suggest a partial one
  • Upper tractFlank pain with stones; often painless when slow, as with fibrosis or tumor
  • InfectionAn infected, obstructed kidney needs urgent drainage; antibiotics alone fail
  • Post-obstructive diuresisUrine output of 200 mL/h or more for 2 hours, or over 3 L in 24 hours, after relief; it can cause hypovolemia and losses of Na+, K+, phosphate, and Mg2+

Diagnosis

Look for the obstruction early, because it is reversible: a bladder scan and catheter at the bedside, then ultrasound for hydronephrosis; the urine indices are compared with the other types on .

ForObtain
Bladder outlet (1, 2)Bladder scan for post-void residual; a urethral catheter that drains a large volume is diagnostic and therapeutic; digital rectal examination
Upper tract (3–5)Kidney ultrasound for hydronephrosis and hydroureter; CT for stones and masses
Prostate cancerPSA when the prostate is hard or nodular, with weight loss or hematuria
InfectionUrine culture

Treatment

Relieve the obstruction at its level, then watch for post-obstructive diuresis; the general care of AKI is on .

CauseTreatment
Urethra and prostate (1)A urethral catheter (a Coudé tip when the prostate is large); a suprapubic catheter if it cannot pass; then BPH treatment, from drugs to TURP
Bladder (2)Catheter drainage; intermittent self-catheterization for neurogenic bladder; treat clots and fecal impaction
Ureters (3–5)A ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, urgently if infected; then treat the stone or mass
Post-obstructive diuresisCheck Na+, K+, phosphate, Mg2+, urea, and creatinine every 12–24 hours; replace losses with care, so the diuresis is not driven by the fluid itself; risk is highest when 1500 mL or more drains at once
