Review article

Postrenal AKI: obstruction to urine flow

Postrenal AKI follows obstruction to urine flow at the urethra, bladder, or both ureters, or the ureter of a single working kidney. Rising pressure in Bowman space lowers GFR within hours, and lasting obstruction causes vasoconstriction, tubular atrophy, and fibrosis. It is found with a bladder scan, a catheter, and ultrasound for hydronephrosis, and relieved by catheter, stent, or nephrostomy, after which post-obstructive diuresis may follow. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes by level, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment.

Key points

  • Obstruction raises Bowman space pressure and lowers GFR within hours; AKI needs both kidneys, or a single working kidney, to be blocked.
  • BPH is the most common cause in older men, pelvic masses in older women, and stones in younger patients; retroperitoneal fibrosis, clots, and neurogenic bladder also obstruct.
  • A bladder scan and catheter find bladder outlet obstruction; ultrasound shows hydronephrosis.
  • An infected, obstructed kidney needs urgent stent or nephrostomy.
  • Post-obstructive diuresis, 200 mL/h or more for 2 hours or over 3 L in 24 hours, follows relief in up to 50% and needs electrolyte monitoring every 12–24 hours.

Pathophysiology and etiology

Obstruction raises pressure up the urinary tract and in Bowman space within hours, opposing filtration, and lasting obstruction causes renal vasoconstriction, inflammation, tubular atrophy, interstitial fibrosis, and eventually bladder atony, chronic interstitial nephritis, secondary FSGS, and ESRD. A gradual blockage of one ureter may cause no AKI. BPH is the most common cause in older men, with stricture, phimosis, valves, and prostate cancer; at the bladder, neurogenic bladder, clots, tumors, fecal impaction, and prolapse; and at both ureters, stones, the most common cause in younger patients, pelvic masses, the most common in older women, retroperitoneal fibrosis, pregnancy, and endometriosis.

Presentation and diagnosis

Lower tract obstruction causes difficulty voiding, retention, and a distended bladder; sudden anuria suggests complete obstruction; stones cause flank pain, whereas slow obstruction is often painless. A bladder scan and a catheter that drains a large volume find bladder outlet obstruction, with digital rectal examination and PSA when cancer is suspected, and ultrasound shows hydronephrosis, with CT for stones and masses, as in the review of .

Management

A urethral catheter, with a Coudé tip for a large prostate or a suprapubic catheter if it cannot pass, relieves outlet obstruction, followed by treatment of BPH; neurogenic bladder may need intermittent self-catheterization; and ureteral obstruction needs a stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, urgently if infected. Post-obstructive diuresis, 200 mL/h or more for 2 hours or over 3 L in 24 hours, follows relief in up to 50%, most likely when 1500 mL or more drains; Na+, K+, phosphate, Mg2+, urea, and creatinine are checked every 12–24 hours and losses replaced with care.

AKI: Comparison and Workup

Definition and staging

AKI is a sudden fall in kidney function, defined by KDIGO as any of: a rise in creatinine of 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline or more within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.

KDIGO stageCreatinineUrine output
11.5–1.9 times baseline, or a rise of 26.5 µmol/L or moreBelow 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours
22.0–2.9 times baselineBelow 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours or more
33 times baseline, 354 µmol/L or more, or starting dialysisBelow 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 hours, or no urine for 12 hours

How long kidney function has been abnormal

  • Within 7 daysAKI, by the KDIGO criteria above
  • 7–90 daysAcute kidney disease (AKD): function has not yet recovered
  • Over 3 monthsCKD

Note: Creatinine lags behind the injury, so a fall in urine output can be the only early sign; cystatin C rises sooner and is not affected by muscle mass.

Phases

  • AInitiationHours to days. The insult; GFR begins to fall, but creatinine lags behind the injury and may still be normal, so the insult usually lies in the 24–48 hours before creatinine rises
  • BExtensionDays. Ongoing hypoxia and inflammation keep killing cells in the outer medulla after the insult has passed
  • COliguric (maintenance) phaseAbout 1–2 weeks. Low urine output, with overload, hyperkalemia, and acidosis most likely; dialysis is most often needed here, usually for a few days to a few weeks; oliguria carries a higher mortality than non-oliguric AKI
  • DDiuretic (polyuric) phaseDays to about 1–2 weeks. GFR returns before the tubules can concentrate urine, so large volumes of Na+, K+, Mg2+, and water are lost: watch for hypovolemia and hypokalemia
  • ERecoveryWeeks to months. Often to a new, higher baseline creatinine; repeated AKI adds up and can lead to CKD

When creatinine rises and recovers, by cause

CauseCreatinine risesRecovery
PrerenalWith the fall in perfusionWithin 24–72 hours of restoring volume
Contrast-associatedWithin 48–72 hours, peaking at 2–5 daysBack to baseline by about 2 weeks
AIN1–2 weeks after a new drugAfter stopping the drug; corticosteroids if no improvement in 3–7 days
STEC-HUS5–13 days after the diarrhea startsAbout half need dialysis
AtheroemboliDays to weeks after a vascular procedureVariable, with no specific treatment
Ischemic or toxic ATNOver days, after the insultWeeks to months, often incompletely
ObstructionWhile the blockage lastsAfter relief, often with a post-obstructive diuresis

What the urine output suggests

  • OliguriaFavors AKI over CKD
  • Sudden anuriaComplete obstruction, severe glomerulonephritis, or a blocked renal artery
  • PolyuriaA concentrating defect, as in AIN, or post-obstructive diuresis
  • After an obstruction is relievedPost-obstructive diuresis in up to 50%: 200 mL/h or more for 2 hours, or over 3 L in 24 hours; usually physiological and over within 24 hours, but a salt-wasting form can last 48 hours or more, with K+, Mg2+, and phosphate losses, so electrolytes are checked every 12–24 hours

Symptoms and complications

AKI is often silent and found on bloods; when symptoms come, they reflect what the kidney can no longer excrete.

ProblemWhat is seen
Fluid overloadEdema, pulmonary edema, and HF, especially in the oliguric phase
HyperkalemiaArrhythmias; above 6.5 mmol/L or with ECG changes, an emergency
Metabolic acidosisKussmaul breathing; may need HCO3− or dialysis
Other electrolytesHyperphosphatemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia
UremiaNausea, vomiting, anorexia, pruritus, lethargy, confusion, asterixis, seizures, pericarditis, and bleeding from poorly functioning platelets
Drug toxicityRenally cleared drugs build up unless their doses are adjusted
InfectionMore common, and a major cause of death

Note: In-hospital mortality is 40–50%, and over 50% in ICU; 12–15% of patients later need long-term dialysis, and repeated AKI adds up to CKD.

Comparison

The tubules decide the pattern: in prerenal AKI they work and conserve Na+ and water; in ATN they cannot; and in postrenal AKI the pattern varies with how long the obstruction has lasted.

FeaturePrerenalIntrarenal (ATN)Postrenal
UCRHigh above 100Normal below 100Variable
Urine Na+Low below 20 mmol/LHigh above 40 mmol/LVariable
FENaLow below 1%High above 2%Often above 2% once established
FEUrea (with diuretics)Low below 35%High above 50%
Urine osmolalityHigh above 500 mOsm/kgLow below 450 mOsm/kgVariable
SedimentBland, or hyaline castsMuddy brown granular casts and tubular cellsOften bland; blood with stones
Creatinine riseSlowAbout 26.5–44 µmol/L a dayVariable
Response to fluidCreatinine falls within 24–72 hoursNoneNone until the obstruction is relieved
UltrasoundNormalNormal-sized kidneysHydronephrosis

Urinalysis at a glance

DipstickPoints to
Blood, with many red cells on microscopyGlomerular disease if the cells are dysmorphic; stones or a tumor (postrenal) if not
Blood, with few red cellsMyoglobin in rhabdomyolysis, or hemoglobin in intravascular hemolysis
Protein 3+ or moreGlomerular disease, especially nephrotic
Little protein despite suspected light chainsMyeloma: the dipstick detects albumin and misses light chains
Leukocyte esterase or nitriteInfection; white cells with a negative culture (sterile pyuria) point to AIN
Specific gravityHigh in prerenal AKI; fixed near 1.010, about 300 mOsm/kg (isosthenuria), when the tubules cannot concentrate, as in ATN
MicroscopyPoints to
Hyaline casts, otherwise blandPrerenal, or normal
Muddy brown granular casts and tubular cellsATN
Red cell casts and dysmorphic red cellsGlomerulonephritis
White cell casts and sterile pyuriaAIN, or pyelonephritis if the culture is positive
CrystalsUrate in TLS, acyclovir, or calcium oxalate in ethylene glycol poisoning
Fatty casts and oval fat bodiesNephrotic syndrome
EosinophilsUnreliable for AIN; also seen in atheroemboli

Reading the urine indices

  • FENaFENa = (UNa × plasma Cr) ÷ (PNa × urine Cr) × 100Falsely high with diuretics; low despite intrinsic disease in HF, cirrhosis, contrast-associated AKI, glomerulonephritis, and vasculitis, where GFR falls but tubules still work
  • FEUreaFEUrea = (Uurea × plasma Cr) ÷ (Purea × urine Cr) × 100Urea is handled in the proximal tubule, before diuretics act, so it stays useful in patients taking them
  • Underlying CKDWeakens Na+ conservation and concentration, so all the indices become less reliable

Diagnosis

Workup

  1. 1. Is it AKI, and how severe?Compare creatinine with a baseline; stage by KDIGO
  2. 2. Any immediate danger?K+, ECG, blood gas, and signs of fluid overload
  3. 3. Volume and drugsOrthostatic vital signs, JVP, and fluid balance; NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, diuretics, nephrotoxins, and contrast in the last 24–48 hours
  4. 4. Obstruction?Bladder scan and catheter; kidney ultrasound
  5. 5. The urineDipstick, microscopy, Na+, osmolality, FENa or FEUrea, and albumin-to-creatinine ratio, read as in Urinalysis at a glance above
  6. 6. The bloodElectrolytes, Ca2+, phosphate, FBC, CK; SPEP and UPEP in older patients; serology and complement if glomerular disease is likely
  7. 7. BiopsyFor unexplained or rapidly falling function, or suspected glomerulonephritis

AKI or CKD?

ClueFavors AKIFavors CKD
HistoryA recent insult; a normal creatinine beforeFatigue, anorexia, nocturia, polyuria, pruritus, and a high creatinine before
UltrasoundNormal-sized kidneysSmall kidneys
BloodAnemia, high phosphate, and high PTH

Treatment

Treat the cause, protect the kidney from further injury, and manage what it can no longer do, with dialysis when that fails.

GoalTreatment
Restore perfusionA monitored fluid challenge when hypovolemia is likely; improvement supports a prerenal component
Prevent further injuryStop NSAIDs and nephrotoxins; hold ACEi and ARBs; avoid contrast; adjust drug doses for GFR
HyperkalemiaCalcium gluconate for ECG changes, insulin with dextrose and salbutamol, binders, and dialysis if refractory (see Potassium disorders)
Fluid overloadHigh-dose IV loop diuretics; they may increase urine output, but turning oliguric into non-oliguric AKI does not improve recovery, the need for dialysis, or survival
Metabolic acidosisHCO3− when severe
NutritionProtein of 1.2–1.5 g/kg a day, preferably enteral, because AKI is catabolic; limit K+ and phosphate

Dialysis: the AEIOU indications

If there isThen
A: AcidosisSevere metabolic acidosis that does not respond to treatment
E: ElectrolytesHyperkalemia that does not respond to treatment
I: IntoxicationA dialyzable poison, such as methanol, ethylene glycol, or lithium
O: OverloadFluid overload that does not respond to diuretics
U: UremiaEncephalopathy, pericarditis, neuropathy, seizures, or bleeding

In AKI, dialysis runs through a temporary venous catheter, is reassessed daily, and usually lasts days to weeks, with CRRT for unstable patients.

Review article

Acute kidney injury: staging, phases, the urine indices, and shared management

Acute kidney injury is a sudden fall in kidney function, defined and staged by KDIGO from creatinine and urine output. It is often silent but causes fluid overload, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, uremia, and drug toxicity, and carries a high mortality. The urine indices and sediment separate prerenal AKI, in which the tubules conserve Na+ and water, from ATN, in which they cannot, and ultrasound finds obstruction. Management treats the cause, protects the kidney, controls K+, fluid, and acid, and uses dialysis by the AEIOU indications. Here, we review the definition, staging, phases, complications, comparison, workup, and shared treatment of AKI.

Key points

  • KDIGO defines AKI as a creatinine rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours, staged 1–3.
  • Phases run from initiation through an oliguric phase, with most complications, and a diuretic phase to recovery over weeks to months.
  • Prerenal AKI has urine Na+ below 20 mmol/L, FENa below 1% (FEUrea below 35% with diuretics), osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg, and a UCR above 100; ATN has FENa above 2%, osmolality below 450, and muddy brown casts.
  • The workup checks for immediate danger, volume, drugs, obstruction, the urine, and the blood, with biopsy for unexplained AKI.
  • Treatment restores perfusion, stops nephrotoxins, adjusts doses, manages K+, fluid, and acid, and dialyzes for acidosis, electrolytes, intoxication, overload, or uremia.

Definition, staging, and phases

KDIGO defines AKI as a creatinine rise of 26.5 µmol/L or more within 48 hours, a rise to 1.5 times baseline or more within 7 days, or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Stage 1 is 1.5–1.9 times baseline or a rise of 26.5 µmol/L, stage 2 is 2.0–2.9 times, and stage 3 is 3 times, 354 µmol/L or more, or dialysis, with urine output thresholds of 6–12 hours, 12 hours or more, and 24 hours below 0.3 mL/kg/h or 12 hours of anuria. Creatinine lags behind injury, and cystatin C rises sooner. AKI is defined by changes within 7 days; function that has not recovered by 7–90 days is acute kidney disease (AKD), and abnormality beyond 3 months is CKD. AKI passes through five phases. In initiation, over hours to days, GFR begins to fall while creatinine lags behind, so the insult usually lies in the 24–48 hours before creatinine rises. In extension, over days, ongoing hypoxia and inflammation keep killing cells in the outer medulla. The oliguric, or maintenance, phase lasts about 1–2 weeks; overload, hyperkalemia, and acidosis are most likely, dialysis is most often needed, usually for a few days to a few weeks, and oliguria carries a higher mortality than non-oliguric AKI. In the diuretic phase, lasting days to about 1–2 weeks, recovering filtration outpaces tubular concentration, so Na+, K+, Mg2+, and water are lost. Recovery takes weeks to months, often to a higher baseline, and repeated AKI can lead to CKD. Oliguria favors AKI, sudden anuria suggests complete obstruction, severe glomerulonephritis, or arterial occlusion, and polyuria a concentrating defect or post-obstructive diuresis. Post-obstructive diuresis, 200 mL/h or more for 2 hours or over 3 L in 24 hours, follows relief in up to 50%; it is usually physiological and over within 24 hours, but a salt-wasting form can last 48 hours or more with K+, Mg2+, and phosphate losses, so electrolytes are checked every 12–24 hours.

Each cause has its own timecourse. Prerenal AKI recovers within 24–72 hours of restoring volume. Contrast-associated AKI rises within 48–72 hours, peaks at 2–5 days, and returns to baseline by about 2 weeks. AIN follows a new drug by 1–2 weeks and improves once it is stopped, with corticosteroids if there is no improvement in 3–7 days. STEC-HUS follows the diarrhea by 5–13 days, and about half of patients need dialysis. Atheroemboli cause AKI days to weeks after a vascular procedure, with variable recovery and no specific treatment. Ischemic or toxic ATN develops over days and recovers over weeks to months, often incompletely, and obstruction recovers after relief, often with a post-obstructive diuresis.

Complications

AKI is often silent but causes fluid overload with edema, pulmonary edema, and HF; hyperkalemia with arrhythmias; metabolic acidosis; hyperphosphatemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia; uremia, with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, pruritus, lethargy, confusion, asterixis, seizures, pericarditis, and platelet dysfunction; drug toxicity; and infection. In-hospital mortality is 40–50%, and over 50% in ICU, and 12–15% of patients later need long-term dialysis.

Comparison and diagnosis

Prerenal AKI has a UCR above 100, urine Na+ below 20 mmol/L, FENa below 1%, FEUrea below 35%, osmolality above 500 mOsm/kg, bland sediment, and a response to fluid within 24–72 hours; ATN has a normal UCR, urine Na+ above 40, FENa above 2%, FEUrea above 50%, osmolality below 450, muddy brown casts, and a creatinine rise of about 26.5–44 µmol/L a day; and postrenal AKI shows hydronephrosis. FENa is falsely high with diuretics and low despite intrinsic disease in HF, cirrhosis, contrast-associated AKI, glomerulonephritis, and vasculitis, whereas FEUrea, handled proximally, stays useful with diuretics, and CKD weakens all the indices. The workup stages the AKI, checks K+, the ECG, the blood gas, and volume, reviews drugs and recent contrast, looks for obstruction with a bladder scan and ultrasound, examines the urine and blood, and reserves biopsy for unexplained or rapidly progressive AKI; a prior normal creatinine and normal-sized kidneys favor AKI, whereas small kidneys, anemia, and high phosphate and PTH favor CKD.

On the dipstick, blood with many red cells suggests glomerular disease when they are dysmorphic and stones or a tumor when they are not, while blood with few red cells suggests myoglobin or hemoglobin. Protein of 3+ or more suggests glomerular disease, especially nephrotic, and the dipstick misses light chains because it detects albumin. Leukocyte esterase or nitrite suggests infection, and white cells with a negative culture suggest AIN. Specific gravity is high in prerenal AKI and fixed near 1.010, about 300 mOsm/kg, when the tubules cannot concentrate, as in ATN. Under the microscope, hyaline casts in otherwise bland urine fit prerenal AKI; muddy brown granular casts and tubular cells, ATN; red cell casts and dysmorphic red cells, glomerulonephritis; white cell casts and sterile pyuria, AIN or, with a positive culture, pyelonephritis; crystals, urate in TLS, acyclovir, or calcium oxalate; and fatty casts and oval fat bodies, nephrotic syndrome. Eosinophils are unreliable for AIN and also occur in atheroemboli.

Management

A monitored fluid challenge treats likely hypovolemia, and NSAIDs, nephrotoxins, ACEi, ARBs, and contrast are avoided, with drug doses adjusted. Hyperkalemia is treated as in the review of , fluid overload with high-dose IV loop diuretics, which may increase urine output without improving recovery, the need for dialysis, or survival, and severe acidosis with HCO3−, and protein of 1.2–1.5 g/kg a day supports the catabolic state. Dialysis, through a temporary catheter and reassessed daily, is indicated for refractory acidosis, refractory hyperkalemia, dialyzable intoxications, refractory overload, and uremia with encephalopathy, pericarditis, neuropathy, seizures, or bleeding, with CRRT for unstable patients.

Metabolic Acidosis

Pathophysiology

A gain of acid or a loss of HCO3− lowers plasma HCO3− and pH, and the lungs hyperventilate to lower pCO2 and pull the pH back toward normal.

H+ + HCO3− ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ CO2 + H2O
FeatureNAGMAAGMA
What happensHCO3− is lost from the kidney or gut, or the kidney fails to make new HCO3−An acid is added; H+ uses up HCO3−, and the acid's anion stays in the blood
HCO3− is replaced byCl−, so it is also called hyperchloremic acidosisAn unmeasured anion: lactate, ketoanions, formate, glycolate, sulfate, or phosphate
Anion gapNormalHigh
Main sourcesKidney: CKD, RTA. Gut: diarrhea, fistulasGOLDMARK: glycols, oxoproline, L-lactate, D-lactate, methanol, aspirin, renal failure, ketoacidosis

What acidosis does to K+

  • AH+ moves into cellsCells buffer excess H+, which softens the fall in plasma pH
  • BK+ moves outK+ leaves cells to keep the charge balanced → hyperkalemia, most marked when the acid is a mineral acid such as HCl or NH4Cl
  • COrganic acids enter with their anionLactate and ketoanions cross into cells together with H+, so little K+ has to leave; organic acidoses shift less K+

Exceptions to the H+ and K+ shift

  • Organic acidosesLactic acidosis and ketoacidosis raise K+ less than a mineral acid does, because the anion enters cells with its H+ (C)
  • DKAK+ is high mainly from insulin deficiency and high osmolality, although total body K+ is low; insulin moves K+ back into cells and can cause hypokalemia
  • RTA types 1 and 2, and diarrheaK+ is low despite acidosis, because K+ is lost in urine or stool faster than it shifts out of cells
  • Correcting acidosisK+ moves back into cells, so treating acidosis can unmask a low total body K+

Etiology

Causes

  • NAGMA: kidney, low GFR
  • 1CKDFewer nephrons make less NH4+, so less acid is excreted and less new HCO3− is made; a NAGMA in earlier CKD becomes an AGMA (14) as GFR falls further
  • NAGMA: kidney, normal GFR
  • 2RTA type 1 (distal)α-intercalated cells cannot secrete H+, so urine cannot be acidified; autoimmune disease (Sjögren syndrome, SLE), lithium, amphotericin B, and toluene
  • 3RTA type 2 (proximal)The proximal tubule, which normally reclaims 85–90% of filtered HCO3−, reclaims less, so HCO3− spills into urine until plasma HCO3− falls below the lowered threshold; multiple myeloma, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide, topiramate), tenofovir, and Fanconi syndrome
  • 4RTA type 4 (hypoaldosteronism) Most common RTAToo little aldosterone, or resistance to it, cuts H+ and K+ secretion, and the high K+ suppresses NH4+ production; diabetic nephropathy, ACEi, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim, and adrenal insufficiency
  • NAGMA: gut and other
  • 5DiarrheaIntestinal fluid beyond the stomach is rich in HCO3−, so losing it lowers HCO3−, and the kidney keeps Cl− in its place; K+ is lost too; secretory diarrhea loses more HCO3− than inflammatory diarrhea
  • 6Pancreatic fistulas and other bicarbonate-rich lossesPancreatic, biliary, and small bowel fluid drains outside the body; a ureterosigmoidostomy lets the colon swap urinary Cl− for HCO3−
  • 7Cl− load and drugsLarge volumes of 0.9% saline, which has 154 mmol/L Cl− and no HCO3−; TPN without acetate; cholestyramine
  • AGMA: GOLDMARK
  • 8GlycolsEthylene glycol in antifreeze is made into glycolic acid, which causes the acidosis, and oxalic acid, which forms calcium oxalate crystals in the tubules → AKI and hypocalcemia; propylene glycol is made into lactate
  • 9Oxoproline5-oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid) builds up with chronic paracetamol use, especially with malnutrition or chronic illness
  • 10L-lactateType A: too little oxygen delivered (shock, sepsis, ischemia) → anaerobic glycolysis. Type B: no hypoxia, but mitochondria cannot use pyruvate (metformin, liver failure, thiamine deficiency)
  • 11D-lactateIn short bowel syndrome, colonic bacteria ferment unabsorbed carbohydrate into D-lactate, which humans metabolize poorly
  • 12MethanolWindscreen washer fluid, solvents, and contaminated spirits; made into formic acid, which damages the retina and basal ganglia
  • 13AspirinSalicylates stimulate the respiratory center first (respiratory alkalosis), then uncouple oxidative phosphorylation → lactate and ketoacids
  • 14Renal failure (uremic acidosis)Advanced CKD or AKI retains sulfate, phosphate, urate, and hippurate; rhabdomyolysis releases acids and phosphate
  • 15KetoacidosisLow insulin and high glucagon → lipolysis → β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate; DKA, AKA after a binge followed by vomiting and poor intake, and starvation

Symptoms and complications

EffectWhat happens
BreathingKussmaul breathing: deep, rapid breaths to blow off CO2; the respiratory muscles can tire
PotassiumOften hyperkalemia (B), but not always: organic acidoses shift less K+, and RTA types 1 and 2 and diarrhea cause hypokalemia
CalciumMore ionized Ca2+; chronic acidosis draws on bone to buffer acid → osteomalacia, rickets, and stones
Heart and vesselsWeaker contraction, vasodilation, and poor response to catecholamines → hypotension; arrhythmias
OxygenDissociation curve shifts right: more O2 released to tissues
BrainHeadache, lethargy, confusion, and coma
OtherNausea, vomiting, anorexia, and fatigue; insulin resistance; long term, muscle wasting and faster CKD progression

Diagnosis

Confirm the acidosis, check the compensation, and calculate the anion gap, delta-delta ratio, and osmolal gap as on ; the gap then sorts the causes below.

NAGMA: kidney or gut?

Urine AG = urine Na+ + urine K+ − urine Cl−
  • Negative urine AGThe kidney is excreting plenty of NH4+, which leaves with Cl− → a normal renal response to HCO3− lost elsewhere: diarrhea (5), fistulas (6), or saline (7)
  • Positive urine AGThe kidney cannot excrete NH4+ → RTA types 1 and 4 (2, 4) or CKD (1)
FindingRTA type 1 (2)RTA type 2 (3)RTA type 4 (4)CKD (1)
DefectDistal H+ secretionProximal HCO3− reabsorptionAldosterone deficiency or resistanceToo few nephrons to make NH4+
GFRNormalNormalNormal or mildly lowLow
Plasma K+LowLowHighNormal or high
Urine pHAbove 5.5, even in severe acidosisBelow 5.5 once HCO3− is below the threshold; above 5.5 when HCO3− is givenBelow 5.5Usually below 5.5
Plasma HCO3−Can fall below 10 mmol/LUsually 12–18 mmol/LUsually above 17 mmol/LFalls as GFR falls
Urine AGPositiveVariablePositivePositive

Note: Before diagnosing an RTA, exclude a UTI with a urease-producing organism, which raises urine pH, and low volume, which limits distal H+ secretion (urine Na+ should be above 25 mmol/L).

CauseBloodUrineHistory
Glycols (8)High osmolal gap early; low Ca2+; rising creatinineCalcium oxalate crystals; hematuriaAntifreeze; inebriation, then flank pain and oliguria
Oxoproline (9)Normal lactate and no ketones5-oxoprolineChronic paracetamol use, malnutrition

Treatment

Treat the cause, and replace volume and K+ as needed; HCO3− is given only when it has truly been lost, as set out on .

Metabolic acidosis

CauseTreatment
CKD (1)Oral NaHCO3 to protect bone and muscle and slow progression; dialysis when advanced (14)
RTA type 1 (2)Oral alkali in modest doses; potassium citrate also replaces K+ and prevents stones; treat the cause
RTA type 2 (3)Large doses of alkali with K+, because HCO3− given above the threshold is lost in urine and carries K+ with it; a thiazide can help by shrinking volume; phosphate and vitamin D for Fanconi bone disease
RTA type 4 (4)Stop culprit drugs, low-potassium diet, and a loop or thiazide diuretic; fludrocortisone for aldosterone deficiency without hypertension or edema
Diarrhea and fistulas (5, 6)Treat the cause; replace fluid, K+, and HCO3−, and control the fistula
Saline (7)Switch to a balanced crystalloid such as Hartmann solution or Plasma-Lyte
Toxic alcohols (8, 12)Fomepizole, or ethanol if it is unavailable, to block alcohol dehydrogenase; hemodialysis for severe acidosis, visual change, AKI, or instability; thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol
Oxoproline (9)Stop paracetamol
L-lactate (10)Type A: restore perfusion with fluids, vasopressors, ABX, and source control. Type B: thiamine; stop metformin, with hemodialysis if severe
D-lactate (11)Treat the short bowel cause and limit carbohydrate reaching the colon
Aspirin (13)Activated charcoal; IV NaHCO3 to alkalinize urine and trap salicylate there; hemodialysis if severe
Renal failure (14)Dialysis
DKA (15)IV fluids, then insulin once K+ is at least 3.5 mmol/L, with K+ replacement; continue insulin until the gap closes
AKA and starvation (15)IV fluids with dextrose and thiamine; feed gradually and watch for refeeding syndrome

Review article

Metabolic acidosis: the anion gap, the urine, and the acid behind it

Metabolic acidosis is a fall in plasma HCO3− from a gain of acid or a loss of HCO3−, to which the lungs respond by hyperventilating to lower pCO2. The anion gap divides it into a normal gap form (NAGMA), in which HCO3− lost from the kidney or gut is replaced by Cl−, and a high gap form (AGMA), in which an added acid leaves its anion in the blood. The urine anion gap, plasma K+, and urine pH separate the renal causes of NAGMA, and the delta-delta ratio and osmolal gap refine AGMA. Here, we review the mechanisms, causes, consequences, diagnosis, and management of metabolic acidosis, and consider its relationship to disorders of potassium, aldosterone, kidney function, and metabolic alkalosis.

Key points

  • The anion gap separates NAGMA, in which HCO3− is lost and replaced by Cl−, from AGMA, in which an acid adds an unmeasured anion; the gap, compensation, and delta-delta calculations are on the comparison and workup page.
  • A negative urine anion gap points to gut losses, and a positive one to RTA types 1 and 4 or CKD; K+ is low in RTA types 1 and 2 and high in type 4, and urine pH stays above 5.5 only in type 1.
  • The causes of AGMA follow GOLDMARK; an osmolal gap above 15 with an AGMA suggests methanol or ethylene glycol.
  • HCO3− is replaced in NAGMA but is not routine in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis, whose anions are metabolized back into HCO3− once the cause is treated.

Pathophysiology

Plasma pH is set by the balance H+ + HCO3− ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ CO2 + H2O, with the kidney regulating HCO3− and the lungs regulating CO2. In NAGMA, HCO3− is lost from the kidney or gut, or the kidney fails to make new HCO3−, and Cl− takes its place, giving a hyperchloremic acidosis with a normal anion gap. In AGMA, an added acid uses up HCO3−, and its anion (lactate, ketoanions, formate, glycolate, sulfate, or phosphate) stays in the blood and widens the gap. In both, the lungs hyperventilate to lower pCO2.

In acidosis, cells take up H+, which softens the fall in pH, and K+ leaves them to keep the charge balanced, causing hyperkalemia that is most marked with mineral acids such as HCl and NH4Cl. Organic acids such as lactate and ketoacids enter cells together with their H+, so they shift less K+. There are exceptions to the usual shift: in DKA, K+ is high mainly from insulin deficiency and high osmolality although total body K+ is low, and insulin moves K+ back into cells; in RTA types 1 and 2 and in diarrhea, K+ is low despite acidosis because it is lost in urine or stool faster than it shifts out of cells; and correcting any acidosis moves K+ back into cells and can unmask a low total body K+.

Etiology and mechanisms

NAGMA. In CKD, fewer nephrons make less NH4+, so less acid is excreted and less new HCO3− is made; the NAGMA of earlier CKD becomes an AGMA as GFR falls further. With a normal GFR, the renal causes are the RTAs. In RTA type 1 (distal), α-intercalated cells cannot secrete H+, so urine cannot be acidified; causes include autoimmune disease (Sjögren syndrome and SLE), lithium, amphotericin B, and toluene. In RTA type 2 (proximal), the proximal tubule, which normally reclaims 85–90% of filtered HCO3−, reclaims less, so HCO3− spills into urine until plasma HCO3− falls below the lowered threshold; causes include multiple myeloma, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (acetazolamide and topiramate), tenofovir, and Fanconi syndrome. RTA type 4, the most common RTA, results from too little aldosterone or resistance to it, which cuts H+ and K+ secretion, while the resulting high K+ suppresses NH4+ production; causes include diabetic nephropathy, ACEi, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, heparin, trimethoprim, and adrenal insufficiency. Among gut causes, intestinal fluid beyond the stomach is rich in HCO3−, so diarrhea lowers HCO3−, the kidney keeps Cl− in its place, and K+ is lost too; secretory diarrhea loses more HCO3− than inflammatory diarrhea. Pancreatic fistulas and other bicarbonate-rich losses act in the same way, as pancreatic, biliary, or small bowel fluid drains outside the body, and a ureterosigmoidostomy lets the colon swap urinary Cl− for HCO3−. A Cl− load causes NAGMA when large volumes of 0.9% saline, with 154 mmol/L Cl− and no HCO3−, are given, and TPN without acetate and cholestyramine can do the same.

AGMA. The causes follow GOLDMARK. Ethylene glycol in antifreeze is made into glycolic acid, which causes the acidosis, and oxalic acid, which forms calcium oxalate crystals in the tubules, causing AKI and hypocalcemia; propylene glycol is made into lactate. 5-oxoproline (pyroglutamic acid) builds up with chronic paracetamol use, especially with malnutrition or chronic illness. L-lactic acidosis is type A when too little oxygen is delivered, as in shock, sepsis, and ischemia, driving anaerobic glycolysis, and type B when there is no hypoxia but mitochondria cannot use pyruvate, as with metformin, liver failure, and thiamine deficiency. D-lactate forms in short bowel syndrome, when colonic bacteria ferment unabsorbed carbohydrate into an isomer that humans metabolize poorly. Methanol, found in windscreen washer fluid, solvents, and contaminated spirits, is made into formic acid, which damages the retina and basal ganglia. Salicylates first stimulate the respiratory center, causing a respiratory alkalosis, then uncouple oxidative phosphorylation, producing lactate and ketoacids. Renal failure, in advanced CKD or AKI, retains sulfate, phosphate, urate, and hippurate, and rhabdomyolysis releases acids and phosphate. In ketoacidosis, low insulin and high glucagon drive lipolysis and the production of β-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate, as in DKA, AKA after a binge followed by vomiting and poor intake, and starvation.

Clinical presentation and complications

Metabolic acidosis causes Kussmaul breathing, deep and rapid breaths that blow off CO2 and can tire the respiratory muscles. K+ is often high, but not always: organic acidoses shift less K+, and RTA types 1 and 2 and diarrhea cause hypokalemia. Ionized Ca2+ rises, and chronic acidosis draws on bone to buffer acid, causing osteomalacia, rickets, and stones. The heart contracts more weakly, vessels dilate, and the response to catecholamines is poor, causing hypotension, with arrhythmias. The oxygen dissociation curve shifts right, releasing more O2 to tissues. Patients have headache, lethargy, confusion, and coma, with nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and fatigue; acidosis causes insulin resistance, and in the long term, muscle wasting and faster CKD progression.

Some findings point to the cause. Hypotension, tachycardia, and dry mucous membranes suggest volume loss from diarrhea or adrenal insufficiency. Fruity breath, polyuria, and polydipsia suggest DKA; blurred vision after drinking, methanol; inebriation, flank pain, hematuria, and tetany, ethylene glycol; and tinnitus with fast breathing, aspirin. Calcium phosphate stones and nephrocalcinosis suggest RTA type 1, with alkaline urine, high urine Ca2+, and low urine citrate, and bone pain and osteomalacia with glycosuria suggest RTA type 2 with Fanconi syndrome. Pruritus, nocturia, oliguria, and asterixis suggest renal failure.

Diagnosis

On an ABG or VBG, metabolic acidosis is a pH below 7.35 with a low HCO3−, which moves the same way as the pH. The expected compensation, the anion gap and its correction for low albumin, the delta-delta ratio, and the osmolal gap are calculated as set out in the review of ; a high osmolal gap with an AGMA suggests methanol or ethylene glycol, and the anion gap sorts the causes below.

In NAGMA, the urine anion gap (urine Na+ + urine K+ − urine Cl−) separates kidney from gut. A negative gap means the kidney is excreting plenty of NH4+, which leaves with Cl−, a normal renal response to HCO3− lost elsewhere, as in diarrhea, fistulas, or saline. A positive gap means the kidney cannot excrete NH4+, as in RTA types 1 and 4 or CKD. RTA type 1 has a normal GFR, low K+, a urine pH above 5.5 even in severe acidosis, plasma HCO3− that can fall below 10 mmol/L, and a positive urine anion gap, with high urine Ca2+, low urine citrate, calcium phosphate stones, and nephrocalcinosis. RTA type 2 has a normal GFR, low K+, a urine pH below 5.5 once HCO3− is below the threshold but above 5.5 when HCO3− is given, plasma HCO3− usually 12–18 mmol/L, and a variable urine anion gap, with Fanconi syndrome (glycosuria with normal blood glucose, phosphaturia, aminoaciduria, and low urate) and bone disease. RTA type 4 has a normal or mildly low GFR, high K+, a urine pH below 5.5, plasma HCO3− usually above 17 mmol/L, and a positive urine anion gap, with diabetes or culprit drugs and high urine Na+ despite a low-salt diet. CKD has a low GFR, normal or high K+, a urine pH usually below 5.5, HCO3− that falls as GFR falls, a positive urine anion gap, and high urea and creatinine. Before diagnosing an RTA, a UTI with a urease-producing organism, which raises urine pH, and low volume, which limits distal H+ secretion, are excluded; urine Na+ should be above 25 mmol/L.

Each AGMA cause has its own findings. Glycols give a high osmolal gap early, low Ca2+, rising creatinine, calcium oxalate crystals, and hematuria, after inebriation followed by flank pain and oliguria. Oxoproline gives normal lactate, no ketones, and 5-oxoproline in urine, with chronic paracetamol use and malnutrition. L-lactate is above 4 mmol/L in shock, sepsis, ischemia, metformin use, and liver failure, and D-lactate is high in short bowel syndrome. Methanol gives a high osmolal gap early, with blurred vision, dilated pupils, and papilledema. Aspirin gives a respiratory alkalosis with an AGMA and a measurable salicylate level, with tinnitus, nausea, and fast breathing. Renal failure gives high urea, creatinine, and phosphate, with reduced urine output. DKA gives high glucose and β-hydroxybutyrate, with K+ normal or high, and ketones and glucose in urine, after missed insulin, infection, or new diabetes. AKA and starvation give low or normal glucose with high β-hydroxybutyrate, and the urine dipstick, which detects acetoacetate, can show few ketones.

Management

Treatment is aimed at the cause, with volume and K+ replaced as needed. HCO3− is given when it has truly been lost, as oral alkali in RTA and CKD, but not routinely in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis, for the reasons set out in the review of .

In CKD, oral NaHCO3 protects bone and muscle and slows progression, and dialysis is needed when the disease is advanced. RTA type 1 responds to oral alkali in modest doses, with potassium citrate also replacing K+ and preventing stones, alongside treatment of the cause. RTA type 2 needs large doses of alkali with K+, because HCO3− given above the threshold is lost in urine and carries K+ with it; a thiazide can help by shrinking volume, and phosphate and vitamin D treat Fanconi bone disease. RTA type 4 is managed by stopping culprit drugs, a low-potassium diet, and a loop or thiazide diuretic, with fludrocortisone for aldosterone deficiency without hypertension or edema. Diarrhea and fistulas are managed by treating the cause, replacing fluid, K+, and HCO3−, and controlling the fistula, and saline-induced acidosis by switching to a balanced crystalloid such as Hartmann solution or Plasma-Lyte. Toxic alcohols are treated with fomepizole, or ethanol if it is unavailable, to block alcohol dehydrogenase, with hemodialysis for severe acidosis, visual change, AKI, or instability, and thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol. Oxoproline acidosis is treated by stopping paracetamol. Type A lactic acidosis is treated by restoring perfusion with fluids, vasopressors, ABX, and source control, and type B with thiamine and by stopping metformin, with hemodialysis if severe. D-lactic acidosis is treated by addressing the short bowel cause and limiting carbohydrate reaching the colon. Aspirin poisoning is treated with activated charcoal, IV NaHCO3 to alkalinize the urine and trap salicylate there, and hemodialysis if severe. Renal failure is treated with dialysis. DKA is treated with IV fluids, then insulin once K+ is at least 3.5 mmol/L, with K+ replacement, continuing insulin until the gap closes, and AKA and starvation with IV fluids with dextrose and thiamine and gradual feeding, watching for refeeding syndrome.

Relationships to other conditions

and . Acidosis usually raises K+, but the K+ in an acidosis points to its cause: a low K+ points to RTA types 1 or 2 or diarrhea, whereas a high K+ points to RTA type 4, CKD, or DKA before insulin. Correcting the acidosis moves K+ into cells, so K+ is replaced before or with alkali.

. Too little aldosterone, or resistance to it, causes the hyperkalemic NAGMA of RTA type 4, as in diabetic nephropathy, with ACEi, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, trimethoprim, and heparin, and in adrenal insufficiency.

. CKD causes a NAGMA early, as NH4+ production falls, and an AGMA late, as sulfate and phosphate are retained, so it appears on both sides of the anion gap; acidosis in turn speeds CKD progression, and oral NaHCO3 is used to slow it.

. Fluid lost below the stomach, as in diarrhea and pancreatic fistulas, causes a NAGMA, whereas fluid lost from the stomach causes a metabolic alkalosis. The two can coexist, as in DKA with vomiting, which the delta-delta ratio reveals as a value above 2.

Metabolic Alkalosis

Pathophysiology

A loss of H+ or a gain of HCO3− raises plasma HCO3− and pH, and the lungs hypoventilate to raise pCO2; the alkalosis lasts only while low volume, Cl−, or K+, or aldosterone excess keeps the kidney from excreting the extra HCO3−.

H+ + HCO3− ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ CO2 + H2O
FeatureChloride-responsiveChloride-resistant

What keeps it goingLow volume, Cl−, and K+Ongoing mineralocorticoid effect or tubular salt wasting
Urine Cl−Below 20 mmol/LAbove 20 mmol/L
Main sourcesVomiting, NG tube suction, past diuretics, after hypercapniaAldosterone excess and its mimics, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, diuretics still acting

What alkalosis does to K+ and Ca2+

  • AAlkalosis reverses the shiftH+ leaves cells and K+ enters them → hypokalemia, made worse by K+ lost in urine
  • BAlbumin binds more Ca2+In alkalosis, albumin gives up H+ and binds more Ca2+ in its place → ionized Ca2+ falls while total Ca2+ is unchanged → tetany

Why metabolic alkalosis lasts

Healthy kidneys excrete extra HCO3− quickly, so an alkalosis lasts only while something keeps the kidney reabsorbing it.

  1. GenerationH+ lost from the stomach or kidney, or HCO3− added
  2. Low volumeAngiotensin II increases proximal HCO3− reabsorption; aldosterone increases distal H+ and K+ secretion
  3. Low Cl−Too little Cl− reaches the collecting duct to swap for HCO3−, so HCO3− cannot be secreted
  4. Low K+Increases H+ secretion and NH4+ production, which makes new HCO3−
  5. Maintained alkalosisLasts until volume, Cl−, and K+ are replaced

Etiology

Causes

  • Gut
  • 1Vomiting and NG tube suctionLosing HCl leaves the HCO3− made by parietal cells in the blood; the volume and Cl− loss then keeps the kidney reabsorbing HCO3−; also chloride-losing diarrhea (villous adenoma, congenital chloridorrhea) and Cl− lost in the sweat of cystic fibrosis
  • Kidney
  • 2Loop and thiazide diureticsMore Na+ reaches the collecting duct, where aldosterone, raised by the volume loss, swaps it for H+ and K+; the extracellular fluid also shrinks around the same amount of HCO3− (contraction alkalosis)
  • 3Primary hyperaldosteronismAn adrenal adenoma (Conn syndrome) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia makes aldosterone regardless of renin → Na+ retention, hypertension, H+ and K+ loss
  • 4Secondary hyperaldosteronismHigh renin drives aldosterone: renal artery stenosis and renin-secreting tumors; low effective volume (heart failure, cirrhosis) does the same and keeps other alkaloses going
  • 5Apparent mineralocorticoid excessThe collecting duct acts as if aldosterone were high: Cushing syndrome (cortisol on the mineralocorticoid receptor), licorice (blocks 11β-HSD2, which normally inactivates cortisol), and Liddle syndrome (overactive ENaC)
  • 6Bartter and Gitelman syndromesInherited loss of NKCC2 in the loop (Bartter, like a lifelong loop diuretic) or NCC in the distal tubule (Gitelman, like a lifelong thiazide)
  • Other
  • 7Alkali loadMilk-alkali syndrome from calcium carbonate, HCO3− tablets or infusions, citrate from massive transfusion, and acetate in TPN; lasts mainly when the kidney cannot excrete HCO3− (CKD, low volume)
  • 8After hypercapniaIn chronic respiratory acidosis (COPD), the kidney retains HCO3−; when ventilation lowers pCO2 quickly, the extra HCO3− is left behind

Review article

Metabolic alkalosis: generation, maintenance, and the urine chloride

Metabolic alkalosis is a rise in plasma HCO3− from a loss of H+ or a gain of HCO3−, to which the lungs respond by hypoventilating to raise pCO2. Because healthy kidneys excrete extra HCO3− quickly, an alkalosis persists only while low volume, Cl−, or K+, or a mineralocorticoid effect, keeps the kidney reabsorbing it. Urine Cl− divides alkalosis into chloride-responsive forms, which correct with saline, and chloride-resistant forms, which BP, renin, and aldosterone then separate. Here, we review the mechanisms, causes, consequences, diagnosis, and management of metabolic alkalosis, and consider its relationship to disorders of potassium, aldosterone, volume, and metabolic acidosis.

Key points

  • Vomiting and NG tube suction remove HCl and generate an alkalosis; low volume, Cl−, and K+ maintain it.
  • Urine Cl− below 20 mmol/L marks a chloride-responsive alkalosis that corrects with saline and KCl; above 20, BP, renin, and aldosterone separate the causes.
  • Alkalosis moves K+ into cells and makes albumin bind more Ca2+, so hypokalemia and tetany with a normal total calcium are typical.
  • Acetazolamide treats an alkalosis when saline cannot be given, as in heart failure.

Pathophysiology

Plasma pH is set by the balance H+ + HCO3− ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ CO2 + H2O, with the kidney regulating HCO3− and the lungs regulating CO2. In metabolic alkalosis, H+ is lost from the stomach or kidney, or HCO3− is gained, and Cl− often falls too; the lungs hypoventilate to raise pCO2. In a chloride-responsive alkalosis, H+ and Cl− are lost from the stomach or by a diuretic that has worn off, and low volume, Cl−, and K+ keep it going; in a chloride-resistant alkalosis, the kidney loses H+ and K+ because aldosterone, or something acting like it, is high, or a diuretic is still acting.

Alkalosis moves H+ out of cells and K+ into them, causing hypokalemia that urinary K+ loss makes worse, and makes albumin give up H+ and bind more Ca2+, so ionized Ca2+ falls while total Ca2+ is unchanged.

Healthy kidneys excrete extra HCO3− quickly, so a metabolic alkalosis lasts only while something keeps the kidney reabsorbing it. After the alkalosis is generated, low volume raises angiotensin II, which increases proximal HCO3− reabsorption, and aldosterone, which increases distal H+ and K+ secretion. Low Cl− leaves too little Cl− in the collecting duct to exchange for HCO3−, so HCO3− cannot be secreted, and low K+ increases H+ secretion and NH4+ production, which makes new HCO3−. The alkalosis lasts until volume, Cl−, and K+ are replaced.

Etiology and mechanisms

Vomiting and NG tube suction remove HCl, leaving the HCO3− made by parietal cells in the blood, and the volume and Cl− loss then keeps the kidney reabsorbing HCO3−; chloride-losing diarrhea (villous adenoma and congenital chloridorrhea) and the Cl− lost in the sweat of cystic fibrosis act similarly. Loop and thiazide diuretics deliver more Na+ to the collecting duct, where aldosterone, raised by the volume loss, exchanges it for H+ and K+, and the extracellular fluid shrinks around the same amount of HCO3−, a contraction alkalosis. In primary hyperaldosteronism, an adrenal adenoma (Conn syndrome) or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia makes aldosterone regardless of renin, causing Na+ retention, hypertension, and H+ and K+ loss. In secondary hyperaldosteronism, high renin drives aldosterone, as in renal artery stenosis and renin-secreting tumors, and low effective volume in heart failure and cirrhosis does the same and keeps other alkaloses going. In apparent mineralocorticoid excess, the collecting duct behaves as if aldosterone were high: in Cushing syndrome, cortisol acts on the mineralocorticoid receptor; licorice blocks 11β-HSD2, which normally inactivates cortisol; and in Liddle syndrome, ENaC is overactive. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes are inherited losses of NKCC2 in the loop, like a lifelong loop diuretic, and of NCC in the distal tubule, like a lifelong thiazide. An alkali load, from calcium carbonate in milk-alkali syndrome, HCO3− tablets or infusions, citrate from massive transfusion, or acetate in TPN, lasts mainly when the kidney cannot excrete HCO3−, as in CKD or low volume. Finally, in chronic respiratory acidosis from COPD, the kidney retains HCO3−, and when ventilation lowers pCO2 quickly, the extra HCO3− is left behind.

Clinical presentation and complications

Metabolic alkalosis causes shallow, slow breathing that is usually mild but can worsen hypercapnia and hypoxemia in COPD or obesity hypoventilation. Hypokalemia causes muscle weakness and arrhythmias. Ionized Ca2+ falls, causing perioral numbness, paresthesias, carpopedal spasm, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and tetany. Arrhythmias come from low K+ and low Ca2+, and vessels constrict, including in the brain. The oxygen dissociation curve shifts left, releasing less O2 to tissues, and patients may have confusion, delirium, seizures, muscle cramps, and weakness.

Some findings point to the cause. Hypotension, tachycardia, and dry mucous membranes suggest volume loss from vomiting or diuretics, and hypertension with low K+ suggests aldosterone excess or its mimics. Failure to thrive, polyuria, and vomiting in a child suggest Bartter or Gitelman syndrome, and recent ventilation for COPD suggests an alkalosis left behind after hypercapnia.

Diagnosis

On an ABG or VBG, metabolic alkalosis is a pH above 7.45 with a high HCO3−, which moves the same way as the pH, and the compensation is checked as set out in the review of ; the urine Cl− then sorts the causes.

In metabolic alkalosis, urine Cl− below 20 mmol/L marks a chloride-responsive alkalosis, in which the kidney holds on to Cl− because volume and Cl− are low: vomiting and NG tube suction, diuretics that have worn off, chloride-losing diarrhea, cystic fibrosis, and the period after hypercapnia. Urine Cl− above 20 mmol/L marks a chloride-resistant alkalosis: diuretics still acting, aldosterone excess and its mimics, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, and severe hypokalemia. Urine Cl− is high while a diuretic acts and low once it wears off, so a changing result suggests hidden diuretic use. Vomiting and diuretics give low or normal BP with high renin and aldosterone and K+ lost mostly in urine. Primary hyperaldosteronism gives high BP, low renin, high aldosterone, and a high aldosterone-to-renin ratio; secondary hyperaldosteronism gives high BP with both high; and apparent mineralocorticoid excess gives high BP with both low. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes give low or normal BP with high renin and aldosterone, with high urine Ca2+ in Bartter syndrome and low urine Ca2+ with low Mg2+ in Gitelman syndrome. An alkali load gives variable values, with high Ca2+ in milk-alkali syndrome.

Management

Chloride-responsive alkalosis, from vomiting, NG tube suction, or after hypercapnia, is treated with 0.9% saline with KCl, which restores volume and Cl− so the kidney can excrete HCO3−, and the cause of vomiting is treated. Diuretic-induced alkalosis is managed by stopping or reducing the diuretic, replacing KCl, or adding a potassium-sparing diuretic, with acetazolamide if the patient is fluid overloaded. Primary hyperaldosteronism is treated with spironolactone or eplerenone, or adrenalectomy for a unilateral adenoma, and secondary hyperaldosteronism by treating its cause, such as renal artery stenosis or a renin-secreting tumor. In apparent mineralocorticoid excess, Cushing syndrome is treated, licorice is stopped, and Liddle syndrome is treated with amiloride, since its ENaC does not need aldosterone. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes need KCl and Mg2+, with potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, ACEi, or ARBs if K+ stays low. An alkali load is treated by stopping the source, with saline for milk-alkali syndrome. When saline cannot be given, as in heart failure, acetazolamide is used, and severe or refractory alkalosis is treated with dialysis against a low-bicarbonate bath or dilute HCl.

Relationships to other conditions

. Alkalosis lowers K+ by moving it into cells and by urinary loss, and hypokalemia itself maintains an alkalosis by increasing H+ secretion and NH4+ production, so K+ is replaced along with Cl−.

. Aldosterone excess causes a hypokalemic, chloride-resistant alkalosis with hypertension, and renin separates primary from secondary causes. Apparent mineralocorticoid excess resembles primary hyperaldosteronism but has low aldosterone, and Bartter and Gitelman syndromes resemble diuretic use with high renin but normal or low BP.

and . Volume loss maintains a metabolic alkalosis through angiotensin II and aldosterone, and saline corrects a chloride-responsive alkalosis by restoring it. In volume overload, where saline would worsen fluid retention, acetazolamide is used instead.

. Fluid lost from the stomach causes a metabolic alkalosis, whereas fluid lost below the stomach causes a NAGMA. An alkalosis can hide inside an AGMA, as in DKA with vomiting, where the delta-delta ratio is above 2.

Acid-base Disorders: Comparison and Workup

Comparison

Metabolic acidosis and alkalosis are mirror images: a primary fall or rise in HCO3− moves the pH the same way, the lungs compensate by changing pCO2, and one test, the anion gap or the urine Cl−, sorts each into its causes.

FeatureMetabolic acidosisMetabolic alkalosis
Primary changeFalls HCO3−: acid gained or HCO3− lostRises HCO3−: H+ lost or HCO3− gained
pHLow below 7.35High above 7.45
CompensationHyperventilation lowers pCO2Hypoventilation raises pCO2, rarely above 55 mmHg
BreathingKussmaul breathing: deep and rapidShallow and slow
Plasma K+High as K+ leaves cells, less so in organic acidoses; low in RTA types 1 and 2 and diarrheaLow as K+ enters cells and is lost in urine
Ionized Ca2+Rises; chronic acidosis draws on boneFalls as albumin binds more Ca2+ → tetany
O2 dissociation curveShifts right: more O2 releasedShifts left: less O2 released
Sorting testAnion gap: normal (NAGMA) or high (AGMA)Urine Cl−: below 20 mmol/L (chloride-responsive) or above (chloride-resistant)
Treatment principleTreat the cause; HCO3− only when it has truly been lostTreat the cause; saline and KCl when chloride-responsive; acid only if severe

The steps for reading any blood gas, and the compensation for every primary disorder, including the respiratory ones, are on Acid-base balance.

Diagnosis

  • pH 7.35–7.45
  • pCO2 35–45 mmHg
  • HCO3− 22–26 mmol/L
  • AG 12–16 mmol/L

Workup

1. Is the pH low or high? (ABG or VBG)Acidemia below 7.35; alkalemia above 7.45
2. Did HCO3− move the same way?Yes: a metabolic disorder. No: a respiratory one
3. Is the compensation what is expected?If not, a respiratory disorder is present as well
Acidosis
4. Anion gapNormal: urine AG, K+, and urine pH. High: delta-delta, osmolal gap, lactate, ketones, creatinine
Alkalosis
4. Urine Cl−Below 20 mmol/L: chloride-responsive. Above 20: check BP, renin, and aldosterone

3. Expected compensation

  • Metabolic acidosisExpected pCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 (± 2)The Winter formula. Other rules: pCO2 is about the last two digits of the pH, or falls about 1.2 mmHg for each 1 mmol/L fall in HCO3−
  • pCO2 higher than expectedA respiratory acidosis as well
  • pCO2 lower than expectedA respiratory alkalosis as well, as in aspirin poisoning
  • Metabolic alkalosisExpected pCO2 = 0.7 × HCO3− + 20 (± 5)Another rule: pCO2 rises 0.6–0.7 mmHg for each 1 mmol/L rise in HCO3− above 24. It rarely passes 55 mmHg, because hypoxia drives breathing
  • pCO2 higher than expectedA respiratory acidosis as well
  • pCO2 lower than expectedA respiratory alkalosis as well

4. Anion gap

Plasma has as many positive as negative charges; the gap is the negative charge that is not measured, mostly albumin. An acid with an unmeasured anion widens it, while HCO3− lost and replaced by Cl− leaves it unchanged.

AG = (Na+ + K+) − (Cl− + HCO3−); normal 12–16 mmol/L
  • Without K+AG = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−); normal 8–12 mmol/L
  • Low albuminEach 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers the gap by about 2.5, which can hide an AGMA; some add 2.5 for each 10 g/L below 40

A high anion gap: one disorder or two?

Delta-delta ratio = (AG − 16) ÷ (24 − HCO3−)

In a pure AGMA, each H+ that uses up one HCO3− leaves one unmeasured anion behind, so the rise in the gap roughly matches the fall in HCO3−. A mismatch shows a second metabolic disorder. Without K+ in the gap, use 12 in place of 16.

  • Below 1HCO3− fell more than the gap rose → an AGMA with a NAGMA, as in DKA with diarrhea
  • 1–2A pure AGMA
  • Above 2HCO3− fell less than the gap rose → an AGMA with a metabolic alkalosis, as in DKA with vomiting, or a high HCO3− from before
Osmolal gap = measured osmolality − (2 × Na+ + glucose + urea); normal below 10, concerning above 15
  • Other formulas2 × (Na+ + K+) + glucose + urea; some add ethanol when it is present
  • High osmolal gap with AGMAToxic alcohol: methanol or ethylene glycol
  • High osmolal gap without acidosisEarly toxic alcohol, before it is metabolized; isopropyl alcohol, which is made into acetone, an uncharged ketone (ketosis without acidosis)
  • Normal osmolal gap late after ingestionDoes not exclude a toxic alcohol: as the alcohol becomes acid, the osmolal gap closes and the anion gap widens

Patterns

If there isPoints to
Low pH, low HCO3−, normal gap, negative urine AGHCO3− lost from the gut or given saline:
Low pH, low HCO3−, normal gap, positive urine AGRTA or CKD
Low pH, low HCO3−, high gap, high osmolal gapMethanol or ethylene glycol
High gap with a delta-delta ratio above 2AGMA with a metabolic alkalosis, as in DKA with vomiting
AGMA with pCO2 lower than expectedA respiratory alkalosis as well, as in aspirin poisoning
High pH, high HCO3−, urine Cl− below 20 mmol/LVomiting, NG suction, or past diuretics:
High pH, high HCO3−, urine Cl− above 20 mmol/L, high BPAldosterone excess or its mimics
High pH, high HCO3−, urine Cl− above 20 mmol/L, normal BPDiuretics still acting, or Bartter or Gitelman syndrome

Treatment

Both disorders are corrected by treating the cause and replacing volume and K+; the kidney then restores HCO3− itself, so HCO3− or acid is given only in specific situations.

Giving HCO3− in acidosis

  • NAGMAHCO3− has truly been lost, so oral alkali (NaHCO3 or potassium citrate) is used for RTA and CKD
  • AGMA from lactate or ketoacidsNot routine: once the cause is treated, lactate and ketoanions are metabolized back into HCO3−, so added HCO3− can overshoot into alkalosis
  • RisksHypernatremia, fluid overload, low ionized Ca2+, and hypokalemia as K+ moves into cells

Correcting an alkalosis

  • Chloride-responsive0.9% saline with KCl restores volume and Cl−, so the kidney can excrete the extra HCO3−
  • Chloride-resistantSaline does not correct it; treat the aldosterone excess or tubular defect and replace K+
  • Saline cannot be givenAcetazolamide, as in heart failure
  • Severe or refractoryDialysis with a low-bicarbonate bath, or dilute HCl

Review article

Metabolic acid-base disorders: a shared approach to the blood gas, compensation, and the sorting tests

Metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis are mirror images in which a primary fall or rise in plasma HCO3− moves the pH in the same direction and the lungs compensate by changing pCO2. A single approach serves both: the pH and HCO3− identify a metabolic disorder, an expected pCO2 tests whether a respiratory disorder coexists, and one further test sorts the causes, the anion gap in acidosis and the urine Cl− in alkalosis. Here, we compare the two disorders, describe the stepwise workup and its calculations, and set out the principles of correction, including when HCO3− or acid should be given.

Key points

  • A metabolic disorder is present when HCO3− moves in the same direction as the pH.
  • Expected pCO2 is 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 (± 2) in acidosis (Winter formula) and 0.7 × HCO3− + 20 (± 5) in alkalosis; a pCO2 outside this range means a respiratory disorder as well.
  • The anion gap, (Na+ + K+) − (Cl− + HCO3−), is normally 12–16 mmol/L and falls by about 2.5 for each 10 g/L fall in albumin.
  • A delta-delta ratio below 1 adds a NAGMA, and above 2 a metabolic alkalosis; a high osmolal gap with an AGMA suggests a toxic alcohol.
  • Urine Cl− below 20 mmol/L marks a chloride-responsive alkalosis, corrected by saline with KCl.
  • HCO3− is given when it has truly been lost, as in RTA and CKD, but not routinely in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis.

Comparison

A metabolic acidosis follows a gain of acid or a loss of HCO3−, and the lungs hyperventilate to lower pCO2; a metabolic alkalosis follows a loss of H+ or a gain of HCO3−, and the lungs hypoventilate to raise pCO2, rarely above 55 mmHg. The disorders have opposite effects beyond the pH: acidosis moves K+ out of cells, raises ionized Ca2+, and shifts the O2 dissociation curve to the right, whereas alkalosis moves K+ into cells, lowers ionized Ca2+ as albumin binds more of it, and shifts the curve to the left. Acidosis causes Kussmaul breathing, and alkalosis shallow, slow breathing. Plasma K+ in acidosis is often high, but less so in organic acidoses, and low in RTA types 1 and 2 and diarrhea.

Diagnosis

An ABG or VBG first shows whether the pH is low or high, and a HCO3− that has moved the same way identifies a metabolic disorder. The expected pCO2 is then calculated, by the Winter formula, 1.5 × HCO3− + 8 (± 2), in acidosis, or 0.7 × HCO3− + 20 (± 5) in alkalosis; a higher pCO2 than expected means a respiratory acidosis as well, and a lower one a respiratory alkalosis, as in aspirin poisoning.

In acidosis, the anion gap, (Na+ + K+) − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally 12–16 mmol/L or 8–12 mmol/L without K+, separates NAGMA from AGMA. The gap is mostly albumin, so each 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers it by about 2.5 and can hide an AGMA. In an AGMA, the delta-delta ratio, (AG − 16) ÷ (24 − HCO3−), is 1–2 when the acidosis is pure, below 1 when a NAGMA coexists, and above 2 when a metabolic alkalosis coexists, as in DKA with vomiting. An osmolal gap, measured osmolality − (2 × Na+ + glucose + urea), above 15 with an AGMA suggests methanol or ethylene glycol; it can be high without acidosis early after ingestion or with isopropyl alcohol, and it closes as the alcohol is metabolized, so a normal value late does not exclude poisoning. In a NAGMA, a negative urine AG shows a normal renal response to HCO3− lost from the gut or to saline, and a positive one points to RTA or CKD. In alkalosis, urine Cl− below 20 mmol/L marks a chloride-responsive disorder and above 20 mmol/L a chloride-resistant one, which BP, renin, and aldosterone then separate.

Management

Both disorders are corrected by treating the cause and replacing volume and K+. HCO3− is given when it has truly been lost, as oral alkali in RTA and CKD, but not routinely in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis, whose anions are metabolized back into HCO3− once the cause is treated, so that added HCO3− can overshoot into alkalosis; its risks are hypernatremia, fluid overload, low ionized Ca2+, and hypokalemia. A chloride-responsive alkalosis is corrected by 0.9% saline with KCl, which lets the kidney excrete the extra HCO3−; acetazolamide is used when saline cannot be given, and dialysis or dilute HCl for severe or refractory alkalosis.

Relationships to other conditions

and . The condition reviews set out the causes that the anion gap and urine Cl− sort, with their specific findings and treatment. The two disorders can coexist, which the delta-delta ratio reveals, as when vomiting complicates DKA.

and potassium. Volume loss drives a chloride-responsive alkalosis and can cause a lactic acidosis, and the shifts of K+ in both disorders link them to and .

Hypovolemia

Pathophysiology

Losing salt and water from the ECF faster than they are replaced shrinks the circulating volume and lowers tissue perfusion, until the sympathetic system, RAAS, and ADH make the kidney retain Na+ and water to restore it.

How the loss changes the compartments

Where the fluid comes from depends on what is lost; the compartments themselves are described on Fluids.

  • Isotonic lossBleeding, vomiting, and diarrhea remove fluid with about as much Na+ as plasma, so only the ECF shrinks and plasma Na+ is unchanged
  • More water than Na+Sweat and osmotic diuresis concentrate the ECF, which draws water out of cells, so both compartments shrink and plasma Na+ rises
  • Third spacingFluid leaves plasma for the interstitium or a body cavity; total body water is unchanged, but the circulating volume falls

Note: Hypovolemia is a loss of salt and water, whereas dehydration is a loss of water alone, which raises plasma Na+ (see Hypernatremia).

How the body responds

  1. Less stretchBaroreceptors, the atria, and the afferent arteriole sense a lower volume
  2. Sympathetic system, RAAS, ADHFaster heart rate and vasoconstriction; angiotensin II and aldosterone retain Na+; ADH retains water
  3. RetentionConcentrated urine with Na+ below 20 mmol/L, until volume is restored

Each step is described on Volume and Osmolality Regulation.

Etiology

Causes

  • Renal loss
  • 1DiureticsLoop diuretics block NKCC2 and thiazides block NCC, so Na+ and water leave in the urine; too high a dose, or continued use while eating and drinking little
  • 2Osmotic diuresisGlucose in DKA and HHS, mannitol, and urea hold water in the tubule, and Na+ is lost with it; more water than Na+ is lost
  • 3Aldosterone deficiencyIn adrenal insufficiency and hypoaldosteronism, the collecting duct cannot reclaim Na+, so Na+ is lost with K+ retained; salt craving, and skin pigmentation in primary adrenal insufficiency
  • 4Cerebral salt wastingAfter SAH or other brain injury, the kidney wastes Na+, possibly through BNP or reduced sympathetic drive to the kidney rather than low aldosterone; unlike SIADH, the patient is hypovolemic
  • 5Salt-wasting nephropathyKidney disease that cannot reclaim Na+, and Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, which act like lifelong loop and thiazide diuretics
  • Extra-renal loss: the big 5
  • 6VomitingGastric fluid, including NG tube suction, is lost → metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia
  • 7DiarrheaThe gut secretes 3–6 L a day and normally reabsorbs it, so diarrhea, high-output stomas, and fistulas lose large volumes → NAGMA and hypokalemia
  • 8SweatingExercise in heat can lose 1–2 L an hour; sweat has less Na+ than plasma
  • 9BurnsFluid is lost from the burned surface, and histamine and free radicals make capillaries leak, so burns also cause third spacing
  • 10BleedingTrauma most often, then GI bleeding, surgery, ruptured aneurysm, and postpartum hemorrhage; whole blood is lost, red cells with the plasma
  • Third spacing
  • 11PancreatitisIL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α make capillaries leak, and fluid moves into the interstitium and retroperitoneum
  • 12PeritonitisThe inflamed peritoneum leaks fluid into the peritoneal cavity and bowel wall
  • 13SepsisCytokines released throughout the body make capillaries leak everywhere, while vasodilation adds a distributive shock
  • 14Bowel obstruction and surgeryFluid pools in obstructed bowel and in inflamed tissue after surgery

Symptoms and complications

Features

FeatureWhat is seenWhy
Early symptomsThirst, fatigue, muscle cramps, postural dizziness, and less urineMild loss is compensated, so BP is still normal
TachycardiaRising heart rate, often the first signThe baroreceptor reflex: less arterial stretch → more sympathetic and less vagal drive
HypotensionFirst on standing (orthostatic), then lying down; late in children and young adultsCompensation fails after about 20–25% of the effective arterial volume is lost
Poor skin perfusionCool, pale, clammy, or mottled skin; capillary refill above 2 seconds; dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; low JVPSympathetic vasoconstriction diverts blood from skin to vital organs
High lactateLactate rises, with a high anion gap acidosis and fast breathingToo little oxygen reaches tissues → anaerobic glycolysis turns pyruvate into lactate (type A lactic acidosis); used to judge severity and response
Organ hypoperfusionConfusion and lethargy, abdominal pain, chest pain, oliguriaBrain, gut, heart, and kidneys are underperfused
Prerenal AKIUrea and creatinine rise, UCR above 100, urine Na+ below 20 mmol/L, FENa below 1%Low renal perfusion lowers GFR; the intact tubules reclaim Na+ and water, and urea with them; prolonged ischemia leads to ATN
Hypovolemic shockHypotension, lactic acidosis, and failing organsCompensated (pre-shock) at about 10% loss, shock at 20–25%, then irreversible organ damage

Clues to the cause

If there isPoints to
Metabolic alkalosis with low K+Vomiting (6) or diuretics (1)
NAGMA with low K+Diarrhea, stomas, or fistulas (7)
High K+ and low Na+ with salt cravingAldosterone deficiency (3)
High glucose and polyuriaOsmotic diuresis in DKA or HHS (2)
Low Na+ and high urine Na+ after SAHCerebral salt wasting (4)
Falling hemoglobinBleeding (10)
Edema or ascites with low BPThird spacing (11–14) or low albumin

Diagnosis

Assess volume status at the bedside and with tests as on ; bleeding comes first, then the urine Na+ shows whether the kidney is the source.

Urine Na+: is the kidney the source?

  • Urine Na+ below 20 mmol/LThe kidney is retaining Na+, as it should: extra-renal loss or third spacing
  • Urine Na+ above 20 mmol/L despite hypovolemiaDiuretics, kidney disease, aldosterone deficiency, or cerebral salt wasting (1–5); also metabolic alkalosis, where Na+ leaves with HCO3−

Treatment

Restore volume and treat the cause, while watching for fluid overload.

Steps and fluids

  1. Bleeding or not?Bleeding needs source control and blood products (plasma, platelets, and red cells in a 1:1:1 ratio), with crystalloid kept to a minimum
  2. Isotonic crystalloidGive boluses and reassess after each one; take care in HF, CKD, and cirrhosis
  3. Treat the causeStop diuretics, give antiemetics, insulin for DKA, ABX and source control for sepsis
  4. VasopressorsOnly if hypotension persists despite adequate fluid
  5. MaintenanceOnce stable, maintenance fluid plus ongoing losses, or stop fluid

Choosing between crystalloids, albumin, and hypotonic fluids is set out on .

  • KClAdded when K+ is low or about to fall: vomiting (6), diarrhea (7), diuretics (1), and DKA once insulin starts (2)
  • HCO3−Replaces HCO3− lost in diarrhea and fistulas (7) with a NAGMA
  • Dextrose (D5)Added to NS or ½NS when glucose falls in DKA, so insulin can continue until the ketoacidosis clears
  • MonitorHeart rate, BP, urine output, mental state, and lactate; crackles, edema, and JVP for overload; daily weight and fluid balance; Na+, K+, Cl−, glucose, and creatinine, raising a low Na+ by no more than 8 mmol/L in 24 hours
