Review article

Disorders of plasma sodium: tonicity, the urine, and the pace of correction

Plasma Na+ reflects water rather than total body Na+: hyponatremia means too much water for the Na+ in the body and hypernatremia too little. Both disorders are approached by asking what the kidney is doing with water, using serum and urine osmolality, volume status, and urine Na+, and both are corrected at a limited rate once the brain has adapted, because rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination or cerebral edema. Here, we compare the two disorders, describe the workup of each, and review the fluids and drugs that raise or lower plasma Na+.

Key points

  • Serum osmolality separates true, hypotonic hyponatremia from hypertonic hyponatremia and pseudohyponatremia.
  • In hyponatremia, urine osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg means ADH is suppressed, as in primary polydipsia and low solute intake.
  • Urine Na+ below 30 mmol/L in hyponatremia means the kidney is holding Na+ because it senses low effective volume.
  • In hypernatremia, urine osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg suggests DI, 300–600 a renal water loss, and above 600 a loss elsewhere or Na+ gained.
  • Water deficit = total body water × (Na+ ÷ 140 − 1), replaced over 48–72 hours with ongoing losses.
  • Chronic hyponatremia is raised by no more than 6–8 mmol/L in 24 hours, and chronic hypernatremia lowered by no more than 10–12 mmol/L.

Comparison

Because Na+ cannot move without water but water can move without Na+, a change in plasma Na+ concentration reflects a change in water. In hyponatremia, plasma becomes dilute, water enters brain cells, and cerebral edema follows; in hypernatremia, water leaves brain cells and the brain shrinks, so bridging veins can tear. Over about 48 hours, brain cells adapt by shedding or gaining solutes, which is why chronic disorders cause fewer symptoms and why correcting them too fast causes osmotic demyelination syndrome after hyponatremia and cerebral edema after hypernatremia.

Diagnosis

In hyponatremia, serum osmolality, 2 × Na+ + glucose + urea, normally 275–295 mOsm/kg, is checked first: it is high when glucose, mannitol, or radiocontrast draw water out of cells, normal in pseudohyponatremia from very high lipids or proteins, and low in true hyponatremia. Urine osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg then shows that ADH is suppressed and intake outruns excretion, while a higher value shows that ADH is acting. Volume status and urine Na+ complete the workup: urine Na+ below 30 mmol/L means the kidney is holding Na+, after extra-renal loss or in HF and cirrhosis, while a higher value points to renal loss, SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, or kidney failure.

In hypernatremia, the cause is usually clear from the history and volume status. Urine osmolality below 300 mOsm/kg means ADH is missing or ignored, as in DI; 300–600 mOsm/kg means a solute, a loop diuretic, kidney disease, or partial DI; and above 600 mOsm/kg means the kidney is concentrating, so water has been lost elsewhere or not taken in, or Na+ has been gained, which urine Na+ separates. The water deficit, total body water × (Na+ ÷ 140 − 1), guides replacement.

Management

Low Na+ is raised with 3% saline for severe symptoms, NS for hypovolemic forms, and water restriction, salt restriction, loop diuretics, vaptans, oral urea, or salt tablets according to the cause; desmopressin or D5W bring the Na+ back down if correction is too fast. High Na+ is lowered with water by mouth or tube where possible, otherwise D5W or ½NS, after NS or LR to restore volume in shock; desmopressin treats central DI, a thiazide nephrogenic DI, and a loop diuretic with D5W removes gained Na+. Na+ is checked often during correction.

Relationships to other conditions

and . The condition reviews cover the causes that this workup sorts and their specific treatment.

and . These are the two disorders of ADH itself: too much ADH holds water and causes euvolemic hyponatremia, and too little or ignored ADH loses water and causes hypernatremia with dilute urine.

Hypokalemia

Pathophysiology

A plasma K+ below 3.5 mmol/L means K+ has shifted into cells, too little has been taken in, or K+ has been lost through the gut or, most often, the kidney; because the resting membrane potential depends on the K+ gradient, a low K+ hyperpolarizes muscle and nerve, weakening them, while it slows cardiac repolarization and makes arrhythmias likely.

SeverityPlasma K+Usual picture
MildLow below 3.5 mmol/LOften no symptoms
ModerateLow below 3.0 mmol/LWeakness, cramps, constipation, and ECG changes
SevereLow below 2.5 mmol/LParalysis, rhabdomyolysis, ileus, and arrhythmias

Moving K+ into cells

  • AInsulinActivates the Na+/K+-ATPase in muscle and liver, so K+ enters cells with glucose; why treating DKA and refeeding lower K+
  • Bβ2 agonistsRaise cAMP, which activates the same pump: salbutamol, adrenaline, and the surge of adrenaline in acute illness
  • CAlkalosisH+ leaves cells to buffer the blood and K+ enters in its place; a small effect beside the renal K+ loss that comes with metabolic alkalosis

Losing K+ in the urine

  1. More Na+ reaches the collecting ductWith more flow, from diuretics, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, or osmotic diuresis
  2. ENaC takes up the Na+The lumen becomes more negative; aldosterone adds ENaC channels and pumps
  3. K+ is secreted through ROMKDown its electrical gradient into the urine; low Mg2+ releases the brake on ROMK
  4. K+ fallsAnd low K+ itself increases H+ secretion and NH4+ production, which keeps an alkalosis going

The principal cell and what drives its K+ secretion are drawn on Potassium balance.

Note: The same three levers that lower K+ are used in reverse to treat hyperkalemia: insulin, salbutamol, and HCO3−.

Etiology

  • Shift into cells
  • 1InsulinInsulin treatment, especially when DKA or HHS is treated; refeeding after starvation, which also lowers phosphate and Mg2+
  • 2β2 agonists and catecholaminesHigh-dose salbutamol, adrenaline, the stress of acute illness, and thyrotoxicosis
  • 3AlkalosisMetabolic or respiratory; the shift is small, and metabolic alkalosis lowers K+ mainly through the kidney
  • 4Periodic paralysis, new cells, and coldHypokalemic periodic paralysis, familial or with thyrotoxicosis, causes attacks of weakness with a normal K+ between them; rapid blood cell production, as when megaloblastic anemia is treated, and hypothermia also move K+ into cells
  • Too little taken in
  • 5Poor intakeEating disorders, restrictive diets, and alcohol use; rarely enough alone, because the kidney can cut its excretion, but it adds to other causes such as diuretics
  • Lost through the gut
  • 6Diarrhea and laxativesThe most common cause outside the kidney: diarrhea, laxative abuse, fistulas, and bowel diversion lose K+ with HCO3−, giving a NAGMA
  • 7Vomiting and NG suctionGastric fluid holds little K+; most is lost in the urine, as HCO3− carries Na+ to the collecting duct and volume loss raises aldosterone, giving a metabolic alkalosis
  • Lost through the kidney
  • 8DiureticsLoop and thiazide diuretics deliver more Na+ and flow to the collecting duct, and the volume loss raises aldosterone; the usual reason for a low K+ in HF and cirrhosis
  • 9HyperaldosteronismPrimary, from an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia (Conn syndrome), with hypertension and low renin; secondary, with high renin, from renal artery stenosis, a renin-secreting tumor, or malignant hypertension (see Hypoaldosteronism and hyperaldosteronism)
  • 10AME and Liddle syndromeLicorice, severe Cushing syndrome, and some forms of CAH let other steroids act on the MR; in Liddle syndrome ENaC stays open; all cause hypertension with low renin and low aldosterone
  • 11RTA types 1 and 2A hypokalemic NAGMA: in type 1, the collecting duct cannot secrete H+, so more K+ is secreted; in type 2, HCO3− escapes the proximal tubule and carries Na+ and K+ out (see Metabolic acidosis)
  • 12HypomagnesemiaMg2+ normally limits K+ loss through ROMK, so a low Mg2+ lets more K+ out; from alcohol use, chronic diarrhea such as Crohn disease, diuretics, and PPIs; K+ stays low until Mg2+ is replaced
  • 13Bartter and Gitelman syndromesInherited loss of NKCC2 (Bartter) or NCC (Gitelman), like a lifelong loop or thiazide diuretic: a hypokalemic alkalosis with normal BP and high renin; Gitelman syndrome also lowers Mg2+ and urine Ca2+
  • 14Osmotic diuresis and drugsGlucose in uncontrolled DM and mannitol raise flow; amphotericin B and high-dose penicillins also increase K+ loss

Note: With hypertension, think of aldosterone or its mimics (9, 10); with a normal or low BP, think of diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, RTA, or Bartter and Gitelman syndromes.

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms usually appear below 3.0 mmol/L and are worse when K+ falls quickly; muscle and nerve become less excitable, while the heart becomes more excitable.

Why tissues respond differently

  • Skeletal muscle and nerveThe membrane is hyperpolarized, further from threshold: weakness, cramps, low reflexes, and in severe cases ascending paralysis and respiratory failure
  • Smooth muscleConstipation, and ileus when severe
  • HeartRepolarization slows and the action potential lengthens, so early afterdepolarizations trigger PVCs, PSVT, A-fib, VT, and VF, with TdP when the QT is long

The ECG

  • AFlat or inverted T waveThe earliest sign of slowed repolarization
  • BST depressionSagging below the isoelectric line
  • CU waveAfter the T wave, and larger than it in severe hypokalemia
  • DLong QU intervalT and U merge and can look like a long QT, with a risk of TdP

Complications

  • Arrhythmias and sudden deathMost dangerous with heart disease, an MI, or digoxin
  • Digoxin toxicityA low K+ increases the effect of digoxin, so toxicity appears at usual doses
  • RhabdomyolysisIn severe hypokalemia, with myoglobinuria and AKI
  • Paralysis and ileusRespiratory failure when the breathing muscles are affected
  • KidneyNephrogenic DI with polyuria; more NH4+ production; with long-standing hypokalemia, tubulointerstitial disease and cysts
  • GlucoseLess insulin is released, so glucose tolerance worsens

Diagnosis

Check the ECG and Mg2+ first; the history (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, laxatives, insulin, salbutamol, licorice) usually gives the cause, and urine K+, the blood gas, and BP with renin and aldosterone sort the rest, as on .

By cause

ForObtain
Shift (1–4)Glucose and insulin given, drugs, and TSH when attacks of weakness suggest thyrotoxic periodic paralysis; urine K+ is low
Gut loss (6, 7)Urine K+ low after diarrhea, with a NAGMA; after vomiting, urine K+ is high but urine Cl− low, with an alkalosis
Diuretics (8)Urine K+ and Cl− high while they are taken; a urine diuretic screen if use is hidden
Aldosterone and its mimics (9, 10)Renin and aldosterone: high aldosterone with low renin in primary, both high in secondary, both low in AME and Liddle syndrome
RTA (11)A NAGMA on the blood gas, with urine pH and the urine anion gap (see Metabolic acidosis)
Hypomagnesemia (12)Mg2+, and Ca2+, which often falls with it
Bartter and Gitelman syndromes (13)High renin and aldosterone with normal BP, urine Cl− high; low Mg2+ and low urine Ca2+ in Gitelman syndrome
Osmotic diuresis (14)Glucose and urine osmolality

Treatment

Replace K+, by mouth when possible and IV for severe hypokalemia, paralysis, or arrhythmias, replace Mg2+ at the same time, and treat the cause; the forms, rates, and cautions are on .

By cause

CauseTreatment
Insulin and β2 agonists (1, 2)Replace cautiously and monitor, because K+ returns from cells when the cause stops
Periodic paralysis (4)Small doses of K+, with a high risk of rebound hyperkalemia; treat thyrotoxicosis
Diarrhea (6)K+ citrate or bicarbonate when there is acidosis, otherwise KCl; treat the cause
Vomiting (7)0.9% saline with KCl, which restores volume and Cl− so the kidney stops losing K+
Diuretics (8)Reduce the dose, add KCl, or add a potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone, eplerenone, or amiloride)
Primary hyperaldosteronism (9)Spironolactone or eplerenone; adrenalectomy for a unilateral adenoma
AME and Liddle syndrome (10)Stop licorice and treat Cushing syndrome; amiloride for Liddle syndrome, since its ENaC does not need aldosterone

Review article

Hypokalemia: shifts into cells, losses through the gut and kidney, and a hyperpolarized membrane

Hypokalemia, a plasma K+ below 3.5 mmol/L, follows a shift of K+ into cells, too little intake, or loss through the gut or, most often, the kidney. Because the resting membrane potential depends on the K+ gradient, a low K+ hyperpolarizes skeletal muscle, smooth muscle, and nerve, causing weakness, ileus, and paralysis, while it slows cardiac repolarization and predisposes to tachyarrhythmias. The cause is usually clear from the history, and urine K+, the acid-base state, and blood pressure with renin and aldosterone sort the remainder. Treatment replaces K+ and Mg2+ and addresses the cause. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider its relationships to hyperkalemia, the acid-base disorders, aldosterone excess, and hypovolemia.

Key points

  • Hypokalemia is mild below 3.5 mmol/L, moderate below 3.0, and severe below 2.5.
  • Insulin and β2 agonists activate the Na+/K+-ATPase and move K+ into cells; alkalosis does so through H+ leaving cells.
  • Renal K+ loss follows more Na+ and flow reaching the collecting duct, more aldosterone or a mimic of it, or a low Mg2+; most K+ lost after vomiting is lost in the urine.
  • The ECG shows flat T waves, ST depression, U waves, and a long QU interval, with a risk of TdP and digoxin toxicity.
  • Urine K+ below 15 mmol/L points to loss outside the kidney or low intake; above it, the blood gas and BP separate RTA, vomiting and diuretics, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, and aldosterone excess.
  • K+ is replaced by mouth when possible and IV for severe or symptomatic hypokalemia, with Mg2+ corrected, since a low Mg2+ keeps K+ low.

Pathophysiology

Plasma K+ is a small extracellular share of a large intracellular store, so it falls when K+ moves into cells or when the body loses more than it takes in. Insulin activates the Na+/K+-ATPase in muscle and liver, β2 agonists activate the same pump through cAMP, and in alkalosis H+ leaves cells to buffer the blood while K+ enters in its place, although this shift is small beside the renal loss that accompanies metabolic alkalosis. In the collecting duct, Na+ taken up through ENaC leaves the lumen negative, and K+ is secreted through ROMK down that gradient; more Na+ and flow reaching the duct, as with diuretics, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, or osmotic diuresis, more aldosterone, which adds ENaC channels and pumps, and a low Mg2+, which removes a brake on ROMK, all increase K+ loss. A low K+ in turn increases H+ secretion and NH4+ production and so sustains a metabolic alkalosis. Severity is graded by plasma K+: mild below 3.5 mmol/L, often without symptoms, moderate below 3.0, and severe below 2.5, when paralysis, rhabdomyolysis, ileus, and arrhythmias occur.

Etiology and mechanisms

Shifts into cells. Insulin treatment, especially of DKA or HHS, and refeeding after starvation, which also lowers phosphate and Mg2+, move K+ into cells, as do high-dose salbutamol, adrenaline, the stress of acute illness, thyrotoxicosis, and alkalosis. Hypokalemic periodic paralysis, familial or with thyrotoxicosis, causes attacks of weakness with a normal K+ between them, and rapid blood cell production, as when megaloblastic anemia is treated, and hypothermia also lower K+.

Intake and the gut. Poor intake from eating disorders, restrictive diets, or alcohol use rarely causes hypokalemia alone, because the kidney can cut its excretion, but it adds to other causes. Diarrhea is the most common cause outside the kidney: diarrhea, laxative abuse, fistulas, and bowel diversion lose K+ with HCO3− and cause a NAGMA. Vomiting and NG suction lose little K+ directly; most is lost in the urine, because HCO3− carries Na+ to the collecting duct while volume loss raises aldosterone.

The kidney. Loop and thiazide diuretics are the usual cause of hypokalemia in HF and cirrhosis. Primary hyperaldosteronism, from an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia, causes hypertension with low renin, and secondary hyperaldosteronism, from renal artery stenosis, a renin-secreting tumor, or malignant hypertension, causes it with high renin. Licorice, severe Cushing syndrome, and some forms of CAH let other steroids act on the MR, and in Liddle syndrome ENaC stays open; these cause hypertension with low renin and low aldosterone. RTA type 1, in which the collecting duct cannot secrete H+, and type 2, in which HCO3− escapes the proximal tubule, cause a hypokalemic NAGMA. Hypomagnesemia from alcohol use, chronic diarrhea such as Crohn disease, diuretics, or PPIs increases K+ loss and makes the hypokalemia refractory. Bartter and Gitelman syndromes, inherited loss of NKCC2 or NCC, resemble lifelong loop or thiazide use, with normal BP and high renin, and Gitelman syndrome also lowers Mg2+ and urine Ca2+. Osmotic diuresis, amphotericin B, and high-dose penicillins complete the list.

Clinical presentation and complications

Symptoms usually appear below 3.0 mmol/L and are worse when K+ falls quickly. Hyperpolarized skeletal muscle and nerve cause weakness, cramps, low reflexes, and, when severe, ascending paralysis and respiratory failure; smooth muscle causes constipation and ileus. In the heart, slowed repolarization lengthens the action potential and early afterdepolarizations trigger PVCs, PSVT, A-fib, VT, VF, and TdP. The ECG shows flat or inverted T waves, ST depression, U waves that can exceed the T wave, and a long QU interval that can resemble a long QT. Arrhythmias are most dangerous with heart disease, an MI, or digoxin, whose effect a low K+ increases. Severe hypokalemia causes rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria and AKI, and chronic hypokalemia causes nephrogenic DI, increased NH4+ production, tubulointerstitial disease and cysts, and glucose intolerance from reduced insulin release.

Diagnosis

The ECG and Mg2+ are checked first. The history of diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea, laxatives, insulin, salbutamol, or licorice usually gives the cause, and the workup set out in the review of sorts the rest. A shift leaves urine K+ low, and TSH is checked when attacks of weakness suggest thyrotoxic periodic paralysis. After diarrhea, urine K+ is low with a NAGMA; after vomiting, urine K+ is high but urine Cl− low, with an alkalosis; with current diuretics, urine K+ and Cl− are both high, and a urine diuretic screen detects hidden use. Renin and aldosterone separate primary hyperaldosteronism, with high aldosterone and low renin, from secondary, with both high, and from apparent mineralocorticoid excess and Liddle syndrome, with both low. RTA shows a NAGMA with an abnormal urine pH or urine anion gap, Bartter and Gitelman syndromes high renin and aldosterone with normal BP, and osmotic diuresis a high glucose or urine osmolality.

Management

K+ is replaced by mouth when possible and IV for severe hypokalemia, paralysis, or arrhythmias, with Mg2+ replaced at the same time, as set out in the review of . Shifts from insulin or β2 agonists are replaced cautiously, because K+ returns from cells when the cause stops, and periodic paralysis carries a particular risk of rebound hyperkalemia. Diarrhea is treated with K+ citrate or bicarbonate when there is acidosis and otherwise KCl, and vomiting with 0.9% saline and KCl, which restores volume and Cl− so the kidney stops losing K+. Diuretic-induced loss is managed by reducing the dose, adding KCl, or adding spironolactone, eplerenone, or amiloride. Primary hyperaldosteronism is treated with spironolactone or eplerenone or by adrenalectomy for a unilateral adenoma; licorice is stopped and Cushing syndrome treated, and Liddle syndrome is treated with amiloride. RTA is treated with oral K+ citrate, replacing K+ before or with alkali, hypomagnesemia with Mg2+, IV MgSO4 when severe, and Bartter and Gitelman syndromes with KCl and Mg2+, adding potassium-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, ACEi, or ARBs if K+ stays low.

Relationships to other conditions

. The two disorders share their levers: insulin, β2 agonists, and alkali move K+ into cells and so cause hypokalemia or treat hyperkalemia, and aldosterone excess causes hypokalemia while its deficiency causes hyperkalemia. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes cells and causes tachyarrhythmias, whereas hyperkalemia depolarizes them and causes bradyarrhythmias and AV block. Over-replacement of K+ turns one into the other.

and . Vomiting, diuretics, aldosterone excess, and Bartter and Gitelman syndromes cause a hypokalemic alkalosis that low K+ helps sustain, whereas diarrhea and RTA types 1 and 2 cause a hypokalemic NAGMA; the acid-base state therefore narrows the cause.

. Primary and secondary hyperaldosteronism cause hypokalemia with hypertension, and renin separates them; apparent mineralocorticoid excess and Liddle syndrome resemble them but have low aldosterone.

. Volume loss raises aldosterone and so increases renal K+ loss after vomiting and with diuretics, and saline with KCl corrects both.

Hyperkalemia

Pathophysiology

A plasma K+ above 5.5 mmol/L means K+ has moved out of cells or the kidney cannot excrete what is taken in, from a low GFR, too little aldosterone, or resistance to it; a high K+ depolarizes cells, which first makes them more excitable and then, as Na+ channels stay inactivated, less excitable, so conduction slows and the heart can stop.

SeverityPlasma K+Usual picture
MildHigh above 5.5 mmol/LOften no symptoms
ModerateHigh above 6.0 mmol/LWeakness and peaked T waves
SevereHigh above 6.5 mmol/LConduction block, paralysis, and arrest

Moving K+ out of cells

  • AInsulin deficiencyWithout insulin the Na+/K+-ATPase is less active; in DKA and HHS, high glucose also draws water out of cells, carrying K+ with it (solvent drag)
  • Bβ-blockers and digoxinβ-blockers remove β2-driven uptake; digoxin blocks the pump itself
  • CAcidosisH+ enters cells to be buffered and K+ leaves; larger in a NAGMA than in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis
  • DCell lysisCells hold most of the body's K+, so hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis, and tumor lysis release large amounts

How a high K+ slows the heart

  1. Extracellular K+ risesThe K+ gradient across the membrane narrows
  2. The resting potential becomes less negativeCells sit closer to threshold and are briefly more excitable
  3. K+ channels conduct moreRepolarization speeds up: peaked T waves
  4. Na+ channels stay inactivatedFewer are available to open, so the upstroke is slower and smaller
  5. Conduction slowsWide QRS, bradycardia, and AV block, then a sine wave, VF, or asystole

Note: The rate of rise matters more than the level, so a chronic hyperkalemia can leave the ECG nearly normal, while a fast rise causes changes at a lower K+.

Etiology

  • Not real
  • 1PseudohyperkalemiaK+ released in the tube: hemolysis from a difficult draw, a syringe, a long tourniquet, or fist clenching, and very high white cell or platelet counts; the most common cause of a high result
  • Shift out of cells
  • 2Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolalityDKA and HHS, where K+ is high despite a total body deficit; mannitol draws K+ out the same way
  • 3AcidosisEspecially a NAGMA; organic acidoses shift less K+
  • 4β-blockersReduce β2-driven uptake into cells, and also lower renin (8)
  • 5Digoxin and succinylcholineDigoxin toxicity blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase; succinylcholine depolarizes muscle and lets K+ out, dangerously in neuromuscular disease, whose muscles carry more receptors
  • 6Cell lysisHemolysis, rhabdomyolysis from crush injury or extreme exercise, TLS after chemotherapy, burns, and massive transfusion; hyperkalemic periodic paralysis causes attacks of weakness with a high K+
  • Kidney excretes too little
  • 7AKI and CKDToo little filtration and flow to excrete the daily load; CKD often needs a drug or load to tip it over
  • 8Low reninHyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, or RTA type 4: diabetic nephropathy, NSAIDs, and β-blockers lower renin, so aldosterone falls, with a hyperkalemic NAGMA
  • 9Low aldosteroneACEi, ARBs, and ARNI block angiotensin II; heparin and ketoconazole reduce aldosterone synthesis; adrenal insufficiency and some forms of CAH make too little
  • 10Aldosterone resistanceSpironolactone and eplerenone block the MR; amiloride, triamterene, trimethoprim (in TMP-SMX), and pentamidine block ENaC; CNIs such as tacrolimus activate NCC, so less Na+ reaches ENaC
  • Too much taken in
  • 11K+ loadDiet (dried fruit, potatoes, bananas, oranges, tomatoes), K+ supplements, IV fluids, TPN, and transfusion; rarely a cause alone, but dangerous when excretion is impaired

Note: Most hyperkalemia needs both a load and impaired excretion, such as CKD with an ACEi and spironolactone.

Symptoms and complications

Many patients have no symptoms until the heart is affected; muscle weakness can ascend to paralysis, and conduction slows until the heart stops.

The ECG

  • APeaked T waveTall, narrow, and symmetric; the earliest change, from about 5.5–6.5 mmol/L
  • BFlat P waveAtrial conduction slows, and P waves can disappear from about 6.5–7.5 mmol/L
  • CLong PR intervalSlowed conduction through the AV node
  • DWide QRSFrom about 7–8 mmol/L; at 8–10 it merges with the T wave into a sine wave, before VF or asystole

Complications

  • BradyarrhythmiasBradycardia and AV block, as conduction slows
  • Cardiac arrestVF or asystole, which can come without warning when K+ rises fast
  • Weakness and paralysisDepolarized muscle cannot fire; weakness ascends from the legs
  • Low Ca2+Worsens the cardiac effects, as in kidney failure
  • AcidosisA high K+ reduces NH4+ production, adding to the acidosis of RTA type 4
  • Lost treatmentFear of hyperkalemia stops ACEi, ARBs, and spironolactone in HF and CKD, where they help

Diagnosis

Get an ECG first and treat at once if it is abnormal; otherwise repeat the K+ to exclude pseudohyperkalemia, then look for a shift, a load, and the drugs and kidney function that limit excretion, as on .

By cause

ForObtain

DKA and HHS (2)Glucose, ketones, and a blood gas

AKI and CKD (7)Urea, creatinine, and urinalysis; urine K+, Na+, and osmolality
Aldosterone (8–10)The drug list; renin and aldosterone; cortisol for adrenal insufficiency

Treatment

Treat at once if the ECG is abnormal, K+ is 6.5 mmol/L or more, or there is weakness: stop K+ sources and causative drugs, stabilize the heart with Ca2+, shift K+ into cells, and remove it, as on ; then treat the cause.

Review article

Hyperkalemia: shifts out of cells, failed excretion, and a depolarized heart

Hyperkalemia, a plasma K+ above 5.5 mmol/L, follows a shift of K+ out of cells or excretion that cannot keep up with intake, from a low GFR, too little aldosterone, or resistance to it, and a falsely high result from K+ released in the sample is its most common apparent cause. A high K+ depolarizes cells and inactivates Na+ channels, so conduction slows, and the ECG progresses from peaked T waves to loss of P waves, a wide QRS, a sine wave, and arrest. Management begins with the ECG, stabilizes the heart, shifts K+ into cells, removes it from the body, and treats the cause. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider its relationships to hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, kidney disease, and hypoaldosteronism.

Key points

  • Hyperkalemia is mild above 5.5 mmol/L, moderate above 6.0, and severe above 6.5, but the rate of rise matters more than the level.
  • Pseudohyperkalemia, from hemolysis, a long tourniquet, fist clenching, or very high white cells or platelets, is excluded by repeating the sample when the ECG is normal.
  • K+ leaves cells with insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality, acidosis, β-blockers, digoxin, succinylcholine, and cell lysis.
  • The kidney fails to excrete K+ in AKI and CKD, with low renin (diabetic nephropathy, NSAIDs, β-blockers), low aldosterone (ACEi, ARBs, heparin, adrenal insufficiency), or aldosterone resistance (spironolactone, amiloride, trimethoprim, CNIs).
  • The ECG shows peaked T waves, flat P waves, a long PR interval, and a wide QRS, progressing to a sine wave, VF, or asystole.
  • An abnormal ECG, K+ of 6.5 mmol/L or more, or weakness needs immediate Ca2+, insulin with glucose, and salbutamol, followed by removal of K+.

Pathophysiology

Hyperkalemia arises when K+ leaves cells or when the kidney cannot excrete what is taken in. Without insulin, the Na+/K+-ATPase is less active, and in DKA and HHS high glucose also draws water out of cells, carrying K+ with it; β-blockers remove β2-driven uptake and digoxin blocks the pump; in acidosis, H+ enters cells and K+ leaves, more so in a NAGMA than in lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis; and cell lysis releases the large intracellular store. As extracellular K+ rises, the K+ gradient narrows and the resting potential becomes less negative, bringing cells closer to threshold and briefly more excitable; K+ channels conduct more, speeding repolarization, but Na+ channels stay inactivated, so fewer are available, the upstroke is slower, and conduction slows until the heart stops. Severity is graded as mild above 5.5 mmol/L, moderate above 6.0, and severe above 6.5, but the rate of rise matters more than the level, so chronic hyperkalemia can leave the ECG nearly normal.

Etiology and mechanisms

Pseudohyperkalemia. The most common cause of a high result is K+ released in the tube by hemolysis from a difficult draw, a syringe, a long tourniquet, or fist clenching, or by very high white cell or platelet counts.

Shifts out of cells. Insulin deficiency and hyperosmolality in DKA and HHS raise K+ despite a total body deficit, and mannitol acts the same way. Acidosis, β-blockers, digoxin toxicity, and succinylcholine, dangerous in neuromuscular disease, move K+ out of cells, and hemolysis, rhabdomyolysis from crush injury or extreme exercise, TLS after chemotherapy, burns, and massive transfusion release it. Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis causes attacks of weakness with a high K+.

Failed excretion and intake. AKI and CKD leave too little filtration and flow, and CKD often needs a drug or load to tip it into hyperkalemia. In hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, or RTA type 4, diabetic nephropathy, NSAIDs, and β-blockers lower renin, so aldosterone falls and a hyperkalemic NAGMA follows. ACEi, ARBs, and ARNI block angiotensin II, heparin and ketoconazole reduce aldosterone synthesis, and adrenal insufficiency and some forms of CAH make too little. Spironolactone and eplerenone block the MR, amiloride, triamterene, trimethoprim, and pentamidine block ENaC, and CNIs such as tacrolimus activate NCC, so less Na+ reaches ENaC. A K+ load from the diet, supplements, IV fluids, TPN, or transfusion rarely causes hyperkalemia alone, and most cases need both a load and impaired excretion.

Clinical presentation and complications

Many patients have no symptoms until the heart is affected. The earliest ECG change is a tall, narrow, symmetric T wave, from about 5.5–6.5 mmol/L; P waves flatten and can disappear from about 6.5–7.5, the PR interval lengthens, and the QRS widens from about 7–8, merging with the T wave into a sine wave at 8–10 before VF or asystole. Bradycardia and AV block reflect slowed conduction, and arrest can come without warning when K+ rises fast. Depolarized muscle cannot fire, so weakness ascends from the legs to paralysis. A low Ca2+, as in kidney failure, worsens the cardiac effects, a high K+ reduces NH4+ production and adds to the acidosis of RTA type 4, and fear of hyperkalemia leads to ACEi, ARBs, and spironolactone being withheld in HF and CKD, where they help.

Diagnosis

An ECG comes first, and treatment starts at once if it is abnormal. Otherwise the K+ is repeated from a free-flowing vein without a tourniquet or fist clenching, with an FBC for very high white cells or platelets, before a shift, a load, and the drugs and kidney function that limit excretion are sought, as in the review of . Glucose, ketones, and a blood gas identify DKA, HHS, and acidosis, and a digoxin level identifies toxicity. Low haptoglobin with high LDH and bilirubin indicates hemolysis, CK and urine myoglobin rhabdomyolysis, and high urate and phosphate with low Ca2+ TLS. Urea, creatinine, urinalysis, and urine K+, Na+, and osmolality assess the kidney, and the drug list, renin and aldosterone, and cortisol identify hypoaldosteronism and adrenal insufficiency.

Management

An abnormal ECG, a K+ of 6.5 mmol/L or more, or weakness calls for immediate treatment: K+ sources and causative drugs are stopped, Ca2+ stabilizes the heart, insulin with glucose and salbutamol shift K+ into cells, and K+ is then removed, as set out in the review of . Pseudohyperkalemia needs only a repeat sample. DKA and HHS are treated with insulin and fluids, with K+ monitored and replaced as it falls to normal; metabolic acidosis is treated by its cause, with an IV NaHCO3 infusion; and digoxin toxicity with digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Rhabdomyolysis and TLS need IV fluids and dialysis when the kidneys fail. In CKD, a low-K+ diet, K+ binders, and a loop diuretic in patients passing urine are used, with dialysis for kidney failure or refractory hyperkalemia. NSAIDs, ACEi, ARBs, spironolactone, trimethoprim, and heparin are stopped or reduced, although a binder can let a needed ACEi or spironolactone continue, and hypoaldosteronism is treated with fludrocortisone unless there is hypertension or fluid overload, with hydrocortisone in adrenal insufficiency.

Relationships to other conditions

. The two share their levers in reverse: insulin, β2 agonists, and alkali move K+ into cells, and aldosterone deficiency causes hyperkalemia while its excess causes hypokalemia. Hyperkalemia depolarizes cells and causes bradyarrhythmias and conduction block, whereas hypokalemia hyperpolarizes them and causes tachyarrhythmias; overtreatment of either can cause the other.

. Acidosis moves K+ out of cells, more in a NAGMA than in organic acidoses, and RTA type 4 combines hyperkalemia with a NAGMA, while DKA raises K+ despite a total body deficit.

and . A low GFR and flow limit excretion, so kidney disease is the usual background, often with a drug or load added; dialysis is the definitive treatment when the kidneys fail.

. Low renin, low aldosterone, and aldosterone resistance each reduce K+ secretion; renin and aldosterone separate them, and fludrocortisone replaces a missing hormone.

Potassium Disorders: Comparison and Workup

Comparison

Plasma K+ is a small extracellular share of a large intracellular store, moved across cell membranes within minutes and excreted by the kidney over hours, so both disorders are worked up by asking whether K+ has shifted, been taken in, or been lost or kept by the kidney, and both are judged first by the ECG.

Treatment

Both disorders are treated by their cause, but the urgent step is set by the ECG: a low K+ is replaced, and a high K+ is treated by stabilizing the heart, shifting K+ into cells, and removing it, with K+ checked often in both, because shifts reverse.

Raising a low K+

TreatmentHow it worksUseWatch for

Replacing safely

  • Avoid dextrose fluidsGlucose releases insulin, which drives K+ into cells and lowers it further

Remove: loop or thiazide diureticMore Na+ and flow reach the collecting ductPatients passing urine, especially if overloaded; never alone when symptomaticHypovolemia
Remove: K+ binders (patiromer, SZC, SPS)Take up K+ in the gut in exchange for Ca2+ or Na+Kidney impairment without urgent dialysis; long term to keep an ACEiSPS can cause colonic necrosis, worse with sorbitol
Remove: hemodialysisRemoves K+ directlyHyperkalemia that does not respond to treatment, the E of the AEIOU indications on The definitive treatment
Replace: fludrocortisoneReplaces aldosteroneHypoaldosteronismHypertension and edema

Note: Ca2+, insulin, salbutamol, and NaHCO3 only buy time, because K+ returns from cells; only removal lowers total body K+.

Review article

Disorders of plasma potassium: the ECG, the urine, and stabilize, shift, and remove

Plasma K+ is a small extracellular share of a large intracellular store, so it changes when K+ moves across cell membranes or when renal excretion fails to match intake. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes cells and causes tachyarrhythmias, and hyperkalemia depolarizes them and causes conduction block, so the ECG decides urgency in both. Hypokalemia is worked up by Mg2+, shifts, urine K+, the acid-base state, and blood pressure with renin and aldosterone, and hyperkalemia by excluding a spurious result, then shifts, kidney function, drugs, and renin and aldosterone. A low K+ is replaced at a limited rate, and a high K+ is treated by stabilizing the heart, shifting K+ into cells, and removing it. Here, we compare the two disorders and review their shared workup and treatment.

Key points

  • Hypokalemia is below 3.5 mmol/L and hyperkalemia above 5.5; the ECG, not the level alone, decides urgency.
  • In hypokalemia, urine K+ below 15 mmol/L points to loss outside the kidney or low intake, and above it to renal loss, which the blood gas, urine Cl−, BP, renin, and aldosterone sort.
  • In hyperkalemia, a spurious result from K+ released in the tube is excluded first, then shifts, kidney function, drugs, and renin and aldosterone are assessed.
  • Oral KCl is first line for hypokalemia; IV KCl runs at usually 10 and at most 20 mmol an hour, in saline rather than dextrose, with Mg2+ corrected.
  • Hyperkalemia with ECG changes is treated with IV Ca2+, then insulin with glucose and salbutamol, then removal by diuretics, binders, or dialysis.
  • Shifts reverse, so K+ is checked often during treatment of either disorder.

Comparison

Hypokalemia, below 3.5 mmol/L and severe below 2.5, hyperpolarizes cells, so skeletal and smooth muscle weaken, with cramps, ileus, and rhabdomyolysis, while slowed repolarization causes PVCs, PSVT, A-fib, VT, and TdP, with flat T waves, ST depression, U waves, and a long QU interval. Hyperkalemia, above 5.5 mmol/L and severe above 6.5, depolarizes cells and inactivates Na+ channels, causing weakness ascending to paralysis and bradycardia and AV block before VF or asystole, with peaked T waves, flat P waves, a long PR interval, a wide QRS, and a sine wave. Insulin, β2 agonists, and alkalosis move K+ into cells, and insulin deficiency, β-blockers, acidosis, and cell lysis move it out. Diuretics, aldosterone excess, and a low Mg2+ are the main renal causes of hypokalemia, and AKI, CKD, ACEi, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics of hyperkalemia. A spurious result is rare with a low K+ but common with a high one.

Diagnosis

In hypokalemia, urgency is judged by the ECG, symptoms, and a K+ below 2.5 mmol/L, and Mg2+ is checked because a low Mg2+ keeps K+ low. After shifts from insulin, salbutamol, alkalosis, thyrotoxicosis, or periodic paralysis are considered, a spot urine K+ above 15 mmol/L, or over 30 mmol a day, indicates renal loss. A lower urine K+ points to diarrhea or laxatives, with a NAGMA, poor intake, or a diuretic since stopped. With renal loss, an acidosis points to RTA types 1 and 2 or DKA; an alkalosis with a urine Cl− below 20 mmol/L to vomiting or past diuretics, and with a higher urine Cl− and normal BP to current diuretics or Bartter or Gitelman syndrome; and hypertension to aldosterone excess, separated by renin and aldosterone into primary hyperaldosteronism, with high aldosterone and low renin, secondary hyperaldosteronism, with both high, and apparent mineralocorticoid excess or Liddle syndrome, with both low.

In hyperkalemia, the ECG comes first, and changes, weakness, or a K+ of 6.5 mmol/L or more are treated before anything else. The sample is repeated from a free-flowing vein, looking for hemolysis or very high white cells or platelets. Shifts are sought with glucose, ketones, a blood gas, CK and urine myoglobin for rhabdomyolysis, urate, phosphate, and Ca2+ for TLS, haptoglobin, LDH, and bilirubin for hemolysis, and a digoxin level. Urea and creatinine identify AKI or CKD, usually with a drug or load added, and when the GFR does not explain the K+, the drug list and renin and aldosterone separate hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, with both low, drugs and adrenal insufficiency, with high renin and low aldosterone, and aldosterone resistance, with both high.

Management

A low K+ is replaced with oral KCl, 60–80 mmol a day, for mild and moderate hypokalemia, or with K+ citrate or bicarbonate when there is acidosis. IV KCl, usually at 10 mmol an hour and at most 20 with monitoring, in saline rather than dextrose, whose glucose releases insulin, is used for severe or symptomatic hypokalemia, arrhythmias, digoxin toxicity, or no oral route; faster infusion risks arrhythmia, arrest, and rebound hyperkalemia. K+ is checked every 2–4 hours during IV replacement. Each 0.3 mmol/L fall reflects about 100 mmol lost, so the deficit is replaced over days, and less is given when a shift is the cause. Mg2+ is corrected, and spironolactone, eplerenone, or amiloride reduce renal loss.

A high K+ with ECG changes is first treated with IV calcium gluconate, which protects the heart without lowering K+; calcium chloride holds more Ca2+ but damages veins, and Ca2+ is never given in the same line as NaHCO3. K+ is then shifted into cells with 10 units of regular insulin and 50 mL of D50, with a D10 infusion to lower the risk of hypoglycemia, with nebulized salbutamol at higher doses than for asthma, and with an IV NaHCO3 infusion only in metabolic acidosis. Because shifts reverse, K+ must then be removed: loop or thiazide diuretics in patients passing urine, never alone when symptomatic; binders such as patiromer and SZC, or SPS, which can cause colonic necrosis; and hemodialysis, the definitive treatment, for hyperkalemia that does not respond, one of the AEIOU indications for dialysis set out in the review of . Fludrocortisone replaces a missing aldosterone.

Relationships to other conditions

and . The condition reviews cover the numbered causes, their specific tests, and their specific treatment.

. Renin and aldosterone are the last step of both workups: excess causes hypokalemia with hypertension, and deficiency or resistance causes hyperkalemia.

. The blood gas sorts renal K+ loss, acidosis shifts K+ out of cells and alkalosis into them, and correcting an acidosis lowers K+, so K+ is replaced before or with alkali.

Hypocalcemia

Pathophysiology

A low ionized Ca2+ means PTH is missing or cannot act, calcitriol is too low to absorb Ca2+, or Ca2+ is bound, precipitated, or moved into bone; a low ionized Ca2+ lowers the threshold for depolarization, so nerve and muscle fire too easily, causing tetany, seizures, and a long QT.

Total and ionized Ca2+

  • Normal rangeTotal Ca2+ about 2.1–2.6 mmol/L; ionized Ca2+ about 1.16–1.31 mmol/L, the active fraction
  • Correct for albuminAdd 0.02 mmol/L for each 1 g/L that albumin falls below 40 g/L; a low total Ca2+ with a normal ionized Ca2+ is pseudohypocalcemia
  • Measure ionized Ca2+ when pH is abnormalAlkalosis binds more Ca2+ to albumin and lowers the ionized fraction; no reliable correction exists

How a low Ca2+ makes nerve and muscle fire

  1. Ionized Ca2+ fallsFewer Ca2+ ions sit on the outside of the membrane
  2. The threshold fallsNa+ channels open more easily, closer to the resting potential
  3. Nerves fire on their ownPerioral and fingertip tingling, cramps, and tetany
  4. Severe or fast fallsLaryngospasm, seizures, and a long QT that can lead to TdP

Note: Symptoms follow the speed of the fall as much as its depth, which is why tetany is common in respiratory alkalosis, when ionized Ca2+ drops within minutes.

Etiology

  • Too little PTH, or PTH that cannot act
  • 1Postsurgical hypoparathyroidismAbout 75% of hypoparathyroidism, after thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, or radical neck surgery; most recover within a month
  • 2Autoimmune and genetic hypoparathyroidismAutoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 (hypoparathyroidism, mucocutaneous candidiasis, and adrenal insufficiency), DiGeorge syndrome, infiltration (hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, amyloidosis), and neck irradiation (see Hypoparathyroidism)
  • 3Magnesium disordersA low Mg2+ causes PTH resistance and, when severe, stops PTH release; a very high Mg2+ also suppresses PTH through the CaSR
  • PTH high, but Ca2+ still low
  • 4Vitamin D deficiencyLow intake, malabsorption, little sun, or liver disease; less Ca2+ is absorbed, and PTH rises (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
  • 5CKDThe kidney retains phosphate and makes too little calcitriol, so PTH rises but cannot restore Ca2+
  • 6PseudohypoparathyroidismInherited resistance to PTH: low Ca2+, high phosphate, and high PTH
  • Bone and drugs
  • 7Hungry bone and osteoblastic metastasesAfter parathyroidectomy for severe hyperparathyroidism, bone takes up Ca2+ rapidly, with low phosphate and Mg2+; osteoblastic metastases such as prostate cancer do the same
  • 8DrugsBisphosphonates and denosumab block bone resorption; cinacalcet lowers PTH; cisplatin acts through low Mg2+; foscarnet binds ionized Ca2+
  • Ca2+ bound or precipitated
  • 9Low albuminPseudohypocalcemia: total Ca2+ is low, ionized Ca2+ normal
  • 10AlkalosisMore Ca2+ binds albumin, so ionized Ca2+ falls although total Ca2+ is normal
  • 11CitrateMassive transfusion and citrate anticoagulation during CRRT bind Ca2+
  • 12Acute hyperphosphatemiaTLS, rhabdomyolysis, and kidney failure; Ca2+ and phosphate precipitate in the tissues
  • 13Acute pancreatitisCa2+ binds fatty acids released from digested fat (saponification); a poor sign in the Ranson criteria
  • 14Sepsis and critical illnessImpaired PTH release, Mg2+ disturbances, and less calcitriol

Note: The most common causes are surgery, CKD, vitamin D deficiency, low Mg2+, and acute pancreatitis.

Symptoms and complications

Mild hypocalcemia is often silent; symptoms follow neuromuscular excitability, and a fall below about 1.75 mmol/L, or a fast fall, can cause seizures and arrhythmias.

Features

SystemWhat is seen
Nerve and musclePerioral and fingertip paresthesias, cramps, and tetany; laryngospasm
Chvostek signTapping the facial nerve in front of the ear twitches the facial muscles on that side
Trousseau signA blood pressure cuff above systolic for 2–3 minutes causes carpopedal spasm
BrainSeizures; anxiety, depression, or emotional lability
HeartLong QT, TdP, and heart failure
ChronicDry skin, thin hair, and brittle nails

The ECG

  • ALong ST segmentCa2+ sets the plateau of the cardiac action potential, and a low Ca2+ lengthens it
  • BLong QT intervalMostly from the long ST segment; a risk of TdP
  • CNormal T waveIts shape is preserved but it comes late, unlike the flat T and U wave of hypokalemia

Complications

  • Seizures and laryngospasmWith severe or rapid falls
  • TdPFrom the long QT
  • Kidney stones and CKDIn poorly controlled hypoparathyroidism, and with long-term high-dose calcium and vitamin D, because PTH no longer holds Ca2+ in the kidney

Diagnosis

Confirm it with albumin-corrected or ionized Ca2+, check the ECG, then find the cause from Mg2+, phosphate, PTH, and vitamin D, as on .

By cause

ForObtain
Hypoparathyroidism (1, 2)Low Ca2+, high phosphate, and low or inappropriately normal PTH on two measurements
Magnesium (3)Mg2+ in every patient; PTH can be low until Mg2+ is replaced
Vitamin D deficiency (4)Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, low or normal phosphate, and high PTH
CKD (5)Creatinine and eGFR, high phosphate, and high PTH
Pseudohypoparathyroidism (6)High phosphate with high PTH and normal kidney function
Bone (7)Recent parathyroidectomy; low phosphate and Mg2+; imaging for osteomalacia or metastases
Binding and precipitation (9–13)Albumin, ionized Ca2+, a blood gas, CK, urate and phosphate, and lipase

Treatment

Give IV calcium gluconate for severe symptoms, a long QT, or acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, otherwise oral Ca2+ with vitamin D, correct Mg2+ first, and treat the cause; the forms and cautions are on .

Postsurgical hypoparathyroidism (1)Prophylactic Ca2+ after neck surgery, tapered as Ca2+ settles
Chronic hypoparathyroidism (1, 2)Oral Ca2+ with calcitriol, aiming for low-normal Ca2+ to limit urine Ca2+; PTH analogs such as palopegteriparatide when control is poor
Low Mg2+ (3)Replace Mg2+ before or with Ca2+, which will not correct otherwise
Vitamin D deficiency (4)Vitamin D repletion, without which Ca2+ cannot be corrected
CKD (5)Calcitriol, with phosphate control (see Chronic kidney disease)

Review article

Hypocalcemia: too little PTH or calcitriol, bound Ca2+, and an excitable membrane

Hypocalcemia, a low ionized or albumin-corrected Ca2+, follows deficient or ineffective PTH, too little calcitriol, binding or precipitation of Ca2+ in plasma, or its uptake into bone. Because a low ionized Ca2+ lowers the threshold for depolarization, it causes paresthesias, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, seizures, and a long QT. The diagnosis is confirmed with corrected or ionized Ca2+, and Mg2+, phosphate, PTH, and vitamin D identify the cause. Treatment gives IV calcium gluconate for severe or symptomatic hypocalcemia, oral Ca2+ with vitamin D or calcitriol otherwise, and Mg2+ first when it is low. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider its relationships to hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, CKD, and alkalosis.

Key points

  • Total Ca2+ is corrected by adding 0.02 mmol/L for each 1 g/L that albumin falls below 40 g/L, and ionized Ca2+ is measured when pH is abnormal, because alkalosis lowers it.
  • A low ionized Ca2+ lowers the threshold for depolarization, causing paresthesias, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, laryngospasm, seizures, and a long QT.
  • Hypoparathyroidism, about 75% postsurgical, gives low Ca2+, high phosphate, and low or inappropriately normal PTH.
  • Vitamin D deficiency and CKD raise PTH but leave Ca2+ low; vitamin D deficiency has low or normal phosphate, and CKD high phosphate.
  • A low Mg2+ causes PTH resistance and, when severe, stops PTH release, so Mg2+ is corrected before Ca2+.
  • Severe or symptomatic hypocalcemia, or a long QT, is treated with IV calcium gluconate; chronic hypocalcemia with oral Ca2+ and vitamin D or calcitriol.

Pathophysiology

Plasma Ca2+ is about half ionized and half bound, mostly to albumin, so total Ca2+ is about 2.1–2.6 mmol/L and ionized Ca2+ about 1.16–1.31 mmol/L. A low albumin lowers total Ca2+ without changing the ionized fraction, and total Ca2+ is corrected by adding 0.02 mmol/L for each 1 g/L that albumin falls below 40 g/L; alkalosis binds more Ca2+ to albumin, so ionized Ca2+ is measured when pH is abnormal. Hypocalcemia follows deficient or ineffective PTH, too little calcitriol to absorb Ca2+, binding or precipitation of Ca2+ in plasma, or its uptake into bone. A low ionized Ca2+ lowers the threshold for depolarization, so Na+ channels open closer to the resting potential and nerves fire on their own, causing tingling, cramps, and tetany, and, with severe or rapid falls, laryngospasm, seizures, and a long QT; symptoms follow the speed of the fall as much as its depth.

Etiology and mechanisms

Too little PTH, or PTH that cannot act. Postsurgical hypoparathyroidism, after thyroidectomy, parathyroidectomy, or radical neck surgery, accounts for about 75% of hypoparathyroidism, and most patients recover within a month. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1, with mucocutaneous candidiasis and adrenal insufficiency, DiGeorge syndrome, infiltration by hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, or amyloidosis, and neck irradiation are rarer causes. A low Mg2+ causes PTH resistance and, when severe, stops PTH release, and a very high Mg2+ suppresses PTH through the CaSR.

High PTH, but Ca2+ still low. Vitamin D deficiency, from low intake, malabsorption, little sun, or liver disease, reduces Ca2+ absorption and causes secondary hyperparathyroidism. In CKD, the kidney retains phosphate and makes too little calcitriol, so PTH rises without restoring Ca2+. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is inherited resistance to PTH, with low Ca2+, high phosphate, and high PTH.

Bone, drugs, and binding. After parathyroidectomy for severe hyperparathyroidism, bone takes up Ca2+ rapidly, the hungry bone syndrome, with low phosphate and Mg2+, and osteoblastic metastases such as prostate cancer act similarly. Bisphosphonates and denosumab block bone resorption, cinacalcet lowers PTH, cisplatin acts through low Mg2+, and foscarnet binds ionized Ca2+. A low albumin causes pseudohypocalcemia, alkalosis lowers ionized Ca2+, citrate from massive transfusion or CRRT binds it, acute hyperphosphatemia from TLS, rhabdomyolysis, or kidney failure precipitates it, acute pancreatitis binds it to fatty acids, and sepsis lowers it by several mechanisms. Surgery, CKD, vitamin D deficiency, low Mg2+, and pancreatitis are the most common causes.

Clinical presentation and complications

Mild hypocalcemia is often silent. Symptoms include perioral and fingertip paresthesias, cramps, tetany, and laryngospasm; the Chvostek sign, facial twitching on tapping the facial nerve, and the Trousseau sign, carpopedal spasm with a cuff inflated above systolic pressure for 2–3 minutes, reveal neuromuscular excitability. Seizures, anxiety, depression, and emotional lability may occur, and the heart shows a long QT, from a long ST segment with a normal T wave, with a risk of TdP and heart failure. Chronic hypocalcemia causes dry skin, thin hair, and brittle nails, and poorly controlled hypoparathyroidism and long-term high-dose treatment cause kidney stones and CKD. Falls below about 1.75 mmol/L, or rapid falls, can cause seizures and arrhythmias.

Diagnosis

Hypocalcemia is confirmed with albumin-corrected or ionized Ca2+, the ECG is checked, and Mg2+, phosphate, PTH, and vitamin D identify the cause, as set out in the review of . Hypoparathyroidism gives low Ca2+, high phosphate, and low or inappropriately normal PTH on two measurements; vitamin D deficiency gives low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, low or normal phosphate, and high PTH; CKD gives a low eGFR, high phosphate, and high PTH; and pseudohypoparathyroidism gives high phosphate and high PTH with normal kidney function. Mg2+ is measured in every patient. Albumin, ionized Ca2+, a blood gas, CK, urate, phosphate, and lipase identify binding and precipitation, and imaging may show osteomalacia or metastases.

Management

IV calcium gluconate is given for severe symptoms, a long QT, or acute symptomatic hypocalcemia, and oral Ca2+ with vitamin D otherwise; Mg2+ is replaced first or with Ca2+, which will not correct otherwise. Prophylactic Ca2+ follows neck surgery and is tapered as Ca2+ settles. Chronic hypoparathyroidism is treated with oral Ca2+ and calcitriol, aiming for low-normal Ca2+ to limit urine Ca2+, with PTH analogs such as palopegteriparatide when control is poor. Vitamin D deficiency needs vitamin D repletion, CKD calcitriol and phosphate control, and hungry bone large doses of IV Ca2+. Vitamin D and Ca2+ are corrected before bisphosphonates or denosumab, ionized Ca2+ is monitored with foscarnet, and a low albumin with a normal ionized Ca2+ needs no Ca2+.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both are read against PTH: in hypocalcemia, a low PTH points to the parathyroids and a high PTH to vitamin D, the kidney, or PTH resistance, whereas in hypercalcemia, a high PTH points to the parathyroids and a suppressed PTH to everything else. Hypocalcemia lowers the threshold for firing and lengthens the QT; hypercalcemia does the reverse. Parathyroidectomy for hypercalcemia can end in the hungry bone syndrome.

. A low Mg2+ causes PTH resistance and stops PTH release, so hypocalcemia with hypomagnesemia corrects only once Mg2+ is replaced; both cause tetany and arrhythmias.

. Phosphate retention and too little calcitriol cause hypocalcemia with secondary hyperparathyroidism, treated with calcitriol and phosphate control.

. Alkalosis binds more Ca2+ to albumin and lowers ionized Ca2+ without changing total Ca2+, which is why tetany can appear with vomiting or overbreathing.

Hypercalcemia

Pathophysiology

A high Ca2+ means Ca2+ enters the blood from bone or gut faster than the kidney excretes it, driven by PTH, PTHrP, calcitriol, or bone breakdown; a high Ca2+ raises the threshold for depolarization, so nerve and muscle become sluggish, the kidney cannot concentrate urine, and the QT shortens.

SeverityCorrected Ca2+Usual picture
MildHigh 2.6–3.0 mmol/LOften found by chance, with no symptoms
ModerateHigh 3.0–3.5 mmol/LPolyuria, thirst, constipation, weakness, and confusion
CrisisHigh above 3.5 mmol/LDehydration, AKI, arrhythmias, stupor, and coma

How a high Ca2+ affects the body

  1. Ionized Ca2+ risesMore Ca2+ on the outside of the membrane
  2. The threshold risesNerve and muscle are harder to fire: weakness, low reflexes, constipation, and confusion
  3. The kidney is affectedNa+ reabsorption falls and aquaporin-2 is lost, so urine cannot be concentrated: polyuria
  4. Volume fallsVasoconstriction and volume loss lower the GFR, so less Ca2+ is excreted and Ca2+ rises further

Note: The rise in Ca2+ and the fall in volume feed each other, which is why IV saline comes first.

Etiology

  • PTH-mediated: PTH high or inappropriately normal
  • 1Primary hyperparathyroidismUsually a parathyroid adenoma; often mild and found by chance, but it can cause osteoporosis, fractures, stones, and kidney failure; part of MEN syndromes (see Hyperparathyroidism)
  • 2Tertiary hyperparathyroidismHyperplasia after years of overstimulation in kidney failure, persisting after a kidney transplant
  • 3FHHAn inherited, autosomal dominant loss of function of the CaSR, so a higher Ca2+ is needed to suppress PTH; urine Ca2+ is low
  • 4Lithium and PTH analogsLithium raises the set point at which Ca2+ suppresses PTH; teriparatide and abaloparatide cause transient rises
  • Not PTH-mediated: PTH suppressed
  • 5PTHrP from a tumorThe most common mechanism in malignancy: PTHrP acts on PTH receptors
  • 6Bone metastasesOsteolytic metastases release Ca2+ locally
  • 7Calcitriol excessLymphoma and granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB), whose macrophages make calcitriol without control
  • 8Vitamin D toxicityExcess vitamin D or calcitriol supplements
  • 9ThiazidesIncrease Ca2+ reabsorption in the distal tubule
  • 10Milk-alkali syndromeExcess calcium carbonate, with metabolic alkalosis and kidney injury
  • 11Immobilization and hyperthyroidismBone resorption outpaces formation
  • 12Other endocrine causesAdrenal insufficiency, through volume loss; pheochromocytoma; vitamin A derivatives

Note: Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy cause about 90% of hypercalcemia.

Symptoms and complications

Mild hypercalcemia is often silent; symptoms usually appear above 3.0 mmol/L and are summed up as stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones.

Features

SystemWhat is seen
Kidney (stones and thrones)Polyuria and thirst from nephrogenic DI; kidney stones; AKI
BoneBone pain; osteoporosis and fractures in hyperparathyroidism
Gut (groans)Nausea, vomiting, anorexia, constipation, pancreatitis, and peptic ulcers
Brain (psychiatric overtones)Fatigue, depression, confusion, stupor, and coma
MuscleWeakness, low tone, and low reflexes
HeartShort QT, long PR, wide QRS, bradycardia, and heart block

The ECG

  • AShort or absent ST segmentThe plateau of the action potential shortens
  • BShort QT intervalThe classic sign; the PR can lengthen and the QRS widen
  • CT waveFollows the QRS almost at once

Complications

  • AKIFrom volume loss and vasoconstriction
  • Stones and nephrocalcinosisFrom high urine Ca2+
  • ArrhythmiasBradycardia, heart block, and, when severe, arrest
  • Pancreatitis and peptic ulcersIn chronic hypercalcemia

Diagnosis

Confirm it with corrected or ionized Ca2+ and review the drugs; then PTH divides the causes: high or inappropriately normal in PTH-mediated disease and suppressed in everything else, as on .

By cause

ForObtain
Primary hyperparathyroidism (1)High or normal PTH, high urine Ca2+; neck ultrasound or a parathyroid scan to find the adenoma; DEXA and kidney ultrasound
FHH (3)High or normal PTH with low urine Ca2+: a CCCR below 0.01
PTHrP (5)Suppressed PTH, high PTHrP; age-appropriate cancer screening and imaging
Bone metastases (6)Suppressed PTH; high ALP; imaging; serum and urine electrophoresis
Calcitriol excess (7)Suppressed PTH with high calcitriol; chest imaging for sarcoidosis or lymphoma
Vitamin D toxicity (8)High 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Other causes (9–12)Drug history, TSH, and metanephrines when suggested

Treatment

Treat moderate or symptomatic hypercalcemia with IV 0.9% saline, then calcitonin for speed and a bisphosphonate or denosumab to hold Ca2+ down, and treat the cause; the drugs are compared on .

By cause

CauseTreatment
Primary hyperparathyroidism (1)Parathyroidectomy if Ca2+ is more than 0.25 mmol/L above normal, with osteoporosis or a fragility fracture, urine Ca2+ above 10 mmol a day, kidney stones, or age under 50; cinacalcet when surgery is not possible
Tertiary hyperparathyroidism (2)Parathyroidectomy or cinacalcet
FHH (3)Usually no treatment; it is benign and surgery does not help
Malignancy (5, 6)Saline, then zoledronic acid or denosumab, which suits kidney impairment; treat the cancer
Calcitriol excess (7)Glucocorticoids, which block calcitriol production
Drugs and supplements (4, 8–10)Stop lithium if possible, thiazides, vitamin D, and calcium carbonate
Severe, with kidney failureDialysis with a low- or no-calcium bath

Review article

Hypercalcemia: PTH, PTHrP, calcitriol, and a sluggish membrane

Hypercalcemia follows Ca2+ entering the blood from bone or gut faster than the kidney excretes it, through PTH, PTHrP, calcitriol, bone breakdown, or reduced excretion; primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy cause about 90%. A high Ca2+ raises the threshold for depolarization and impairs urine concentration, causing weakness, constipation, confusion, polyuria, kidney stones, and a short QT. PTH divides the causes into PTH-mediated disease, separated by urine Ca2+, and PTH-independent disease, investigated with PTHrP, vitamin D metabolites, and imaging. Treatment restores volume with saline, lowers Ca2+ with calcitonin and bisphosphonates or denosumab, and treats the cause. Here, we review its mechanisms, causes, presentation, diagnosis, and treatment, and consider its relationships to hypocalcemia, diabetes insipidus, and metabolic alkalosis.

Key points

  • Hypercalcemia is mild at 2.6–3.0 mmol/L, moderate at 3.0–3.5, and a crisis above 3.5; symptoms usually appear above 3.0.
  • A high Ca2+ raises the threshold for firing, causes nephrogenic DI through lost aquaporin-2, and lowers volume, which reduces Ca2+ excretion further.
  • A high or inappropriately normal PTH points to primary or tertiary hyperparathyroidism, FHH, or lithium; a suppressed PTH to PTHrP, bone metastases, calcitriol excess, vitamin D, thiazides, or milk-alkali syndrome.
  • FHH, a loss of function of the CaSR, has low urine Ca2+, with a CCCR below 0.01, and needs no surgery.
  • The ECG shows a short QT, with a long PR, wide QRS, bradycardia, and heart block when severe.
  • Treatment is IV saline, calcitonin within hours, a bisphosphonate or denosumab over days, glucocorticoids for calcitriol excess, and parathyroidectomy for primary hyperparathyroidism that meets the criteria.

Pathophysiology

Hypercalcemia occurs when Ca2+ enters the blood from bone or gut faster than the kidney excretes it. PTH and PTHrP increase bone resorption and renal Ca2+ reabsorption, calcitriol increases gut absorption, bone metastases and immobility release Ca2+ from bone, and thiazides and volume loss reduce excretion. A high ionized Ca2+ raises the threshold for depolarization, so nerve and muscle are harder to fire, causing weakness, low reflexes, constipation, and confusion. In the kidney, it reduces Na+ reabsorption and aquaporin-2, so urine cannot be concentrated, and its vasoconstriction and the resulting volume loss lower the GFR, which reduces Ca2+ excretion and raises Ca2+ further; this loop is why saline comes first. Hypercalcemia is mild at 2.6–3.0 mmol/L, moderate at 3.0–3.5, and a crisis above 3.5.

Etiology and mechanisms

PTH-mediated. Primary hyperparathyroidism, usually from an adenoma and sometimes part of a MEN syndrome, is often mild and found by chance but can cause osteoporosis, fractures, stones, and kidney failure. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism follows years of overstimulation in kidney failure. FHH, an autosomal dominant loss of function of the CaSR, raises the Ca2+ needed to suppress PTH, with low urine Ca2+. Lithium raises the PTH set point, and teriparatide and abaloparatide cause transient rises.

Not PTH-mediated. In malignancy, PTHrP acting on PTH receptors is the most common mechanism, and osteolytic metastases release Ca2+ locally. Lymphoma and granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis and TB make calcitriol without control, and excess vitamin D or calcitriol supplements raise Ca2+ directly. Thiazides increase distal Ca2+ reabsorption, excess calcium carbonate causes milk-alkali syndrome with metabolic alkalosis and kidney injury, and immobilization and hyperthyroidism increase bone resorption. Adrenal insufficiency, pheochromocytoma, and vitamin A derivatives are rarer causes. Primary hyperparathyroidism and malignancy account for about 90% of cases.

Clinical presentation and complications

Mild hypercalcemia is often found by chance. Above about 3.0 mmol/L, it causes polyuria and thirst, kidney stones, and AKI; bone pain, osteoporosis, and fractures in hyperparathyroidism; nausea, vomiting, anorexia, constipation, pancreatitis, and peptic ulcers; fatigue, depression, confusion, stupor, and coma; and weakness with low reflexes, the stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones. The ECG shows a short QT from a short or absent ST segment, with a long PR, a wide QRS, bradycardia, and heart block when severe, and arrest can follow.

Diagnosis

Hypercalcemia is confirmed with corrected or ionized Ca2+, the drugs are reviewed, and PTH divides the causes, as set out in the review of . A high or inappropriately normal PTH with high urine Ca2+ indicates primary hyperparathyroidism, localized by neck ultrasound or a parathyroid scan, with DEXA and kidney ultrasound to assess its effects; a high or normal PTH with low urine Ca2+, a CCCR below 0.01, indicates FHH. A suppressed PTH leads to PTHrP and cancer screening, ALP, imaging, and electrophoresis for bone involvement, calcitriol and chest imaging for granulomatous disease or lymphoma, 25-hydroxyvitamin D for toxicity, and TSH and metanephrines when suggested.

Management

Moderate or symptomatic hypercalcemia is treated with IV 0.9% saline until volume and urine output are restored, calcitonin, which lowers Ca2+ within hours but for only a few days, and a bisphosphonate, such as zoledronic acid, which takes about 3 days, or denosumab, which suits kidney impairment, as compared in the review of . Primary hyperparathyroidism is treated by parathyroidectomy when Ca2+ is more than 0.25 mmol/L above normal, with osteoporosis or a fragility fracture, urine Ca2+ above 10 mmol a day, kidney stones, or age under 50, and with cinacalcet when surgery is not possible; tertiary hyperparathyroidism by parathyroidectomy or cinacalcet. FHH usually needs no treatment. Malignancy is treated with saline and zoledronic acid or denosumab along with the cancer, calcitriol excess with glucocorticoids, and drug causes by stopping lithium where possible, thiazides, vitamin D, and calcium carbonate. Dialysis with a low- or no-calcium bath is used for severe hypercalcemia with kidney failure.

Relationships to other conditions

. Both are read against PTH, and the two mirror each other at the membrane and on the ECG: a high Ca2+ raises the threshold and shortens the QT, a low Ca2+ lowers it and lengthens the QT. Treating hypercalcemia can overshoot, and parathyroidectomy can end in the hungry bone syndrome.

. Hypercalcemia is a cause of nephrogenic DI, through loss of aquaporin-2, and the resulting polyuria and volume loss worsen the hypercalcemia.

. Milk-alkali syndrome combines hypercalcemia, metabolic alkalosis, and kidney injury from excess calcium carbonate, and thiazides raise Ca2+ while causing a contraction alkalosis.

Hypomagnesemia

Pathophysiology

A plasma Mg2+ below 0.7 mmol/L means too little is taken in, Mg2+ is lost through the gut or kidney, or it has moved into cells or bone; because Mg2+ is needed to release PTH and to limit K+ loss through ROMK, a low Mg2+ also lowers Ca2+ and K+, and those three together make nerve, muscle, and heart irritable.

Why a low Mg2+ lowers Ca2+ and K+

  1. Mg2+ fallsSymptoms usually start below 0.5 mmol/L
  2. PTH failsMg2+-dependent adenylyl cyclase makes less cAMP, so less PTH is released and it works less well: hypocalcemia
  3. ROMK is releasedWithout Mg2+ limiting it, more K+ is secreted in the collecting duct: hypokalemia in about 60%
  4. Cells are irritableTetany and arrhythmias, even before Ca2+ falls

Note: Serum Mg2+ is about 1% of the body's Mg2+, so a normal level does not rule out a deficit, and replacement continues after the level normalizes.

Etiology

  • Too little taken in
  • 1Poor intakeAlcohol use disorder, in about 30%, starvation, anorexia nervosa, and TPN without enough Mg2+
  • Lost through the gut
  • 2DiarrheaAcute or chronic diarrhea, including Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis, and laxative abuse
  • 3PPIsLong-term use reduces Mg2+ absorption
  • 4Malabsorption and gastric bypassLess of the small bowel absorbs Mg2+
  • Moved into cells and bone
  • 5Shifts into cellsInsulin for DKA, refeeding, correcting acidosis, alcohol withdrawal, and acute pancreatitis
  • 6Hungry boneBone takes up Mg2+ after parathyroidectomy or thyroidectomy
  • Lost through the kidney
  • 7Loop and thiazide diureticsLoop diuretics remove the lumen-positive voltage that drives Mg2+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb
  • 8Nephrotoxic drugsAminoglycosides, amphotericin B, pentamidine, cisplatin, ciclosporin, and EGFR antibodies such as cetuximab
  • 9Inherited tubular disordersGitelman syndrome, Bartter syndrome, and familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis (claudin-16 or -19)
  • 10Recovering tubulesRecovery from ATN, after an obstruction is relieved, and after a kidney transplant

Note: Hypomagnesemia is common in hospital, at 12–20%, and in about 65% of critically ill patients in one study.

Symptoms and complications

Symptoms usually start below 0.5 mmol/L and come from neuromuscular excitability, arrhythmias, and the low Ca2+ and K+ that follow.

Features

SystemWhat is seen
EarlyNausea, vomiting, anorexia, fatigue, and weakness
Nerve and muscleTremor, tetany with Chvostek and Trousseau signs (even with a normal Ca2+), cramps, choreoathetosis, vertical nystagmus, and seizures
BrainApathy, depression, agitation, delirium, psychosis, and coma
HeartWide QRS and peaked T in mild to moderate deficiency; long PR and smaller T when severe; atrial and ventricular ectopics, A-fib, VT, and TdP
ElectrolytesHypocalcemia and hypokalemia

Complications

  • TdPA polymorphic VT with a long QT; IV Mg2+ treats it
  • Ventricular arrhythmias after an MIMore likely in the first 24 hours when Mg2+ is low
  • Digoxin toxicityLow Mg2+ inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase and depletes cell K+
  • Refractory hypokalemia and hypocalcemiaNeither corrects until Mg2+ is replaced
  • ChondrocalcinosisWith long-standing deficiency, as in Gitelman syndrome

Diagnosis

Measure Mg2+ with Ca2+, phosphate, K+, creatinine, and glucose, and an ECG; the cause is usually clear from the history, and the FEMg separates renal from gut loss, as on .

By cause

ForObtain
Gut loss and low intake (1–4)FEMg below 2%: the kidney is holding Mg2+
Renal loss (7–10)FEMg above 2% with normal kidney function; the drug list
Inherited disorders (9)Genetic testing with a family history, unexplained hypomagnesemia, or onset in infancy; urine Ca2+ is low in Gitelman syndrome and high in claudin defects
Shifts (5, 6)Recent insulin, refeeding, or parathyroidectomy; phosphate, which falls with them

Treatment

Give IV MgSO4 for instability, arrhythmias, or severe symptoms and oral Mg2+ otherwise, halve the dose in kidney failure, and correct K+ and Ca2+ after it; the doses are on .

By cause

CauseTreatment
Alcohol and poor intake (1)Mg2+ with thiamine and other replacement; reduce alcohol
PPIs (3)Stop or reduce the PPI if possible
Refeeding and DKA (5)Monitor and replace Mg2+, K+, and phosphate as treatment starts

Nephrotoxic drugs (8)Monitor Mg2+ during treatment and replace it
